citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 306 (Book Page): Blood ammonia level would expected to be elevated in ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency but not in UMP synthase deficiency.

category: Interpret the Lesh-Nhyan syndrome
statement: A pediatric neurologist is differentiating between primary idiopathic gout and Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Which clinical feature is uniquely characteristic of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and would typically be absent in a standard adult-onset case of gout?
options: Hyperuricemia resulting from purine degradation
Formation of uric acid stones in the kidneys (urolithiasis)
Inflammatory response to monosodium urate crystals
Deposition of urate crystals in the joints causing arthritis
Compulsive behavior including biting of lips and fingers
correctOption: Compulsive behavior including biting of lips and fingers
optionExplanations: Hyperuricemia is the biochemical hallmark of both gout and Lesch-Nyhan syndrome; it simply refers to elevated levels of uric acid in the blood.
Urolithiasis occurs in both conditions due to the high concentration of uric acid in the urine, making it a shared feature rather than a differentiating one.
The inflammatory response to urate crystals is the underlying mechanism of the pain in gouty arthritis, which can occur in both conditions.
Gouty arthritis is the classic presentation of primary gout but can also occur in Lesch-Nyhan patients due to the severe hyperuricemia.
Self-mutilation (lip and finger biting) is a specific behavioral manifestation of the neurological damage in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, distinguishing it from standard gout.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): ...the syndrome is characterized by motor dysfunction, cognitive deficits, and behavioral disturbances that include self-mutilation (biting of lips and fingers, Figure 22.11).

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
coreConcept: Energy and Substrate Requirements for AMP Synthesis
statement: The synthesis of Adenosine Monophosphate (AMP) from Inosine Monophosphate (IMP) is a meticulously regulated two-step process. Which of the following best describes the energetic and mechanistic requirement for the first step of this specific conversion?
options: It involves the release of pyrophosphate to drive the reaction to completion.
It requires GTP as an energy source and aspartate as a nitrogen donor.
It utilizes NADH for reductive amination of the hypoxanthine ring.
It requires FAD as a prosthetic group for the synthesis of adenylosuccinate.
It requires ATP as an energy source and glutamine as a nitrogen donor.
correctOption: It requires GTP as an energy source and aspartate as a nitrogen donor.
optionExplanations: The release of pyrophosphate (PPi) occurs in the GMP synthetase reaction and PRPP reactions, but the conversion of IMP to adenylosuccinate involves the hydrolysis of GTP to GDP and Pi.
The synthesis of adenylosuccinate from IMP requires GTP as the specific energy source and the amino acid aspartate to provide the nitrogen atom at position 6 of the purine ring.
NADH is not used for reductive amination in this pathway; rather, NAD+ is used as an oxidizing agent in the separate IMP to GMP pathway.
FAD is involved in the pyrimidine pathway (dihydroorotate dehydrogenase) but does not play a role in the conversion of IMP to adenylosuccinate or AMP.
The requirement for ATP and glutamine is characteristic of the GMP synthesis pathway (specifically the conversion of XMP to GMP), not the AMP pathway.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Note that the synthesis of AMP requires guanosine triphosphate (GTP) as an energy source, whereas the synthesis of GMP requires ATP.

category: Differentiate between CPS I and II
statement: Which of the following describes the specific nitrogen source utilized by the mitochondrial isoform, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I)?
options: Free Ammonia (NH3)
The ring nitrogens of Histidine
The amide group of Asparagine
The α-amino group of Glutamate
Urea
correctOption: Free Ammonia (NH3)
optionExplanations: CPS I is specialized to use free ammonium ions/ammonia derived from the breakdown of amino acids to start the urea cycle.
Nitrogens from the histidine ring enter the one-carbon pool via FIGlu, they are not direct donors for the carbamoyl phosphate synthetase reaction.
Asparagine is not the nitrogen donor for either CPS isoform; glutamine is the donor for CPS II.
While glutamate can provide ammonia via glutamate dehydrogenase, the CPS I enzyme itself uses the resulting free ammonia as its direct substrate.
Urea is the final product of the cycle initiated by CPS I; it is not a substrate for its synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): Figure 22.20 Summary of the differences between carbamoyl phosphate synthetase (CPS) I and II. ... CPS I: Source of nitrogen: Ammonia.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: A 14-month-old child presents with failure to thrive and severe megaloblastic anemia. Laboratory tests reveal normal serum B12 and folate levels, but significant crystals are noted in the urine. A diagnosis of hereditary orotic aciduria is made. Which of the following treatments is most appropriate for this patient?
options: Intravenous Hydroxyurea
Dietary restriction of protein
High-dose Folic acid supplementation
Administration of Allopurinol
Oral administration of Uridine
correctOption: Oral administration of Uridine
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and would further worsen the anemia by inhibiting DNA synthesis.
Incorrect. Protein restriction is used in urea cycle defects (like OTC deficiency) but is not the primary treatment for hereditary orotic aciduria.
Incorrect. The megaloblastic anemia in orotic aciduria does not respond to folate because the block is in the de novo synthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides, not one-carbon metabolism.
Incorrect. Allopurinol is used to treat gout by inhibiting xanthine oxidase; it would not address a pyrimidine synthesis defect.

Correct. Uridine can be salvaged by nucleoside kinases to UMP, bypassing the deficient UMP synthase, thereby providing the necessary pyrimidines for RNA/DNA synthesis and reducing orotate production through feedback inhibition.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Administration of uridine results in improvement of the anemia and decreased excretion of orotate.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II) is the regulated, rate-limiting step of pyrimidine synthesis in human cells. Which of the following best describes the allosteric regulation of this enzyme?
options: Activated by ATP and inhibited by CTP
Activated by inorganic phosphate and inhibited by AMP
Activated by PRPP and inhibited by UTP
Activated by N-acetylglutamate and inhibited by UTP
Activated by UTP and inhibited by PRPP
correctOption: Activated by PRPP and inhibited by UTP
optionExplanations: While ATP activates CPS II in some bacterial models, in mammalian cells, PRPP is the primary activator; CTP inhibition is more characteristic of bacterial aspartate transcarbamoylase.
Inorganic phosphate is an activator for PRPP synthetase, and AMP is an inhibitor for the purine pathway's amidotransferase, not CPS II.
CPS II is allosterically activated by 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP), signaling a need for nucleotide synthesis, and inhibited by Uridine Triphosphate (UTP) via feedback inhibition.
N-acetylglutamate is the essential activator for CPS I (mitochondrial, urea cycle), not CPS II (cytosolic, pyrimidine synthesis).
This is incorrect because UTP is the end-product and serves as an inhibitor, while PRPP indicates precursor availability and serves as an activator.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): [CPS II is inhibited by UTP (the end product of this pathway, which can be converted into the other pyrimidine nucleotides), and is activated by PRPP.]

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: The drug 5-fluorouracil is a potent antineoplastic agent that targets the regulation of nucleotide pools. What is the precise metabolic mechanism by which it inhibits the synthesis of thymidine monophosphate (TMP)?
options: It is converted to 5-FdUMP, which covalently binds and inactivates thymidylate synthase.
It prevents the amination of UTP to CTP by inhibiting CTP synthetase.
It acts as a reversible inhibitor of the CAD multifunctional enzyme complex.
It competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, depleting tetrahydrofolate.
It blocks the reduction of UDP to dUDP by ribonucleotide reductase.
correctOption: It is converted to 5-FdUMP, which covalently binds and inactivates thymidylate synthase.
optionExplanations: 5-FU is a prodrug converted to 5-FdUMP, which acts as a suicide inhibitor by forming a permanent covalent bond with thymidylate synthase and its folate cofactor.
CTP synthetase converts UTP to CTP using glutamine; this step is not the target of 5-fluorouracil.
CAD (CPS II, Aspartate transcarbamoylase, Dihydroorotase) is the early part of the pathway; 5-FU acts on the final steps of dTMP synthesis.
Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; 5-FU targets thymidylate synthase directly after metabolic activation.
Hydroxyurea, not 5-FU, is the drug mentioned as inhibiting ribonucleotide reductase's generation of deoxyribonucleotides.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 304 (Book Page): [5-Fluorouracil is metabolically converted to 5-FdUMP, which becomes permanently bound to the inactivated thymidylate synthase; for this reason, the drug is called a “suicide” inhibitor.]

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
coreConcept: Cell Cycle Specificity of Deoxyribonucleotide Synthesis
statement: A 55-year-old male with chronic myelogenous leukemia is started on hydroxyurea therapy. Following treatment, his laboratory results show a significant decrease in the cellular concentration of dCTP and dGTP. This pharmacological effect is most closely associated with which phase of the cell cycle?
options: M phase
G2 phase
G1 phase
G0 phase
S-phase
correctOption: S-phase
optionExplanations: M phase involves mitosis and cell division; DNA synthesis (and thus RNR's primary role) is completed before this phase begins.
G2 is the post-synthetic phase where the cell prepares for mitosis; the bulk of dNTP synthesis has already occurred.
G1 is the pre-synthetic phase; while preparations occur, the peak activity of RNR for deoxyribonucleotide production occurs in the S-phase.
G0 is a quiescent phase where DNA synthesis is not active, and RNR activity is minimal.
Correct. Ribonucleotide reductase is most active during the S-phase to provide the dNTPs necessary for DNA replication.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 297 (Book Page): The nucleotides required for DNA synthesis, however, are 2'-deoxyribonucleotides, which are produced from ribonucleoside diphosphates by the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase during the S-phase of the cell cycle.

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: A 52-year-old patient experiencing an acute gouty attack is prescribed colchicine. Through which mechanism does this pharmacological agent exert its primary effect in reducing joint inflammation?
options: Disruption of microtubule formation to inhibit neutrophil migration
Competitive inhibition of PRPP synthetase
Direct chemical dissolution of monosodium urate crystals
Increasing renal clearance of urate
Inhibition of xanthine oxidase activity
correctOption: Disruption of microtubule formation to inhibit neutrophil migration
optionExplanations: Colchicine binds to tubulin and prevents its polymerization into microtubules, which are essential for the chemotaxis and motility of neutrophils into the inflamed synovium.
Inhibition of PRPP synthetase would reduce de novo purine synthesis but is not the mechanism of colchicine, which has no effect on urate levels.
No standard gout medication works by direct chemical dissolution of crystals; treatment focuses on managing inflammation or lowering systemic urate levels to allow gradual dissolution.
Increasing renal clearance is the mechanism of uricosuric agents like probenecid, which are used to lower serum urate levels long-term.
Inhibition of xanthine oxidase is the mechanism of allopurinol and febuxostat, which are used for chronic management, not acute symptom relief.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): Colchicine prevents formation of microtubules, thus decreasing the movement of neutrophils into the affected area. Like the other anti-inflammatory drugs, it has no effect on uric acid levels.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: Which of the following sets of molecules provides all the atoms required for the de novo construction of the pyrimidine ring?
options: Arginine, Glutamate, and Bicarbonate
Aspartic acid, Glutamine, and CO2
Alanine, Aspartate, and NH3
Glycine, Glutamine, and CO2
Asparagine, Glycine, and Formyl-THF
correctOption: Aspartic acid, Glutamine, and CO2
optionExplanations: Arginine and bicarbonate are components of the urea cycle; while CO2 is often represented as bicarbonate, Arginine is not a precursor for the pyrimidine ring.
The pyrimidine ring is composed of atoms from aspartic acid (N1, C4, C5, C6), glutamine (N3), and CO2 (C2).
Alanine is not a precursor for nucleotides; NH3 is used by CPS I in the mitochondria for the urea cycle, whereas CPS II uses the amide group of glutamine.
Glycine is a major donor for the purine ring, but it does not contribute to the pyrimidine ring structure.
Asparagine and glycine are not used in pyrimidine ring synthesis; Formyl-THF is a donor for purine synthesis (C2 and C8) and dTMP synthesis, but not the initial pyrimidine ring.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): The sources of the atoms in the pyrimidine ring are glutamine, CO 2 , and aspartic acid (Figure 22.19).

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: Which pharmacological agent is specifically classified as a uricosuric drug, used to increase the renal excretion of uric acid in patients who underexcrete it?
options: Allopurinol
Probenecid
Febuxostat
Colchicine
Methotrexate
correctOption: Probenecid
optionExplanations: Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, which reduces the production of uric acid rather than increasing its excretion.
Probenecid inhibits the renal reabsorption of uric acid in the proximal tubule, thereby increasing its excretion in the urine.
Febuxostat is a non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor, similar in therapeutic goal to allopurinol (reducing production).
Colchicine is an anti-inflammatory agent that inhibits microtubule formation but has no effect on urate levels.
Methotrexate is a folate analog that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; it is not used to treat gout and can actually cause hyperuricemia due to cell lysis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): Uricosuric agents, such as probenecid or sulfinpyrazone, that increase renal excretion of uric acid, are used in patients who are “underexcretors” of uric acid.

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: Which specific set of compounds serves as the direct substrates for the catalytic reduction performed by ribonucleotide reductase?
options: Deoxyadenosine diphosphate, Deoxyguanosine diphosphate, Deoxycytidine diphosphate, and Deoxyuridine diphosphate
Adenosine triphosphate, Guanosine triphosphate, Cytidine triphosphate, and Uridine triphosphate
Adenosine diphosphate, Guanosine diphosphate, Cytidine diphosphate, and Uridine diphosphate
Hypoxanthine, Guanine, Cytosine, and Uracil
Adenosine monophosphate, Guanosine monophosphate, Cytidine monophosphate, and Uridine monophosphate
correctOption: Adenosine diphosphate, Guanosine diphosphate, Cytidine diphosphate, and Uridine diphosphate
optionExplanations: Deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates are the products of the ribonucleotide reductase reaction, not the substrates; the enzyme converts ribonucleotides into these deoxy forms.

Nucleoside triphosphates (NTPs) like ATP and GTP are the building blocks for RNA synthesis and provide energy, but they are not the direct substrates for ribonucleotide reductase; they act as allosteric regulators instead.
Ribonucleotide reductase specifically acts on ribonucleoside diphosphates (NDPs), reducing the 2'-hydroxyl group of the ribose sugar to produce deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs).
Free nitrogenous bases are utilized in the salvage pathways (via HGPRT or APRT) or degraded; they cannot be directly reduced to deoxy-forms by ribonucleotide reductase.
Nucleoside monophosphates must first be converted into diphosphates by base-specific kinases (like adenylate kinase) before they can be recognized and reduced by ribonucleotide reductase.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 297 (Book Page): Ribonucleotide reductase (ribonucleoside diphosphate reductase) is composed of two nonidentical dimeric subunits, R1 and R2, and is specific for the reduction of purine nucleoside diphosphates (ADP and GDP), and pyrimidine nucleoside diphosphates, cytidine diphosphate (CDP) and uridine diphosphate (UDP) to their deoxy-forms.

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: An 8-month-old infant presents with severe lymphopenia, lack of a thymus shadow on X-ray, and recurrent fungal and viral infections since birth. Biochemical analysis reveals extremely high levels of dATP and a marked deficiency in dGTP, dCTP, and dTTP. Which enzymatic step is being inhibited to cause this global reduction in deoxyribonucleotides?
options: Xanthine oxidase
Adenosine deaminase
Ribonucleotide reductase
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase
Thymidylate synthase
correctOption: Ribonucleotide reductase
optionExplanations: Xanthine oxidase is involved in purine degradation; its inhibition does not lead to the selective reduction of deoxyribonucleotides or SCID.
While Adenosine deaminase is the deficient enzyme, its lack is the *cause* of dATP accumulation, which then goes on to inhibit a different enzyme downstream.

The excessive accumulation of dATP in ADA deficiency acts as a powerful allosteric inhibitor at the 'activity site' of ribonucleotide reductase, shutting down the production of all deoxyribonucleotides needed for DNA synthesis.
HGPRT deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, characterized by hyperuricemia and behavioral issues, not the profound immunodeficiency seen in SCID.

Thymidylate synthase is required for dTMP synthesis, but the data shows a deficiency in all deoxyribonucleotides (dGTP, dCTP, etc.), which points toward a more central enzyme like ribonucleotide reductase.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): [A deficiency of ADA results in an accumulation of adenosine... As dATP levels rise, ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited, thus preventing the production of all deoxyribose-containing nucleotides (see Page 289 (Book Page)).]

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
statement: Sulfonamides are effective antimicrobial agents because they selectively target bacterial purine synthesis without interfering with human pathways. What is the physiological basis for this selectivity?
options: Humans must obtain preformed folic acid from their diet rather than synthesizing it.
Humans utilize a different nitrogen donor for the conversion of IMP to GMP.
Bacterial purine synthesis occurs in the mitochondria while human synthesis is cytosolic.
Sulfonamides are rapidly degraded by human xanthine oxidase before they can act.
Human cells lack the transport proteins necessary to take up sulfonamides.
correctOption: Humans must obtain preformed folic acid from their diet rather than synthesizing it.
optionExplanations: Sulfonamides inhibit the enzyme that converts PABA into folic acid. Since humans lack this pathway and ingest folate, the drug is non-toxic to human purine synthesis.
Both humans and bacteria utilize glutamine as the nitrogen donor for various steps in purine synthesis; this is not the basis for sulfonamide selectivity.
De novo purine synthesis is primarily cytosolic in both humans and bacteria; the localization does not confer selectivity to sulfa drugs.
Xanthine oxidase is involved in purine degradation to uric acid and does not play a role in the metabolism or deactivation of sulfonamides.
Human cells can take up sulfonamides, but since they do not synthesize folic acid de novo from PABA, the drug has no target to inhibit.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page): Humans cannot synthesize folic acid, and must rely on external sources of this vitamin. Therefore, sulfa drugs do not interfere with human purine synthesis.

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
statement: Sulfonamides function by mimicking which of the following precursors of the folic acid molecule?
options: Glutamic acid
Para-aminobenzoic acid
Ribose 5-phosphate
Pteridine ring
N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate
correctOption: Para-aminobenzoic acid
optionExplanations: While folate contains glutamate, sulfonamides are not analogs of glutamate.
Sulfonamides are structural analogs of para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), allowing them to competitively inhibit the enzymes that incorporate PABA into the folic acid precursor.
Ribose 5-phosphate is the sugar moiety of nucleotides, not a component of the PABA-to-folate pathway.
The folate molecule contains a pteridine ring, but sulfonamides specifically mimic PABA.
N10-formyl-THF is a functional coenzyme of purine synthesis; sulfonamides prevent its synthesis rather than mimicking it.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page): Sulfonamides are structural analogs of para-aminobenzoic acid that competitively inhibit bacterial synthesis of folic acid.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: A clinical comparison is made between two primary immunodeficiency disorders involving purine degradation enzymes. While Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency causes Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID), which of the following best describes the clinical manifestation of Purine Nucleoside Phosphorylate (PNP) deficiency?
options: Less severe immunodeficiency involving T-cells primarily
Excessive production of allantoin leading to nephrolithiasis
Selective depletion of B-cells with normal T-cell count
Complete depletion of T, B, and Natural Killer cells
Isolated hyperuricemia without immunologic impairment
correctOption: Less severe immunodeficiency involving T-cells primarily
optionExplanations: PNP deficiency is characterized as being rarer and less severe than ADA deficiency, primarily impacting T-cell function and numbers.
Humans do not normally produce allantoin, and this is not the mechanism of PNP deficiency pathology.
PNP deficiency affects T-cells more severely than B-cells; B-cell isolation is not characteristic.
This describes SCID caused by ADA deficiency, where T, B, and NK cells are all affected.
Both ADA and PNP deficiencies are characterized by immunodeficiency, not isolated hyperuricemia.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) deficiency results in a less severe immunodeficiency involving T-cells primarily.

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
statement: In bacteria, the administration of sulfonamides leads to a decrease in the cellular concentration of which specific coenzyme required for the addition of carbon atoms 2 and 8 of the purine ring?
options: Adenosine triphosphate (ATP).
Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+).
N5, N10-Methylene tetrahydrofolate.
N10-Formyltetrahydrofolate.
Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD).
correctOption: N10-Formyltetrahydrofolate.
optionExplanations: ATP is an energy source for the pathway, but its levels are not the direct target of sulfonamide-mediated folate depletion.
NAD+ is a redox cofactor used in the conversion of IMP to XMP, but it is not a donor for ring atoms 2 and 8.
N5, N10-methylene THF is primarily used in the synthesis of dTMP from dUMP, not for the C2 and C8 positions of the purine ring.

Two steps in the de novo purine pathway require N10-formyltetrahydrofolate to donate carbons 2 and 8. Sulfonamides deplete the folate pool, thereby reducing the availability of this specific formyl-donor coenzyme.
FAD is involved in pyrimidine synthesis (dihydroorotate dehydrogenase) but not as a carbon donor for the purine ring assembly.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 292 (Book Page): The atoms of the purine ring are contributed by... N10-formyltetrahydrofolate (Figure 22.5)... Page 294 (Book Page): Because purine synthesis requires tetrahydrofolate as a coenzyme, the sulfa drugs slow down this pathway in bacteria.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
coreConcept: Isozyme Comparison of CPS I vs CPS II
statement: A researcher is comparing the mechanisms of nitrogen utilization in nucleotide synthesis. Which of the following best distinguishes Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase II (CPS II) from Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase I (CPS I)?
options: CPS II utilizes the amide group of glutamine as its nitrogen source, while CPS I utilizes free ammonia.
CPS II is activated by N-acetylglutamate, whereas CPS I is activated by PRPP.
CPS II is located in the mitochondria, whereas CPS I is located in the cytosol.
CPS II produces orotic acid directly, whereas CPS I produces carbamoyl aspartate.
CPS II is involved in the urea cycle, whereas CPS I is involved in pyrimidine synthesis.
correctOption: CPS II utilizes the amide group of glutamine as its nitrogen source, while CPS I utilizes free ammonia.
optionExplanations: CPS II (cytosolic) specifically uses glutamine to provide the nitrogen for the pyrimidine ring, while CPS I (mitochondrial) uses ammonia derived from amino acid catabolism.
N-acetylglutamate is the essential activator for CPS I in the urea cycle; CPS II is activated by PRPP and inhibited by UTP.
This is incorrect; CPS I is the mitochondrial enzyme (urea cycle), and CPS II is the cytosolic enzyme (nucleotide synthesis).
Neither enzyme produces orotic acid or carbamoyl aspartate directly; they both produce carbamoyl phosphate, which is then processed by subsequent enzymes in their respective pathways.
The roles are reversed: CPS I is the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle, and CPS II is the rate-limiting step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): CPS I [Source of nitrogen]: Ammonia; CPS II [Source of nitrogen]: γ-Amide group of glutamine.

category: Interpret the Lesh-Nhyan syndrome
statement: A 22-month-old male child is brought to the emergency department with significant bleeding from his lips and fingertips, which appear chewed. His mother reports he has developmental delays and frequently arches his back with involuntary movements. Physical exam reveals swollen, tender joints and choreoathetosis. Labs: Serum Uric Acid 14 mg/dL (Normal <7), Serum Creatinine 0.6 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows numerous orange-tinged crystals. What is the most likely molecular basis for this patient’s condition?
options: Accumulation of dATP leading to ribonucleotide reductase inhibition
Overactivity of PRPP synthetase leading to excess ribose 5-phosphate
Deficiency of UMP synthase resulting in megaloblastic anemia
Inability to degrade adenosine to inosine due to deaminase failure
Failure to convert hypoxanthine to inosine monophosphate (IMP)
correctOption: Failure to convert hypoxanthine to inosine monophosphate (IMP)
optionExplanations: Accumulation of dATP is the mechanism of toxicity in ADA deficiency, which inhibits DNA synthesis in lymphocytes; it is not the mechanism in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.
PRPP synthetase overactivity is a different X-linked cause of gout, but it generally does not present with the characteristic self-mutilation and severe choreoathetosis seen in Lesch-Nyhan.
UMP synthase deficiency causes hereditary orotic aciduria, which features megaloblastic anemia and growth failure, not self-mutilation or choreoathetosis.
This describes Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency, which causes Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) rather than behavioral and gouty symptoms.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is caused by HGPRT deficiency, which prevents the salvage of hypoxanthine to IMP and guanine to GMP. This matches the clinical triad of hyperuricemia, self-mutilation, and motor dysfunction.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): This deficiency results in an inability to salvage hypoxanthine or guanine, from which excessive amounts of uric acid, the end product of purine degradation, are produced.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: The synthesis of guanosine monophosphate (GMP) from inosine monophosphate (IMP) involves a two-step sequence. Which nitrogen donor is required for the second reaction in this specific pathway?
options: N10-formyltetrahydrofolate
Glutamine
Ammonia
Aspartic acid
Glycine
correctOption: Glutamine
optionExplanations: N10-formyltetrahydrofolate is a one-carbon donor used during the construction of the purine ring (specifically for carbons 2 and 8), not for the late-stage conversion of IMP to GMP.
In the second step of GMP synthesis, the enzyme GMP synthetase catalyzes the transfer of an amide group from glutamine to xanthosine monophosphate (XMP) to produce GMP.
While ammonia is a nitrogen source for carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the urea cycle, it is not the specific donor used by GMP synthetase in mammalian cells.
Aspartic acid is the nitrogen donor for the conversion of IMP to adenylosuccinate in the AMP synthesis pathway, not the GMP pathway.
Glycine provides carbons 4 and 5 and nitrogen 7 of the purine ring during the early stages of de novo synthesis but is not the donor for the IMP to GMP conversion.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): [Figure 22.8 shows] Xanthosine monophosphate [converted to] GMP [via] GMP synthetase [using] Glutamine.

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
coreConcept: Mechanism of Action of Hydroxyurea on Ribonucleotide Reductase
statement: A pharmacological researcher is investigating the molecular mechanism of hydroxyurea in the treatment of chronic myelogenous leukemia. Which specific feature of the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase is directly targeted and neutralized by this drug?
options: The essential free radical required for catalysis
The substrate specificity site for pyrimidine diphosphates
The ATP-binding activity site on the R1 subunit
The thiol groups on the thioredoxin coenzyme
The disulfide bridge in the oxidized enzyme
correctOption: The essential free radical required for catalysis
optionExplanations: Hydroxyurea acts specifically by quenching or destroying the stable tyrosyl free radical located in the R2 subunit of ribonucleotide reductase, which is essential for the reduction mechanism.
The substrate specificity site regulates which nucleotides are reduced based on triphosphate levels; hydroxyurea has no direct effect on this allosteric regulatory site.
The activity site on the R1 subunit is where dATP and ATP bind to regulate the enzyme's overall rate, but hydroxyurea does not bind to this site; it acts by destroying a free radical.
Thioredoxin is a peptide coenzyme that provides reducing equivalents; hydroxyurea does not directly target the thiol groups of thioredoxin.

The disulfide bridge is a transient product of the reaction on the enzyme itself that must be reduced; hydroxyurea does not neutralize this bridge but rather prevents the enzyme from reaching this state by stopping the reaction at the radical level.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 298 (Book Page): The drug hydroxyurea destroys the free radical required for enzymic activity of ribonucleotide reductase, and thus inhibits the generation of substrates for DNA synthesis.

category: Differentiate between CPS I and II
statement: A 2-year-old child presents with megaloblastic anemia that is unresponsive to vitamin B12 or folate supplementation. Physical exam shows delayed growth, and urinalysis reveals crystalline sediment identified as orotic acid. The patient's blood ammonia levels are normal. Which enzyme is most likely deficient in this patient?
options: UMP synthase
Ornithine transcarbamylase
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
correctOption: UMP synthase
optionExplanations: UMP synthase deficiency (Hereditary Orotic Aciduria) leads to the accumulation of orotic acid and a failure to produce pyrimidines, causing megaloblastic anemia. Crucially, blood ammonia is normal because the urea cycle is unaffected.
OTC deficiency causes orotic aciduria, but it is characteristically accompanied by severe hyperammonemia, which is absent in this patient.

A deficiency in CPS II would lead to a decrease in pyrimidine synthesis but would not cause an accumulation of orotic acid; instead, it would cause a decrease in all subsequent intermediates of the pathway.
CPS I deficiency would cause hyperammonemia but would result in decreased orotic acid levels because the initial substrate for the urea cycle is missing.
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase deficiency is not the standard cause of the clinical triad of megaloblastic anemia, growth retardation, and orotic aciduria described in the text.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page)-311: Orotate phosphoribosyl transferase and orotidylate decarboxylase are also catalytic domains of a single polypeptide chain called UMP synthase. Orotic aciduria—a rare genetic defect—may be caused by a deficiency of one or both activities of this bifunctional enzyme... results in poor growth, megaloblastic anemia...

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting and committed step in the de novo biosynthesis of purine nucleotides?
options: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase
PRPP synthetase
Adenosine deaminase
Glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase
IMP dehydrogenase
correctOption: Glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase
optionExplanations: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) is a key enzyme in the salvage pathway, not the de novo synthesis pathway. It converts free purine bases back into nucleotides.

PRPP synthetase catalyzes the synthesis of PRPP from ATP and ribose 5-phosphate. While it provides the essential activated pentose, it is not considered the committed step of the purine-specific pathway because PRPP is also used in pyrimidine synthesis and salvage pathways.
Adenosine deaminase is an enzyme involved in the degradation of purines, specifically converting adenosine to inosine. It is not involved in the biosynthetic pathway.

Glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase catalyzes the conversion of PRPP to 5-phosphoribosylamine. This is the first step unique to purine synthesis and is strictly regulated by feedback inhibition from AMP and GMP.
IMP dehydrogenase is involved in the branch point of purine synthesis, specifically converting IMP to XMP for GMP production. It is not the initial committed step of the entire purine pathway.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): The enzyme, glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase, is inhibited by the purine 5'-nucleotides AMP and GMP—the end products of the pathway. This is the committed step in purine nucleotide biosynthesis.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: The allosteric regulation of 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP) synthetase is critical for nucleotide homeostasis. Which of the following best describes the physiological regulation of this X-linked enzyme?
options: Activated by guanosine triphosphate (GTP) and inhibited by glutamine
Activated by ribose 5-phosphate and inhibited by aspartate
Activated by adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and inhibited by inorganic phosphate (Pi)
Activated by 2-deoxyribose and inhibited by uridine triphosphate (UTP)
Activated by inorganic phosphate (Pi) and inhibited by purine nucleotides
correctOption: Activated by inorganic phosphate (Pi) and inhibited by purine nucleotides
optionExplanations: GTP is a purine nucleotide and would therefore likely act as an inhibitor rather than an activator. Glutamine is a substrate for subsequent steps in the pathway but does not directly inhibit PRPP synthetase.

Ribose 5-phosphate is the substrate, and while substrate availability limits the reaction rate, the term 'activator' specifically refers to the role of inorganic phosphate. Aspartate is an atom donor for the rings but not a direct inhibitor of this enzyme.
ATP is a substrate for the reaction, not the primary allosteric activator. Furthermore, inorganic phosphate (Pi) is the activator of the enzyme, not an inhibitor.
2-deoxyribose is not the starting sugar for this enzyme; the enzyme uses ribose 5-phosphate. UTP is the end-product of pyrimidine synthesis and inhibits CPS II, not PRPP synthetase.

PRPP synthetase is highly sensitive to the levels of inorganic phosphate, which acts as an activator. Conversely, purine ribonucleotides (like ADP and GDP) act as allosteric inhibitors, ensuring that the supply of the activated pentose (PRPP) matches the cell's demand for nucleotides.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): This X-linked enzyme [PRPP synthetase] is activated by inorganic phosphate and inhibited by purine nucleotides (end-product inhibition).

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: The conversion of inosine monophosphate (IMP) into the two primary purine nucleotides is governed by a reciprocal energy requirement. Which of the following best describes this metabolic logic?
options: NADH provides the reducing power for both AMP and GMP synthesis branches.
ATP is required for AMP synthesis to ensure high energy levels are maintained.
Both pathways exclusively utilize ATP as the phosphate donor for monophosphate kinases.
GTP provides the energy for GMP synthesis to prevent depletion of guanine pools.
GTP is used as the energy source for the synthesis of AMP, while ATP is used for GMP synthesis.
correctOption: GTP is used as the energy source for the synthesis of AMP, while ATP is used for GMP synthesis.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. While NAD+ is used as an electron acceptor in the conversion of IMP to XMP, NADH does not provide 'reducing power' as an energy driver for the overall synthesis steps.
Incorrect. ATP is actually used for the synthesis of GMP, not AMP. Using the 'other' nucleotide's triphosphate helps balance the ratios of A and G.
Incorrect. This statement refers to the later conversion of NMPs to NDPs/NTPs, but for the initial conversion from IMP to AMP/GMP, the energy sources are specifically GTP and ATP respectively.
Incorrect. GTP is used in the AMP synthesis branch, specifically by adenylosuccinate synthetase, not the GMP branch.

Correct. This reciprocal usage of triphosphates (GTP for AMP and ATP for GMP) serves as a cross-regulatory mechanism to ensure that the production of one purine nucleotide is sensitive to the concentration of the other.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Note that the synthesis of AMP requires guanosine triphosphate (GTP) as an energy source, whereas the synthesis of GMP requires ATP.

category: Interpret the role of synthetic analogues of nucleotides in medicine based on sign/symptoms and data e
statement: Mycophenolic acid is utilized in clinical medicine to prevent graft rejection. Which specific metabolic consequence is responsible for its immunosuppressive effect?
options: Blockade of the methyl group transfer from N5, N10-methylene tetrahydrofolate.
Competitive inhibition of the salvage pathway catalyzed by HGPRT.
Inhibition of the reduction of GDP to dGDP by ribonucleotide reductase.
Deprivation of T and B cells of the key purine components needed for nucleic acid synthesis.
Accumulation of dATP, leading to the inhibition of all deoxyribonucleotide production.
correctOption: Deprivation of T and B cells of the key purine components needed for nucleic acid synthesis.
optionExplanations: This describes the inhibition of thymidylate synthase or the effects of folate analogs like methotrexate, not mycophenolic acid.
Mycophenolic acid inhibits the de novo pathway at IMP dehydrogenase; it does not directly target the HGPRT-mediated salvage pathway.
This describes the action of hydroxyurea or the downstream effect of dATP accumulation, not the direct mechanism of mycophenolic acid.

By inhibiting IMP dehydrogenase, mycophenolic acid blocks the de novo synthesis of GMP. Since T and B lymphocytes are highly dependent on this pathway for proliferation, they are selectively deprived of necessary purines.
Accumulation of dATP is the pathophysiology seen in adenosine deaminase deficiency, not the mechanism of mycophenolic acid.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): The drug deprives rapidly proliferating T and B cells of key components of nucleic acids. The drug is an immunosuppressant used to prevent graft rejection.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed step in the de novo biosynthesis of purine nucleotides?
options: Glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase
PRPP synthetase
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase
Adenylosuccinate synthetase
IMP dehydrogenase
correctOption: Glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase
optionExplanations: Glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase catalyzes the replacement of the pyrophosphate group of PRPP with an amide group from glutamine, marking the first dedicated step toward purine synthesis.
PRPP synthetase is involved in the initial activation of ribose 5-phosphate to PRPP, but it is not the committed step as PRPP is also used in pyrimidine synthesis and salvage pathways.
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) is an enzyme of the salvage pathway, not the de novo biosynthetic pathway.
Adenylosuccinate synthetase is involved later in the pathway, specifically for the conversion of IMP to AMP, rather than the initial committed step.
IMP dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting enzyme for the specific branch leading to GMP synthesis from IMP, not the overall de novo pathway's committed step.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): The enzyme, glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase, is inhibited by the purine 5'-nucleotides AMP and GMP—the end products of the pathway. This is the committed step in purine nucleotide biosynthesis.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: Which metabolite is the immediate precursor to AMP in the two-step sequence starting from IMP?
options: Inosine
Adenylosuccinate
Hypoxanthine
Xanthosine monophosphate
Adenosine
correctOption: Adenylosuccinate
optionExplanations: Inosine is a nucleoside (base + sugar) found in the degradation or salvage pathways. It is not an intermediate in the de novo synthesis sequence of IMP to AMP.
Adenylosuccinate is the intermediate formed by the condensation of IMP and aspartate. It is subsequently cleaved by adenylosuccinate lyase to yield AMP and fumarate.
Hypoxanthine is the nitrogenous base of IMP. While it can be salvaged to IMP, it is not an intermediate between IMP and AMP.
Xanthosine monophosphate (XMP) is the intermediate in the GMP synthesis branch, formed by the oxidation of IMP. It is not on the pathway to AMP.
Adenosine is the nucleoside form of AMP. In the synthesis of nucleotides, the monophosphate (AMP) is formed first from the ribose-containing precursor (adenylosuccinate), not the nucleoside.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): IMP ... Adenylosuccinate ... AMP

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
coreConcept: Feedback regulation of Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase II
statement: Which of the following molecules acts as the primary allosteric inhibitor for the rate-limiting, cytosolic step of de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis in human cells?
options: Adenosine triphosphate (ATP)
Uridine triphosphate (UTP)
Cytidine triphosphate (CTP)
5-Phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP)
Inosine monophosphate (IMP)
correctOption: Uridine triphosphate (UTP)
optionExplanations: ATP is an activator of ribonucleotide reductase but does not serve as an inhibitor for CPS II; in fact, the urea cycle equivalent (CPS I) requires ATP, and CPS II also uses ATP as a substrate.
UTP is the major feedback inhibitor of Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase II (CPS II), which is the regulated, rate-limiting step of the pyrimidine de novo pathway in humans.
While CTP is an inhibitor of aspartate transcarbamoylase in prokaryotic cells, it is not the primary regulated step inhibitor in mammalian pyrimidine synthesis.
PRPP is an allosteric activator, not an inhibitor, of the CPS II enzyme in the pyrimidine biosynthetic pathway.
IMP is the parent purine nucleotide and serves as a precursor for AMP and GMP; it does not directly regulate the pyrimidine pathway.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): CPS II is inhibited by UTP (the end product of this pathway, which can be converted into the other pyrimidine nucleotides), and is activated by PRPP.

category: Differentiate between CPS I and II
statement: A laboratory compares two cell lines: one with a deficiency in UMP synthase and another with a deficiency in ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC). Which laboratory finding would uniquely characterize the OTC-deficient cell line and distinguish it from the UMP synthase-deficient line?
options: Requirement for exogenous uridine for growth
Increased sensitivity to UTP inhibition
Significantly elevated levels of ammonia
Reduced synthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides
Accumulation of orotic acid in the medium
correctOption: Significantly elevated levels of ammonia
optionExplanations: While uridine treatment is the standard for UMP synthase deficiency, both cell lines might benefit from pyrimidines if their internal synthesis is compromised, making it a less specific diagnostic feature than ammonia levels.
UTP inhibition targets CPS II; neither deficiency is characterized specifically by an altered 'sensitivity' to this inhibition as their primary diagnostic hallmark.

OTC is a urea cycle enzyme; its deficiency causes a failure to detoxify ammonia, leading to hyperammonemia. UMP synthase is a cytosolic pyrimidine enzyme, and its deficiency does not affect the urea cycle's ability to process ammonia.

Both conditions can result in impaired pyrimidine synthesis (UMP synthase deficiency directly, and OTC deficiency indirectly via nitrogen imbalance), although it's the primary defect in UMP synthase deficiency.
Both UMP synthase deficiency and OTC deficiency result in the accumulation of orotic acid (orotic aciduria), so this finding does not distinguish between them.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 306 (Book Page): Blood ammonia level would expected to be elevated in ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency but not in UMP synthase deficiency.

category: Differentiate between CPS I and II
statement: A patient is diagnosed with Hereditary Orotic Aciduria due to a deficiency in UMP synthase. A second patient has orotic aciduria due to an X-linked deficiency in Ornithine Transcarbamylase (OTC). Which biochemical finding would most reliably distinguish the OTC deficiency from the UMP synthase deficiency?
options: Activity of Dihydroorotase
Response to uridine administration
Intracellular PRPP levels
Blood ammonia levels
Presence of orotic acid in the urine
correctOption: Blood ammonia levels
optionExplanations: Dihydroorotase activity is unaffected in both of these specific distal or urea cycle blocks.
While uridine treats UMP synthase deficiency, it does not correct the underlying hyperammonemia of OTC deficiency, though this is a therapeutic rather than a diagnostic biochemical finding.
PRPP levels may fluctuate in both conditions due to varying feedback and utilization, but they are not a standard or reliable diagnostic differentiator.
OTC is a urea cycle enzyme; its deficiency causes a failure to detoxify ammonia, leading to hyperammonemia. UMP synthase is purely a pyrimidine enzyme, so ammonia levels remain normal.
Orotic aciduria is present in both conditions, so it cannot be used to distinguish between them.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 306 (Book Page): 22.5 What laboratory test would help in distinguishing an orotic aciduria caused by ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency from that caused by UMP synthase deficiency? ... Blood ammonia level would expected to be elevated in ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency but not in UMP synthase deficiency.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: In the metabolic sequence of pyrimidine biosynthesis, which enzyme is uniquely characterized by its association with the inner mitochondrial membrane rather than the cytosol?
options: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
Dihydroorotase
Aspartate transcarbamoylase
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II
Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase
correctOption: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
optionExplanations: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is the only enzyme in the pyrimidine de novo pathway located on the inner mitochondrial membrane; it catalyzes the oxidation of dihydroorotate to orotate.
Dihydroorotase is the third domain of the cytosolic CAD complex.
Aspartate transcarbamoylase is part of the cytosolic trifunctional CAD complex.
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II) is a cytosolic enzyme and part of the trifunctional CAD complex.
Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase is a cytosolic domain of the bifunctional enzyme UMP synthase.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): The enzyme that produces orotate, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, is associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane. All other enzymes in pyrimidine biosynthesis are cytosolic.

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: Structurally, Ribonucleotide Reductase is characterized as a complex enzyme. Which description accurately reflects its subunit organization?
options: A complex of two nonidentical dimeric subunits, R1 and R2.
A single polypeptide chain with four distinct catalytic domains.
A mitochondrial-bound protein consisting of alpha and beta chains.
A heterodimer that requires a vitamin B12 cofactor.
A homotetramer composed of four identical R1 subunits.
correctOption: A complex of two nonidentical dimeric subunits, R1 and R2.
optionExplanations: Ribonucleotide Reductase is composed of two different types of subunits (R1 and R2), each existing as a dimer, which come together to form the active enzyme complex.
While some enzymes in the pyrimidine pathway (like CAD) are multifunctional single chains, Ribonucleotide Reductase is a multi-subunit complex.
Ribonucleotide Reductase is a cytosolic enzyme, not mitochondrial. Only one enzyme in the pyrimidine pathway, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, is associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane.
The human version of Ribonucleotide Reductase does not require Vitamin B12 (cobalamin); it relies on a tyrosyl radical and iron, whereas some prokaryotic versions use B12.
The subunits are nonidentical; R1 contains the regulatory and catalytic sites, while R2 contains the essential free radical and iron center.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 297 (Book Page): Ribonucleotide reductase (ribonucleoside diphosphate reductase) is composed of two nonidentical dimeric subunits, R1 and R2...

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: The bifunctional enzyme UMP synthase contains two distinct catalytic domains. Which enzyme activities are combined in this single protein?
options: CPS II and Aspartate transcarbamoylase
Thymidylate synthase and Dihydrofolate reductase
Dihydroorotase and Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
Adenosine deaminase and Purine nucleoside phosphorylase
Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and Orotidylate decarboxylase
correctOption: Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and Orotidylate decarboxylase
optionExplanations: CPS II and Aspartate transcarbamoylase are domains of the CAD complex, not UMP synthase.
Thymidylate synthase and Dihydrofolate reductase are separate enzymes, though they are functionally linked in the folate cycle for dTMP production.
Dihydroorotase is a CAD domain, and Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is a separate mitochondrial enzyme.
Adenosine deaminase and Purine nucleoside phosphorylase are distinct, separate enzymes in the purine degradation pathway.
Correct. UMP synthase is the protein that carries out the final two steps of UMP synthesis: transferring ribose-5-phosphate to orotate (OPRT) and then decarboxylating OMP to UMP (ODC).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): Orotate phosphoribosyl transferase and orotidylate decarboxylase are also catalytic domains of a single polypeptide chain called UMP synthase.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: The conversion of dUMP to dTMP is a critical step for DNA synthesis. Which enzyme catalyzes this reaction and requires a specific folate derivative as a methyl donor?
options: CTP synthetase
Ribonucleotide reductase
dUTPase
Thymidylate synthase
Dihydrofolate reductase
correctOption: Thymidylate synthase
optionExplanations: CTP synthetase converts UTP to CTP by adding an amino group from glutamine; it is not involved in thymidylate production.
Ribonucleotide reductase reduces ribonucleoside diphosphates (like UDP) to deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (like dUDP) but does not perform methylation.
dUTPase hydrolyzes dUTP to dUMP to prevent the incorporation of uracil into DNA and provide the substrate for thymidylate synthase.
Thymidylate synthase catalyzes the methylation of dUMP to dTMP using N5,N10-methylene THF, which is simultaneously oxidized to DHF.
Dihydrofolate reductase reduces DHF back to THF; it is essential for regenerating the folate pool but does not catalyze the dUMP to dTMP conversion directly.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 303 (Book Page): dUMP is converted to dTMP by thymidylate synthase, which uses N 5 ,N 10 -methylene tetrahydrofolate as the source of the methyl group.

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: During the catalytic cycle of ribonucleotide reductase, the reduction of the 2'-hydroxyl group of the pentose sugar is directly coupled to which chemical change within the enzyme's structure?
options: Phosphorylation of a conserved threonine residue
Hydrolysis of a high-energy thioester bond
Reduction of a ferric iron center to ferrous iron
Formation of a disulfide bond from two sulfhydryl groups
Decarboxylation of an aspartate residue in the R1 subunit
correctOption: Formation of a disulfide bond from two sulfhydryl groups
optionExplanations: Phosphorylation is a common regulatory mechanism for many enzymes, but the actual catalytic reduction of the ribose sugar involves a redox reaction, not a phosphate transfer.
Thioester bonds are involved in pathways like fatty acid synthesis or the TCA cycle (e.g., Acetyl-CoA), but are not the mechanism by which RNR reduces its substrates.

While the R2 subunit contains a tyrosine-stabilized iron center, the actual reduction of the substrate ribose involves the transfer of hydrogen from sulfhydryl groups, not a simple cycle of iron reduction/oxidation.

Correct. The enzyme uses two cysteine sulfhydryl groups to donate hydrogen atoms to the substrate. In the process, these groups are oxidized to form a disulfide bridge, which must then be reduced by thioredoxin for the next cycle.
Decarboxylation is used in the conversion of OMP to UMP by OMP decarboxylase, but it is not part of the ribonucleotide reductase mechanism.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 297 (Book Page): The immediate donors of the hydrogen atoms needed for the reduction of the 2'-hydroxyl group are two sulfhydryl groups on the enzyme itself, which, during the reaction, form a disulfide bond

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: The chemotherapeutic agent 5-Fluorouracil exerts its primary cytotoxic effect by targeting which specific metabolic step in pyrimidine metabolism?
options: Decarboxylation of OMP to UMP
Methylation of dUMP to dTMP
Reduction of CDP to dCDP
Amination of UTP to CTP
Salvage of uracil to UMP
correctOption: Methylation of dUMP to dTMP
optionExplanations: Decarboxylation of OMP to UMP is catalyzed by OMP decarboxylase (part of UMP synthase); deficiency here leads to orotic aciduria, but it is not the target of 5-FU.

5-Fluorouracil is converted to 5-FdUMP, which acts as a 'suicide inhibitor' of thymidylate synthase, preventing the methylation of dUMP to dTMP and thus starving the cell of thymidine for DNA synthesis.
The reduction of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides is catalyzed by ribonucleotide reductase, which is inhibited by hydroxyurea, not 5-FU.
CTP synthetase converts UTP to CTP using glutamine; this step is not the primary target of 5-Fluorouracil's antineoplastic activity.
While 5-FU is a uracil analog, its primary efficacy comes from the inhibition of de novo dTMP synthesis rather than interfering with the salvage of natural uracil bases.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): dUMP is converted to dTMP by thymidylate synthase... Inhibitors of thymidylate synthase include thymine analogs such as 5-fluorouracil, which serve as successful antitumor agents.

category: Interpret the role of synthetic analogues of nucleotides in medicine based on sign/symptoms and data e
statement: A renal transplant recipient is prescribed mycophenolic acid to prevent acute graft rejection. This drug is particularly effective because it selectively targets the proliferation of T and B lymphocytes. What is the biochemical basis for this selectivity?
options: It prevents the conversion of PRPP to 5-phosphoribosylamine
Lymphocytes lack the salvage pathways for pyrimidine bases
It inhibits the reduction of dihydrofolate in immune cells
It blocks the transport of uric acid out of the cell
It acts as an uncompetitive inhibitor of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase
correctOption: It acts as an uncompetitive inhibitor of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase
optionExplanations: The conversion of PRPP to 5-phosphoribosylamine is inhibited by AMP and GMP, but mycophenolic acid targets a later step (IMP to GMP).
The text does not state that lymphocytes lack pyrimidine salvage; rather, they are dependent on the IMP-to-GMP pathway for purine requirements during proliferation.
Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reduction; mycophenolic acid does not target folate metabolism.
Uric acid transport is affected by uricosuric drugs; mycophenolic acid is an immunosuppressant targeting nucleotide synthesis.
Mycophenolic acid is an uncompetitive inhibitor of IMP dehydrogenase; this enzyme is critical for de novo GMP synthesis, which T and B cells rely on heavily for DNA replication.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): The drug is a reversible, uncompetitive inhibitor of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase... The drug deprives rapidly proliferating T and B cells of key components of nucleic acids.

category: g Methotrexate, 5 Flurouracil and Allupurinol
coreConcept: Allopurinol Effect on PRPP and De Novo Synthesis
statement: A 60-year-old male with chronic lymphocytic leukemia is about to start aggressive chemotherapy. To prevent tumor lysis syndrome, he is started on Allopurinol. Two weeks later, biochemical analysis reveals a significant decrease in his intracellular 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP) levels. What is the most likely mechanism for this decrease?
options: Allopurinol is salvaged by HGPRT, consuming PRPP and creating nucleotides that inhibit the de novo pathway.
Xanthine oxidase inhibition leads to an accumulation of ATP, which competes with PRPP for the amidotransferase enzyme.
Allopurinol directly inhibits PRPP synthetase through allosteric binding.
The drug inhibits the absorption of ribose from the gastrointestinal tract.
Increased uric acid levels exert a retrograde feedback inhibition on the pentose phosphate pathway.
correctOption: Allopurinol is salvaged by HGPRT, consuming PRPP and creating nucleotides that inhibit the de novo pathway.
optionExplanations: Allopurinol is a hypoxanthine analog. When HGPRT levels are normal, it (and the accumulated hypoxanthine) is salvaged into nucleotide forms. This reaction uses PRPP as a substrate, depleting its pool. Furthermore, the resulting nucleotides inhibit the committed step of de novo synthesis.

Xanthine oxidase inhibition does not lead to an accumulation of ATP; in fact, the salvage pathway consumes ATP and PRPP to recycle bases into monophosphates (IMP/GMP/AMP). Balance is maintained via feedback, not ATP competition at that site.
Allopurinol does not directly inhibit PRPP synthetase; its regulatory effects are mediated through the salvage pathway and product inhibition.
Methotrexate and other drugs might cause GI upset, but Allopurinol does not interfere with the nutritional absorption of ribose sugar.
Uric acid levels actually decrease with allopurinol. Even if they were high, they do not inhibit the pentose phosphate pathway in this manner.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): In patients with normal levels of HGPRT, the hypoxanthine can be salvaged, thus reducing the levels of PRPP and, therefore, de novo purine synthesis.

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: In the human metabolic pathway for the catabolism of purine nucleotides, which enzyme is responsible for the production of the final, relatively insoluble nitrogenous waste product?
options: Xanthine oxidase.
Guanase.
Adenosine deaminase.
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase.
Urate oxidase.
correctOption: Xanthine oxidase.
optionExplanations: Xanthine oxidase catalyzes both the conversion of hypoxanthine to xanthine and the final conversion of xanthine to uric acid, the terminal metabolite of purines in humans.
Guanase (guanine deaminase) converts guanine to xanthine, which must then be further processed by xanthine oxidase to become uric acid.
Adenosine deaminase (ADA) converts adenosine to inosine; it is an upstream enzyme in the degradative pathway, not the terminal one.
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) converts nucleosides (inosine/guanosine) into free bases (hypoxanthine/guanine), which are then further oxidized.
Urate oxidase (uricase) is NOT expressed in humans. It converts uric acid to allantoin in other mammals, but its absence in humans is why uric acid is our final product.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 299 (Book Page): Hypoxanthine is oxidized by xanthine oxidase to xanthine, which is further oxidized by xanthine oxidase to uric acid, the final product of human purine degradation.

category: g Methotrexate, 5 Flurouracil and Allupurinol
statement: A 52-year-old male with advanced colorectal cancer is treated with a regimen including 5-fluorouracil. Following administration, his cellular levels of dTMP decrease significantly, leading to 'thymineless death' of the tumor cells. Which of the following best describes the metabolic consequence that occurs in these cells due to the specific mechanism of this drug?
options: Accumulation of dihydrofolate (DHF) due to inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase.
Increased incorporation of uracil into DNA because of dUTPase inhibition.
Direct inhibition of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II by 5-fluorouracil.
Covalent trapping of the enzyme thymidylate synthase in a ternary complex with a folate coenzyme.
Blockade of the conversion of IMP to GMP by reversible inhibition of IMP dehydrogenase.
correctOption: Covalent trapping of the enzyme thymidylate synthase in a ternary complex with a folate coenzyme.
optionExplanations: DHF accumulates when methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, not typically with 5-fluorouracil, which acts on the preceding step.
While uracil can be incorporated into DNA if dUTP levels rise, 5-fluorouracil does not inhibit dUTPase; its primary target is thymidylate synthase.
CPS II is inhibited by UTP and activated by PRPP; 5-fluorouracil does not target this regulated step of pyrimidine synthesis.

5-fluorouracil is converted to 5-FdUMP, which acts as a suicide inhibitor. It binds covalently to thymidylate synthase and the coenzyme N5,N10-methylene-THF, forming a stable ternary complex that permanently inactivates the enzyme.
IMP dehydrogenase is inhibited by Mycophenolic acid, not 5-fluorouracil; 5-fluorouracil targets the pyrimidine pathway, not the purine pathway conversion of IMP to GMP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 303 (Book Page): 5-Fluorouracil is metabolically converted to 5-FdUMP, which becomes permanently bound to the inactivated thymidylate synthase; for this reason, the drug is called a “suicide” inhibitor.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
coreConcept: Energy sources in Purine Nucleotide Synthesis
statement: During the conversion of Inosine Monophosphate (IMP) to Adenosine Monophosphate (AMP), which specific molecule provides the necessary energy for the formation of the intermediate adenylosuccinate?
options: Cytidine Triphosphate (CTP)
Guanosine Triphosphate (GTP)
Flavin Adenine Dinucleotide (FAD)
Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD+)
Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP)
correctOption: Guanosine Triphosphate (GTP)
optionExplanations: CTP is not involved in the purine synthesis pathway; it is a pyrimidine triphosphate used primarily in RNA synthesis and as an energy source for phospholipid synthesis.

GTP is uniquely required by adenylosuccinate synthetase to condense IMP with aspartate, forming the intermediate adenylosuccinate. This provides a regulatory loop where GTP levels drive AMP production.
FAD is a redox cofactor used in pathways like the citric acid cycle or pyrimidine synthesis (dihydroorotate dehydrogenase) but is not a participant in the IMP to AMP pathway.
NAD+ is a coenzyme used in the oxidation of IMP to Xanthosine Monophosphate (XMP) by IMP dehydrogenase, but it does not provide the phosphate-bond energy for adenylosuccinate formation.
ATP is the energy source for the conversion of Xanthosine Monophosphate (XMP) to Guanosine Monophosphate (GMP), not IMP to AMP. This reciprocal use of energy prevents imbalances in purine pools.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Note that the synthesis of AMP requires guanosine triphosphate (GTP) as an energy source, whereas the synthesis of GMP requires ATP.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: In the production of deoxyribonucleotides, a cyclic transfer of reducing equivalents is required to maintain the activity of ribonucleotide reductase. Which of the following best describes the correct sequence of electron flow to the enzyme?
options: NADH → Thioredoxin Reductase → Thioredoxin → Ribonucleotide Reductase
NADPH → Thioredoxin → Thioredoxin Reductase → Ribonucleotide Reductase
NADPH → Thioredoxin Reductase → Thioredoxin → Ribonucleotide Reductase
ATP → Thioredoxin Reductase → Thioredoxin → Ribonucleotide Reductase
FADH2 → Ribonucleotide Reductase → Thioredoxin → NADPH
correctOption: NADPH → Thioredoxin Reductase → Thioredoxin → Ribonucleotide Reductase
optionExplanations: NADH is generally not the primary donor for this pathway; NADPH is the specific coenzyme used by thioredoxin reductase.
Thioredoxin reductase must act on thioredoxin to reduce it; electrons flow from NADPH to the reductase, then to thioredoxin.

Correct. Ribonucleotide reductase uses sulfhydryl groups on thioredoxin to reduce ribonucleoside diphosphates. The resulting oxidized thioredoxin (disulfide) must be reduced by thioredoxin reductase, which utilizes NADPH as the ultimate electron donor.
ATP provides energy for many reactions but does not serve as the source of reducing equivalents (electrons) for this enzyme system.
FADH2 is used in other metabolic steps (like dihydroorotate dehydrogenase) but not in the regeneration of ribonucleotide reductase.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 297 (Book Page): The necessary reducing equivalents are provided by NADPH + H+, and the reaction is catalyzed by thioredoxin reductase... The two sulfhydryl groups of thioredoxin donate their hydrogen atoms to ribonucleotide reductase.

category: Interpret Orotic aciduria in relevance to nucleotides and urea
statement: A 2-year-old child is evaluated for hyperammonemia, lethargy, and vomiting. Laboratory tests show high urinary orotic acid and low blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Genetic testing confirms a mutation in an X-linked gene. Which enzyme is most likely defective?
options: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
UMP synthase
Ornithine transcarbamylase
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II
PRPP synthetase
correctOption: Ornithine transcarbamylase
optionExplanations: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase deficiency would block the pathway before orotic acid is formed, resulting in low orotic acid levels.
UMP synthase deficiency (Hereditary Orotic Aciduria) is autosomal recessive and presents with macrocytic anemia and normal ammonia/BUN levels.

Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is X-linked, causes hyperammonemia, low BUN (due to urea cycle failure), and elevated orotic acid (due to carbamoyl phosphate leakage into the pyrimidine pathway).
CPS II deficiency would lead to a decrease in pyrimidine production and would not cause an accumulation of orotic acid.
PRPP synthetase mutations usually lead to purine overproduction and gout, and are not associated with the urea cycle or hyperammonemic crises.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page) / 531: Defects in ornithine transcarbamylase of the urea cycle promote pyrimidine synthesis due to increased availability of carbamoyl phosphate. ... Carbamoyl phosphate, synthesized by CPS I, is also a precursor of urea.

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: The complex regulation of ribonucleotide reductase ensures that the four dNTPs are produced in balanced amounts. Binding of which molecule to the 'substrate specificity sites' specifically promotes the reduction of GDP to dGDP at the catalytic site?
options: dATP
dCTP
dTTP
ATP
dGTP
correctOption: dTTP
optionExplanations: dATP binding to the activity site inhibits the overall enzyme; its role at the specificity site is more complex but primarily regulates pyrimidine reduction.
dCTP is a product of the pathway, but the specific regulatory link mentioned for GDP reduction is triggered by dTTP.
Correct. dTTP acts as a signal at the specificity site to initiate the reduction of purine GDP into dGDP, ensuring balanced purine/pyrimidine ratios.
ATP bound to the activity site activates the enzyme; when bound to specificity sites, it primarily favors the reduction of pyrimidines (CDP and UDP).
dGTP binding to specificity sites typically promotes the reduction of ADP to dADP, rather than its own precursor (GDP).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 298 (Book Page): For example, deoxythymidine triphosphate (dTTP) binding at the specificity sites causes a conformational change that allows reduction of GDP to dGDP at the catalytic site.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: In the de novo synthesis of purine nucleotides, which specific amino acid provides the nitrogen atom necessary for the conversion of inosine monophosphate (IMP) to adenylosuccinate?
options: Glycine
Glutamine
Alanine
Glutamate
Aspartic acid
correctOption: Aspartic acid
optionExplanations: Glycine is incorporated as a whole molecule into the purine ring during the earlier steps of IMP synthesis (forming glycinamide ribonucleotide), but it is not the donor for the specific conversion of IMP to AMP.
Glutamine is the nitrogen donor for the conversion of xanthosine monophosphate (XMP) to guanosine monophosphate (GMP), catalyzed by GMP synthetase, not for the synthesis of adenylosuccinate.
Alanine is not a primary nitrogen donor in the purine biosynthetic pathway; the major donors are glutamine, aspartate, and glycine.
Glutamate is the byproduct formed when glutamine donates its amide nitrogen for GMP synthesis; it does not serve as a donor for the IMP to adenylosuccinate step.

Aspartic acid (aspartate) provides the amino group that replaces the keto group of IMP to form adenylosuccinate in the first step of AMP synthesis, a reaction catalyzed by adenylosuccinate synthetase.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): [Figure 22.8 shows the conversion of IMP to Adenylosuccinate using Aspartic acid and GTP, catalyzed by Adenylosuccinate synthetase.]

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: A biochemistry researcher is tracing the origins of atoms in the pyrimidine ring. Which combination of molecules provides all the necessary components for the construction of the pyrimidine nucleus?
options: Glutamate, Aspartate, and CO2
Glycine, Glutamine, and CO2
Aspartate, Glutamine, and CO2
Glycine, Aspartate, and N10-formyl-THF
Aspartate, Ammonia, and Formate
correctOption: Aspartate, Glutamine, and CO2
optionExplanations: Glutamine is the specific nitrogen donor for CPS II; glutamate is the byproduct of the reaction, not the substrate.
Glycine is a precursor for the purine ring, not the pyrimidine ring.
The pyrimidine ring is composed of atoms from aspartic acid (N1, C4, C5, C6), CO2 (C2), and the amide nitrogen of glutamine (N3).
Glycine and N10-formyl-THF are both specific to the purine biosynthetic pathway.
Ammonia is used by CPS I (urea cycle), but pyrimidine synthesis uses glutamine; formate (via THF) is a purine precursor.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): The sources of the atoms in the pyrimidine ring are glutamine, CO2, and aspartic acid (Figure 22.19).

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
statement: When comparing the pharmacological mechanisms of sulfonamides and methotrexate, which of the following statements accurately differentiates their roles in nucleotide metabolism?
options: Sulfonamides interfere with bacterial folate synthesis, while methotrexate inhibits human dihydrofolate reductase.
Both drugs act as suicide inhibitors of the enzyme thymidylate synthase.
Sulfonamides target the PRPP amidotransferase step, while methotrexate targets the IMP dehydrogenase step.
Sulfonamides inhibit the reduction of dihydrofolate, whereas methotrexate inhibits folate synthesis.
Methotrexate mimics PABA, while sulfonamides mimic N10-formyltetrahydrofolate.
correctOption: Sulfonamides interfere with bacterial folate synthesis, while methotrexate inhibits human dihydrofolate reductase.
optionExplanations: Sulfonamides selectively target the bacterial synthesis of folic acid from PABA. Methotrexate targets dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) in humans, preventing the recycling of THF.
Neither is a suicide inhibitor of thymidylate synthase; that description applies to 5-fluorouracil (metabolized to 5-FdUMP).
Neither drug targets these specific enzymes; PRPP amidotransferase is inhibited by AMP/GMP, and IMP dehydrogenase is inhibited by mycophenolic acid.
This is the reverse; methotrexate inhibits reduction (DHFR), while sulfonamides inhibit synthesis.
Sulfonamides mimic PABA; methotrexate is a structural analog of folic acid, not N10-formyl-THF.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page): Sulfonamides are structural analogs of para-aminobenzoic acid that competitively inhibit bacterial synthesis of folic acid... Methotrexate and related compounds inhibit the reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, catalyzed by dihydrofolate reductase.

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: Secondary hyperuricemia can occur due to various metabolic disturbances. Why does lactic acidosis specifically predispose a patient to the development of gout?
options: Lactate and urate compete for the same renal transporter for excretion
Acidosis increases the solubility of monosodium urate, causing faster crystal deposition
Lactate inhibits the salvage enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase
Lactate activates PRPP synthetase, increasing purine production
Lactate directly degrades nucleic acids in the extracellular matrix
correctOption: Lactate and urate compete for the same renal transporter for excretion
optionExplanations: In the kidney, lactate and uric acid utilize the same secretory transporters. High levels of lactate competitively inhibit the secretion of uric acid into the urine, leading to hyperuricemia.
