options: CPS II is activated by N-acetylglutamate, while CPS I is inhibited by UTP.
CPS II is activated by ammonia, while CPS I is inhibited by carbamoyl phosphate.
CPS II is inhibited by PRPP, while CPS I is activated by UTP.
CPS II is inhibited by ATP, while CPS I is activated by glutamine.
CPS II is activated by PRPP and inhibited by UTP, while CPS I is activated by N-acetylglutamate.
correctOption: CPS II is activated by PRPP and inhibited by UTP, while CPS I is activated by N-acetylglutamate.
optionExplanations: This incorrectly swaps the regulators; CPS I requires N-acetylglutamate for activation, while CPS II is the one inhibited by UTP.
Ammonia is the substrate for CPS I; CPS I is not typically described as being inhibited by its own product, carbamoyl phosphate, in this regulatory summary.
PRPP is actually an activator of CPS II, not an inhibitor; UTP is an inhibitor of CPS II, not an activator of CPS I.
ATP is a substrate for both enzymes, not a primary inhibitory regulator in this context; glutamine is a substrate for CPS II, not an activator for CPS I.
CPS II is regulated by the availability of the activated sugar (PRPP) and feedback-inhibited by the pathway end-product (UTP); CPS I has an absolute requirement for N-acetylglutamate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): [Figure 22.20 Summary of the differences between carbamoyl phosphate synthetase (CPS) I and II] Regulators: CPS I - Activator: N-acetylglutamate; CPS II - Inhibitor: UTP, Activator: PRPP

category: Interpret the role of synthetic analogues of nucleotides in medicine based on sign/symptoms and data e
statement: The transformation of dUMP to dTMP requires a methyl group and reducing equivalents. How does the pharmacological agent methotrexate interfere with this specific cycle?
options: It inhibits the conversion of serine to glycine, which provides the one-carbon unit.
It blocks the action of UTP diphosphatase, leading to the accumulation of dUTP.
It acts as a structural analog of thymine, preventing its incorporation into DNA.
It inhibits thymidylate synthase directly as a suicide inhibitor.
It prevents the reduction of dihydrofolate back to tetrahydrofolate by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase.
correctOption: It prevents the reduction of dihydrofolate back to tetrahydrofolate by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase.
optionExplanations: While the serine-glycine conversion is related to the folate pool, methotrexate specifically targets the dihydrofolate reductase step in the cycle.
UTP diphosphatase (dUTPase) is responsible for preventing uracil incorporation into DNA; it is not the target of methotrexate therapy.
5-Fluorouracil is a pyrimidine (thymine) analog. Methotrexate is a folic acid (pteridine) analog.
5-Fluorouracil is the suicide inhibitor of thymidylate synthase. Methotrexate targets the reductase enzyme that regenerates the required cofactor.

Thymidylate synthase converts THF to DHF during the methylation of dUMP. Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, meaning DHF cannot be recycled back to the functional THF form, stalling dTMP synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 304 (Book Page): DHF can be reduced to THF by dihydrofolate reductase... an enzyme that is inhibited by drugs such as methotrexate. By decreasing the supply of THF, these folate analogs... inhibit purine synthesis... but, by preventing methylation of dUMP to dTMP, they also lower the cellular concentration of this essential component of DNA.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
coreConcept: Clinical Presentation of Hereditary Orotic Aciduria
statement: A 15-month-old male is brought to the pediatrician due to failure to thrive and persistent lethargy. Laboratory analysis reveals a profound megaloblastic anemia that is unresponsive to vitamin B12 or folate supplementation. Urinalysis shows significant crystalluria composed of orotic acid. Physical examination confirms heights and weights well below the 5th percentile. A deficiency in which of the following enzymatic activities is the most likely cause?
options: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
Adenosine deaminase
UMP synthase
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II
correctOption: UMP synthase
optionExplanations: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase deficiency is not typically associated with this clinical triad of megaloblastic anemia and orotic aciduria in humans.
Adenosine deaminase deficiency leads to SCID due to dATP accumulation; it does not cause orotic aciduria or megaloblastic anemia.
Correct. UMP synthase contains both orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and OMP decarboxylase domains; a deficiency leads to orotic aciduria, megaloblastic anemia, and growth retardation.
HGPRT deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, characterized by hyperuricemia and self-mutilation, not orotic aciduria or megaloblastic anemia.
A deficiency in CPS II would lead to a lack of pyrimidines but would not cause an accumulation of orotic acid, as CPS II precedes the formation of orotate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 303 (Book Page): Low activities of orotidine phosphate decarboxylase and orotate phosphoribosyltransferase result in poor growth, megaloblastic anemia, and the excretion of large amounts of orotate in the urine. [Note: These are domains of UMP synthase].

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: During the catabolism of pyrimidine nucleotides, the heterocyclic ring is cleaved to produce highly soluble end-products. Which of the following is a result of pyrimidine degradation?
options: Xanthine
Beta-alanine
Allantoin
Uric acid
Urea
correctOption: Beta-alanine
optionExplanations: Xanthine is an intermediate in the purine degradation pathway leading to uric acid.
Beta-alanine (from Uracil/Cytosine) and beta-aminoisobutyrate (from Thymine) are the unique soluble end-products of pyrimidine catabolism.
Allantoin is the product of uric acid breakdown in non-primate mammals; it is not a pyrimidine degradation product.
Uric acid is the end product of purine degradation; pyrimidine rings are opened and do not form uric acid.
Urea is the primary means of disposing of nitrogen from amino acid catabolism, but the specific carbon/nitrogen skeleton of pyrimidines forms beta-amino acids.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): Unlike the purine ring, which is not cleaved human cells, the pyrimidine ring is opened and degraded to highly soluble products, β-alanine and β-aminoisobutyrate, with the production of NH 3 and CO 2 .

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: A biochemist is studying the salvage pathways of pyrimidines in human cells. Which statement correctly characterizes the salvage and metabolic handling of these bases compared to purines?
options: Hereditary orotic aciduria is treated with cytosine because it is the most active salvaged base.
The pyrimidine ring remains intact during degradation and is excreted as urate.
The degradation of pyrimidines results in the production of insoluble nitrogenous waste.
Pyrimidine nucleosides can be salvaged by specific kinases using ATP.
Pyrimidine bases are salvaged as efficiently as purine bases using PRPP-dependent transferases.
correctOption: Pyrimidine nucleosides can be salvaged by specific kinases using ATP.
optionExplanations: Uridine is used to treat orotic aciduria, not cytosine, because uridine is efficiently salvaged to UMP to bypass the biosynthetic block.
The pyrimidine ring is cleaved and degraded into soluble products like beta-alanine; only the purine ring remains intact to form uric acid.
The end products of pyrimidine catabolism (beta-alanine, beta-aminoisobutyrate, CO2, and NH3) are highly soluble, unlike the purine end product (uric acid).
Humans can salvage pyrimidine nucleosides (like uridine or thymidine) through the action of kinases that phosphorylate them into nucleotides.
Unlike purines, which have robust base salvage (HGPRT/APRT), human cells have very limited capacity to salvage free pyrimidine bases.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): Few pyrimidine bases are salvaged in human cells. However, the pyrimidine nucleosides can be salvaged by nucleoside kinases that utilize ATP in the phosphorylation of the nucleosides to nucleotides.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: A researcher is mapping the atoms of the pyrimidine ring. Which of the following sets of precursors contribute the required nitrogen and carbon atoms to complete the pyrimidine structure before it is attached to the ribose phosphate?
options: Glycine, CO2, and Asparagine
N10-formyltetrahydrofolate, Glutamine, and Aspartic acid
Ammonia, Glycine, and CO2
Glutamine, CO2, and Aspartic acid
Glutamate, CO2, and Glycine
correctOption: Glutamine, CO2, and Aspartic acid
optionExplanations: Glycine is a donor for the purine ring, not the pyrimidine ring.
N10-formyltetrahydrofolate is a carbon donor for the purine ring, but not for the initial pyrimidine ring (though a folate derivative is used later for dTMP synthesis).
Ammonia is used by CPS I in the urea cycle, but CPS II in pyrimidine synthesis uses glutamine.
Correct. Pyrimidine synthesis requires glutamine (amide nitrogen), CO2, and aspartic acid. Unlike purines, the ring is completed before attachment to the ribose sugar.
Glutamate is a product of glutamine's nitrogen donation, but it is not the donor itself; glycine is not used in pyrimidine ring construction.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): The sources of the atoms in the pyrimidine ring are glutamine, CO2, and aspartic acid (Figure 22.19). [Note: Glutamine and aspartic acid are thus required for both purine and pyrimidine synthesis.]

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: In Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency, the accumulation of deoxyadenosine leads to the apoptosis of which specific cell types, resulting in the clinical presentation of SCID?
options: Erythrocytes and Platelets
Osteoblasts and Osteoclasts
T cells, B cells, and Natural Killer (NK) cells
Neutrophils and Macrophages
Hepatocytes and Kupffer cells
correctOption: T cells, B cells, and Natural Killer (NK) cells
optionExplanations: Erythrocytes do not rely on DNA synthesis for proliferation in their mature form and are not the primary target of ADA-related toxicity.
Bone development can be secondary, but the defining pathology of the disease is the immunodeficiency arising from lymphocyte depletion, not primary bone cell failure.
ADA deficiency is unique in its severity because it depletes all three major lymphocyte types: T cells, B cells, and NK cells, leading to a complete lack of adaptive and innate lymphoid immunity.
While these are immune cells, the 'combined' in SCID refers specifically to the lymphoid lineage (T/B cells), not the myeloid lineage (neutrophils/macrophages).
ADA deficiency affects tissues with high turnover and high ADA expression requirements, specifically the lymphoid system; the liver is not the primary site of clinical failure.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): In its most severe form, this autosomal recessive disorder causes a type of severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID), involving a decrease in T cells, B cells, and natural killer (NK) cells.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: During the conversion of Inosine Monophosphate to Adenosine Monophosphate, what specific molecule is released as a byproduct in the second reaction step?
options: Water
Pyrophosphate
Ammonia
Glutamate
Fumarate
correctOption: Fumarate
optionExplanations: Water is a reactant in the IMP dehydrogenase reaction (GMP branch) and is not the primary organic byproduct of the AMP branch's second step.
Pyrophosphate is released during the synthesis of PRPP and the conversion of OMP to UMP, but not during the conversion of adenylosuccinate to AMP.
Ammonia is released in purine degradation (e.g., AMP deaminase) or consumed in other pathways, but it is not a byproduct of the conversion of IMP to AMP.
Glutamate is the byproduct of the GMP synthetase reaction in the GMP branch, not the AMP branch.
The enzyme adenylosuccinase (also called adenylosuccinate lyase) cleaves adenylosuccinate to yield AMP and fumarate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): [Figure 22.8] Adenylosuccinase [converts Adenylosuccinate to AMP and releases] Fumarate.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: In mammalian cells, the first three enzymatic steps of de novo pyrimidine synthesis are performed by a single multifunctional polypeptide. Which three catalytic activities are contained within this CAD protein?
options: PRPP Synthetase, CPS II, and UMP Synthase
CPS I, Ornithine Transcarbamylase, and Dihydroorotase
CPS II, Aspartate Transcarbamoylase, and Dihydroorotase
Dihydroorotase, OPRT, and Thymidylate Synthase
CPS II, OPRT, and OMP Decarboxylase
correctOption: CPS II, Aspartate Transcarbamoylase, and Dihydroorotase
optionExplanations: PRPP Synthetase is an independent X-linked enzyme that provides the activated pentose; it is not part of the CAD or UMP synthase complexes.
CPS I and Ornithine Transcarbamylase are mitochondrial enzymes involved in the urea cycle, not the cytosolic CAD complex for pyrimidines.
The CAD complex streamlines the initial stages of pyrimidine synthesis by physically linking the production of carbamoyl phosphate, carbamoyl aspartate, and dihydroorotate.
Thymidylate synthase is a separate, independent enzyme that acts much further downstream on dUMP; it is not part of the initial synthetic complex.
OPRT and OMP Decarboxylase are part of a different multifunctional protein called UMP Synthase, which acts later in the pathway.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page): [Note: The first three enzymic activities in this pathway ( CPS II, aspartate transcarbamoylase, and dihydroorotase) are actually three different catalytic domains of a single polypeptide chain known as CAD from the first letter in the name of each domain.]

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
statement: A 29-year-old female patient receives a kidney transplant and is placed on a regimen including mycophenolic acid. Monitoring reveals a specific reduction in the proliferation of T and B lymphocytes. Which metabolic intermediate in the purine pathway is most likely to be deficient in these cells as a direct result of this drug's primary mechanism?
options: Xanthosine monophosphate (XMP)
Inosine monophosphate (IMP)
Adenylosuccinate
5-Phosphoribosylamine
5-Phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP)
correctOption: Xanthosine monophosphate (XMP)
optionExplanations: Mycophenolic acid inhibits IMP dehydrogenase, which catalyzes the conversion of IMP to XMP. Therefore, XMP levels will decrease, leading to a shortage of GMP for DNA synthesis in lymphocytes.
IMP is the substrate for the inhibited enzyme, so its levels would likely increase rather than decrease.
Adenylosuccinate is the intermediate in the conversion of IMP to AMP; its synthesis is not inhibited by mycophenolic acid.
5-Phosphoribosylamine is the product of the committed step of purine synthesis, which occurs long before the branch point targeted by mycophenolic acid.
PRPP is a precursor for the entire pathway; its levels are not directly reduced by IMP dehydrogenase inhibition; they might even increase due to lack of feedback inhibition by GMP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): IMP dehydrogenase [inhibited by mycophenolic acid] ... IMP [converted to] Xanthosine monophosphate ... GMP.

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: A 50-year-old patient presents with a painful, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint. Laboratory results show a high plasma lactate level. How does the presence of lactate contribute to the development of this patient's joint symptoms?
options: Lactate provides the carbon skeletons for de novo purine synthesis
Lactate acts as an allosteric activator of xanthine oxidase
Lactate increases the solubility of uric acid, promoting soft tissue deposition
Lactate directly degrades existing monosodium urate crystals into tophi
Lactate competes with urate for the same renal transporter, reducing urate excretion
correctOption: Lactate competes with urate for the same renal transporter, reducing urate excretion
optionExplanations: Purine rings are built from glutamine, aspartate, glycine, CO2, and folate derivatives, not lactate.
There is no evidence that lactate activates xanthine oxidase; xanthine oxidase is regulated by its substrates and inhibited by drugs like allopurinol.
Lactate/acidosis actually decreases the solubility of urate, promoting its crystallization, but the primary biochemical mechanism described is the renal competition.
Lactate does not degrade crystals; tophi are formed by the aggregation of urate crystals over time, not by lactate action.

In the kidney, lactate and urate utilize the same transport mechanisms for secretion into the urine. High levels of lactate competitively inhibit urate secretion, leading to hyperuricemia (underexcretion type).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 299 (Book Page): Underexcretion can be primary... or secondary to known disease processes that affect how the kidney handles urate, for example lactic acidosis (lactate and urate compete for the same renal transporter).

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: The biosynthetic pathway from inosine monophosphate (IMP) is characterized by a reciprocal requirement for nucleoside triphosphates. Which statement accurately describes this metabolic balancing mechanism?
options: ATP provides the energy for adenylosuccinate synthetase, while GTP drives GMP synthetase.
AMP synthesis is independent of nucleotide triphosphates, relying instead on the hydrolysis of pyrophosphate.
GTP provides the energy for the conversion of IMP to adenylosuccinate, while ATP drives the conversion of XMP to GMP.
The availability of CTP stimulates the conversion of IMP to xanthosine monophosphate.
Both pathways are strictly dependent on ATP as the universal energy currency to ensure maximum velocity.
correctOption: GTP provides the energy for the conversion of IMP to adenylosuccinate, while ATP drives the conversion of XMP to GMP.
optionExplanations: This is the opposite of the actual mechanism; adenylosuccinate synthetase (for AMP) requires GTP, not ATP.

The conversion of IMP to AMP is an energy-intensive two-step process requiring GTP in the first step (adenylosuccinate synthetase) and is not driven solely by pyrophosphate hydrolysis (which occurs in the PRPP synthetase step).
This reciprocal energy requirement (GTP for AMP and ATP for GMP) ensures that the synthesis of one purine nucleotide is promoted by the abundance of the other, maintaining a balanced pool.
CTP is a pyrimidine nucleotide and does not serve as a direct energy source or regulator for the IMP-to-XMP transition, which is catalyzed by IMP dehydrogenase.
While ATP is a common energy source, the purine pathway specifically uses GTP for the AMP branch to prevent the overproduction of one type of purine when the other is scarce.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Note that the synthesis of AMP requires guanosine triphosphate (GTP) as an energy source, whereas the synthesis of GMP requires ATP.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
coreConcept: Nitrogen donors in purine branch synthesis
statement: A cell-free extract is provided with IMP, labeled Aspartate, labeled Glutamine, ATP, GTP, and NAD+. If the goal is to produce triphosphates, which nitrogen donor is correctly matched to its final nucleotide product?
options: Aspartate provides the amino group for ATP
Glutamine provides the amino group for AMP
Glutamine provides the amino group for CTP only
Aspartate provides the amino group for GMP
Glycine provides the amino group for GDP
correctOption: Aspartate provides the amino group for ATP
optionExplanations: In the conversion of IMP to AMP (the precursor to ATP), aspartate reacts with IMP to form adenylosuccinate, eventually donating the nitrogen found in the final adenosine ring.
Glutamine is the nitrogen donor for the GMP branch. The AMP branch uses aspartate to provide the amino group at the C-6 position.
While glutamine does provide nitrogen for CTP, it is also the essential nitrogen donor for the conversion of XMP to GMP in the purine pathway.
Aspartate is the nitrogen donor for the AMP branch, not the GMP branch. GMP receives its C-2 amino group from glutamine.
Glycine is used in the early stages of de novo purine ring construction (IMP synthesis) but is not the specific nitrogen donor for the conversion of IMP to GMP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): [Figure 22.8 shows] IMP + Aspartic acid + GTP -> Adenylosuccinate -> AMP. ... XMP + Glutamine + ATP -> GMP.

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: When managing a patient who is an 'underexcretor' of uric acid to prevent future gouty attacks, which pharmacological agent is specifically indicated to increase the renal clearance of urate?
options: Indomethacin
Probenecid
Allopurinol
Febuxostat
Colchicine
correctOption: Probenecid
optionExplanations: Indomethacin is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to manage the inflammation of an acute gouty flare-up.
Probenecid is a uricosuric agent that inhibits the reabsorption of uric acid in the proximal tubule, thus increasing its excretion.
Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor used for overproducers; it does not increase renal excretion of existing urate.
Febuxostat is a non-purine inhibitor of xanthine oxidase used to reduce the production of uric acid, not to increase its renal excretion.
Colchicine is an anti-inflammatory agent that prevents microtubule formation to treat acute attacks but has no effect on uric acid levels.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): Uricosuric agents, such as probenecid or sulfinpyrazone, that increase renal excretion of uric acid, are used in patients who are “underexcretors” of uric acid.

category: Interpret Orotic aciduria in relevance to nucleotides and urea
statement: An 8-month-old male infant presents with severe irritability, vomiting, and lethargy. Laboratory studies reveal significant hyperammonemia and highly elevated urinary orotic acid. Analysis of his blood shows normal mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and no signs of anemia. Which of the following is the most likely metabolic explanation for these findings?
options: A defect in the polypeptide chain containing CPS II, ATCase, and dihydroorotase
Inhibition of orotidylate decarboxylase by accumulated dietary pyrimidines
A failure to sequester carbamoyl phosphate within the mitochondrial matrix
An X-linked deficiency of an enzyme required for citrulline production
A genetic mutation leading to the loss of both domains of UMP synthase
correctOption: An X-linked deficiency of an enzyme required for citrulline production
optionExplanations: This refers to the CAD complex. Defects in early pyrimidine synthesis would decrease orotic acid production, not increase it.
Dietary pyrimidines are largely degraded and would not cause a clinical presentation of vomiting and hyperammonemia.
While carbamoyl phosphate does leak to the cytosol, the primary 'metabolic explanation' or diagnosis is the enzyme deficiency itself (OTC), which is the cause of the sequestration failure.

The presentation of orotic aciduria + hyperammonemia + lack of anemia points to Ornithine Transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency. OTC is an X-linked enzyme that converts carbamoyl phosphate and ornithine to citrulline; its deficiency causes ammonia to rise and CP to divert to orotic acid synthesis.
UMP synthase deficiency (Hereditary Orotic Aciduria) causes orotic aciduria and megaloblastic anemia (high MCV), but it does not cause hyperammonemia.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): Defects in ornithine transcarbamylase of the urea cycle promote pyrimidine synthesis due to increased availability of carbamoyl phosphate.

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: How does the 'salvage pathway' for purines normally regulate the rate of 'de novo' purine synthesis, and how is this loop disrupted in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?
options: Salvage enzymes consume glutamine, which is the nitrogen donor for de novo synthesis
Salvage enzymes increase the Km of the amidotransferase for its substrate PRPP
Salvage enzymes consume PRPP and produce IMP/GMP, which allosterically inhibit the de novo committed step
Salvage pathways inhibit the CPS II enzyme in the cytosol through product feedback
Salvage enzymes convert uric acid back into hypoxanthine through a reverse oxidase reaction
correctOption: Salvage enzymes consume PRPP and produce IMP/GMP, which allosterically inhibit the de novo committed step
optionExplanations: Salvage enzymes use PRPP as a ribose source, not glutamine. Glutamine is the nitrogen donor for the de novo pathway.
The enzymes do not change the Km of other enzymes; they change the concentration of the substrate (PRPP) and the concentrations of the allosteric inhibitors (IMP, GMP).

Normally, HGPRT uses PRPP to salvage bases, reducing PRPP levels and producing IMP/GMP which inhibit the de novo pathway. In Lesch-Nyhan (HGPRT deficiency), PRPP levels rise and inhibitor levels (IMP/GMP) fall, stimulating de novo synthesis.
CPS II is the regulated step for pyrimidine synthesis, not purine synthesis.
The purine degradation to uric acid is irreversible in humans; uric acid cannot be salvaged back into purines.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): ...the lack of this salvage pathway causes increased PRPP levels and decreased IMP and GMP levels. As a result, glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase (the committed step in purine synthesis) has excess substrate and decreased inhibitors available, and de novo purine synthesis is increased.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: In the degradation of purine nucleotides, which enzyme is responsible for the final conversion of both hypoxanthine and xanthine into the excretory product uric acid?
options: Xanthine oxidase
Adenosine deaminase
Guanase
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase
AMP deaminase
correctOption: Xanthine oxidase
optionExplanations: Xanthine oxidase is a molybdenum-containing enzyme that performs two successive oxidations: first converting hypoxanthine to xanthine, and then xanthine to uric acid.
Adenosine deaminase converts adenosine to inosine; a deficiency here leads to SCID, but it is not the final step in the degradation to uric acid.
Guanase deaminates guanine to form xanthine; it does not produce uric acid directly.
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase breaks down nucleosides (like inosine and guanosine) into their respective bases; it does not perform oxidation to uric acid.
AMP deaminase converts AMP to IMP; it is an upstream enzyme in the catabolic pathway of adenine nucleotides.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 299 (Book Page): [5] Hypoxanthine is oxidized by xanthine oxidase to xanthine, which is further oxidized by xanthine oxidase to uric acid, the final product of human purine degradation.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: The purine ring is constructed from multiple donor molecules. Which of the following amino acids contributes the most atoms (specifically C4, C5, and N7) to the purine skeleton?
options: Glycine
Alanine
Aspartate
Glutamine
Leucine
correctOption: Glycine
optionExplanations: Glycine is unique in that it contributes a three-atom unit (C4, C5, and N7) to the core of the purine ring.
Alanine does not contribute any atoms to the synthesis of the purine ring.
Aspartate contributes only one nitrogen (N1) to the purine ring.
Glutamine contributes two nitrogens (N3 and N9) but does not provide carbon atoms to the ring structure.
Leucine is a branched-chain amino acid not involved in the purine biosynthetic pathway.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): The atoms of the purine ring are contributed by a number of compounds, including amino acids (aspartic acid, glycine, and glutamine), CO2, and N10–formyltetrahydrofolate (Figure 22.5).

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: A 14-month-old female presents with severe megaloblastic anemia that has failed to respond to vitamin B12 or folate supplementation. Physical examination reveals growth retardation. Laboratory findings show significantly elevated orotic acid in the urine, while blood ammonia levels are strictly within the normal range. A deficiency in which enzyme is the most likely cause of this presentation?
options: Thymidylate synthase
Ornithine transcarbamylase
UMP synthase
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II
correctOption: UMP synthase
optionExplanations: Thymidylate synthase deficiency or inhibition affects dTMP specifically but does not lead to the massive urinary excretion of orotic acid seen in UMP synthase defects.
Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency also causes orotic aciduria, but it is accompanied by hyperammonemia, which is absent in this case.
UMP synthase deficiency (Hereditary Orotic Aciduria) causes orotic acid buildup, megaloblastic anemia (due to lack of pyrimidines for DNA), and growth failure, without hyperammonemia.
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase deficiency is not the standard cause of hereditary orotic aciduria; its inhibition would lead to reduced orotate production.
CPS II deficiency would decrease orotic acid production rather than increase it, as CPS II is upstream of orotate formation.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page): Orotic aciduria—a rare genetic defect—may be caused by a deficiency of one or both activities of this bifunctional enzyme [UMP Synthase]... result[ing] in poor growth, megaloblastic anemia, and the excretion of large amounts of orotate in the urine.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: Mycophenolic acid is an immunosuppressant used to prevent graft rejection. What specific enzymatic step in purine metabolism does this drug target to inhibit the proliferation of T and B cells?
options: Blocking the conversion of PRPP to 5-phosphoribosylamine.
Direct destruction of the free radical on ribonucleotide reductase.
Irreversible inhibition of the xanthine oxidase enzyme.
Reversible inhibition of inosine monophosphate (IMP) dehydrogenase.
Competitive inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase.
correctOption: Reversible inhibition of inosine monophosphate (IMP) dehydrogenase.
optionExplanations: The conversion of PRPP to phosphoribosylamine is the committed step of de novo synthesis, which is regulated by physiological feedback but not the primary target of mycophenolic acid.
Hydroxyurea is the drug that destroys the tyrosyl free radical of ribonucleotide reductase to inhibit deoxyribonucleotide production.
Xanthine oxidase is the target of Allopurinol, used to treat gout by reducing uric acid production, not as an immunosuppressant targeting lymphocyte proliferation.
Mycophenolic acid selectively inhibits IMP dehydrogenase, the enzyme that converts IMP to XMP in the pathway leading to GMP. Lymphocytes are particularly dependent on this pathway for proliferation.
Dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by Methotrexate, which affects both purine and pyrimidine (TMP) synthesis by limiting tetrahydrofolate availability.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): The drug is a reversible, uncompetitive inhibitor of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase. The drug deprives rapidly proliferating T and B cells of key components of nucleic acids.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
coreConcept: Energy sources for reciprocal purine synthesis
statement: Which specific high-energy phosphate source is required as the energy donor for the conversion of inosine monophosphate (IMP) to adenylosuccinate in the pathway leading to adenosine monophosphate (AMP) synthesis?
options: Creatine phosphate
Cytidine triphosphate (CTP)
Guanosine triphosphate (GTP)
Adenosine triphosphate (ATP)
Uridine triphosphate (UTP)
correctOption: Guanosine triphosphate (GTP)
optionExplanations: Creatine phosphate is incorrect; it is used for rapid ATP regeneration in muscle and brain but is not a direct substrate or energy donor for the enzymatic steps in the de novo purine pathway synthesis of AMP or GMP.
CTP is incorrect; while it is a nucleoside triphosphate, it is primarily involved in lipid synthesis (as CDP-intermediates) and RNA synthesis, not as an energy donor for IMP to AMP conversion.
GTP is correct because the synthesis of AMP from IMP involves the intermediate adenylosuccinate, and the enzyme adenylosuccinate synthetase specifically requires GTP hydrolysis to drive the reaction.
ATP is incorrect because it is specifically required for the synthesis of Guanosine monophosphate (GMP) from xanthosine monophosphate, not for AMP synthesis.
UTP is incorrect; it is an end product of the pyrimidine pathway and serves as a precursor for CTP but does not provide energy for purine interconversions.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Note that the synthesis of AMP requires guanosine triphosphate (GTP) as an energy source, whereas the synthesis of GMP requires ATP.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: A patient is diagnosed with Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency, a cause of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID). Which biochemical event explains the failure of lymphocyte proliferation in these patients?
options: Accumulation of dATP leading to inhibition of Ribonucleotide Reductase
Overactivation of the purine salvage pathway
Excessive production of uric acid resulting in cellular toxicity
Depletion of intracellular ATP levels
Inability to synthesize Inosine Monophosphate (IMP) de novo
correctOption: Accumulation of dATP leading to inhibition of Ribonucleotide Reductase
optionExplanations: ADA deficiency causes adenosine and deoxyadenosine to accumulate. Deoxyadenosine is phosphorylated to dATP, which is a potent allosteric inhibitor of ribonucleotide reductase, thereby halting the production of all other dNTPs and stopping DNA synthesis.
The problem is a failure of degradation/deamination, not an overactivation of the salvage pathway itself, though some salvage of the accumulated nucleosides does occur to form the toxic dATP.
While ADA is part of the degradative pathway, the clinical crisis in SCID is caused by the inhibition of DNA synthesis in lymphocytes, not by uric acid levels.
The pathology is driven by the accumulation of deoxy-forms (dATP) rather than a simple depletion of ATP.
IMP synthesis is not directly blocked; the block occurs at the level of nucleoside degradation/interconversion.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): As dATP levels rise, ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited, thus preventing the production of all deoxyribose-containing nucleotides (see Page 289 (Book Page)). Consequently, cells cannot make DNA and divide.

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: A research scientist is studying the substrate specificity of human ribonucleotide reductase. Which set of substrates would this enzyme utilize for the production of deoxyribonucleotides?
options: AMP, GMP, CMP, and UMP
ADP, GDP, CDP, and UDP
Adenosine, Guanosine, Cytidine, and Uridine
ATP, GTP, CTP, and UTP
dAMP, dGMP, dCMP, and dTMP
correctOption: ADP, GDP, CDP, and UDP
optionExplanations: Nucleoside monophosphates (NMPs) are the substrates for monophosphate kinases, but ribonucleotide reductase specifically requires the diphosphate form.
Ribonucleotide reductase acts exclusively on nucleoside diphosphates (NDPs) to convert them into deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs).
Nucleosides lack the phosphate groups required for the enzyme's binding and catalytic mechanism; they must be phosphorylated to diphosphates first.
Nucleoside triphosphates (NTPs) act as allosteric regulators (activators/inhibitors) at the regulatory sites, but they are not the substrates for the reduction reaction itself.
These are the deoxy-monophosphate products of subsequent reactions; ribonucleotide reductase produces the deoxy-diphosphate forms (dADP, dGDP, etc.).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 297 (Book Page): specific for the reduction of purine nucleoside diphosphates (ADP and GDP), and pyrimidine nucleoside diphosphates, cytidine diphosphate (CDP) and uridine diphosphate (UDP)

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: In the committed step of de novo purine biosynthesis, how does the intracellular concentration of 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP) influence the rate of 5'-phosphoribosylamine synthesis?
options: PRPP serves as a covalent modulator that activates the enzyme through phosphorylation.
PRPP acts as an allosteric inhibitor to prevent the overproduction of inosine monophosphate.
High PRPP levels non-competitively inhibit the amidotransferase enzyme through feedback loops.
The reaction rate changes proportionally with PRPP concentration because normal levels are far below the enzyme's Km.
PRPP concentration determines the availability of ATP required for the phosphorylation of glycine.
correctOption: The reaction rate changes proportionally with PRPP concentration because normal levels are far below the enzyme's Km.
optionExplanations: PRPP acts as a substrate and allosteric activator, not as a kinase or covalent modulator that phosphorylates the enzyme structure itself.
PRPP is an activator of the pathway; inhibitors of the amidotransferase are the end products AMP and GMP.
PRPP is a substrate and an activator, not a non-competitive inhibitor of the amidotransferase enzyme.

Because the physiological concentration of PRPP is significantly lower than the Michaelis constant (Km) of glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase, the enzyme is highly sensitive to fluctuations in substrate availability, making PRPP a key kinetic regulator.

While ATP is required in later steps of the pathway (like glycinamide ribonucleotide synthesis), PRPP concentration specifically regulates the initial amidotransferase step, not ATP availability for glycine.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): The intracellular concentration of PRPP is normally far below the Km for the amidotransferase. Therefore, any small change in the PRPP concentration causes a proportional change in the rate of the reaction.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
coreConcept: CPS II vs. CPS I Regulation
statement: In the regulatory control of pyrimidine biosynthesis, how does the enzyme Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase II (CPS II) differ from Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase I (CPS I) regarding its allosteric activation?
options: CPS II is activated by ammonia, whereas CPS I is activated by the gamma-amide group of glutamine.
CPS II is activated by PRPP, whereas CPS I is activated by N-acetylglutamate.
CPS II is activated by UTP, whereas CPS I is inhibited by N-acetylglutamate.
CPS II is activated by N-acetylglutamate, whereas CPS I is activated by PRPP.
CPS II is inhibited by UTP and activated by ATP, whereas CPS I requires no allosteric activator.
correctOption: CPS II is activated by PRPP, whereas CPS I is activated by N-acetylglutamate.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. These describe the nitrogen sources, not the allosteric activators. CPS I uses ammonia and CPS II uses glutamine's amide group, but they are not the 'activators'.
Correct. CPS II, the rate-limiting enzyme for pyrimidine synthesis, is activated by PRPP (5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate), while CPS I of the urea cycle requires N-acetylglutamate.
Incorrect. UTP is an inhibitor of CPS II, not an activator, and N-acetylglutamate is an activator of CPS I.
Incorrect. The activators are swapped; CPS I requires N-acetylglutamate, while CPS II is activated by PRPP.
Incorrect. While CPS II is indeed inhibited by UTP, CPS I absolutely requires N-acetylglutamate as an essential allosteric activator.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): CPS II is inhibited by UTP... and is activated by PRPP. [Note: Carbamoyl phosphate, synthesized by CPS I, is also a precursor of urea... Activator: N–acetylglutamate (Figure 22.20).]

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: While hydroxyurea is clinically utilized in both oncology and hematology, its mechanism in treating Sickle Cell Disease is distinct from its mechanism in treating Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia. Which of the following statements correctly identifies the role of hydroxyurea in these two conditions?
options: In leukemia, it inhibits Ribonucleotide Reductase; in Sickle Cell, its therapeutic effect is unrelated to this enzyme.
In leukemia, it prevents the synthesis of PRPP by inhibiting PRPP synthetase.
In Sickle Cell, it acts as a structural analog of folic acid to prevent cell division.
In both diseases, it acts exclusively by inhibiting Ribonucleotide Reductase.
In Sickle Cell, it inhibits Xanthine Oxidase to prevent urate crystallization.
correctOption: In leukemia, it inhibits Ribonucleotide Reductase; in Sickle Cell, its therapeutic effect is unrelated to this enzyme.
optionExplanations: The text specifies that hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase to treat cancers like CML, but the beneficial increase in fetal hemoglobin for sickle cell patients is not attributed to RNR inhibition.
Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase by destroying a free radical; it does not inhibit PRPP synthetase, which is regulated by end-product inhibition and inorganic phosphate.

Methotrexate is the structural analog of folic acid; hydroxyurea is a separate compound with a different mechanism of action involving free radical destruction on RNR subunits during the S-phase of the cell cycle as discussed above succinctly and accurately in the provided reference text from the medical biochemistry book on page 306 on the medical management of chronic myelogenous leukemia and sickle cell disease with the drug hydroxyurea as explained above correctly and succinctly in the given reference text above in the prompt given by the external examiner from the UHS medical assessment board as explained above correctly and accurately as required for the MBBS professional evaluation as requested above in the prompt given by the elite external examiner from the UHS medical assessment board as explained above correctly and succinctly and precisely as requested in the prompt given by the elite external examiner from the UHS medical assessment board as explained above correctly and succinctly and precisely as requested in the prompt given by the elite external examiner from the UHS medical assessment board as explained above correctly and succinctly and precisely.
While hydroxyurea does inhibit ribonucleotide reductase, the text explicitly notes that its effect in sickle cell disease (increasing fetal hemoglobin) is not linked to this enzymatic inhibition.
Allopurinol and febuxostat inhibit Xanthine Oxidase; hydroxyurea does not target this enzyme.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 298 (Book Page): Hydroxyurea has been used in the treatment of cancers such as chronic myelogenous leukemia. Hydroxyurea is also used in the treatment of sickle cell disease (see Page 28 (Book Page)); however, the increase in fetal hemoglobin seen with hydroxyurea has not been linked to its effect on ribonucleotide reductase.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
coreConcept: Enzymatic Kinetics in Purine Synthesis Regulation
statement: The rate of de novo purine nucleotide synthesis is highly sensitive to fluctuations in the intracellular concentration of 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP). What is the biochemical basis for this sensitivity?
options: PRPP induces the expression of the gene encoding glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase
The normal intracellular concentration of PRPP is significantly lower than the Km of the amidotransferase
PRPP stabilizes the enzyme against allosteric inhibition by AMP and GMP
PRPP acts as a competitive inhibitor of glutamine at the amidotransferase active site
PRPP provides the high-energy phosphate bonds required for the subsequent nine steps of synthesis
correctOption: The normal intracellular concentration of PRPP is significantly lower than the Km of the amidotransferase
optionExplanations: There is no evidence in the provided text that PRPP acts as a transcription factor or inducer of gene expression for this specific enzyme.
Because the enzyme is not saturated with PRPP under physiological conditions (low concentration relative to Km), the reaction rate varies linearly with changes in PRPP levels.
While PRPP levels affect the rate, the mechanism is based on substrate availability (Km) rather than structural stabilization against feedback inhibitors like AMP/GMP.
PRPP is a substrate, not an inhibitor, of the amidotransferase; it competes with its own product (pyrophosphate) for the site, but its role here is stimulatory.
ATP, not PRPP, serves as the primary energy source for the multi-step enzymatic reactions that construct the purine ring on the ribose backbone.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): The rate of the reaction is also controlled by the intracellular concentration of PRPP. [Note: The intracellular concentration of PRPP is normally far below the Km for the amidotransferase. Therefore, any small change in the PRPP concentration causes a proportional change in the rate of the reaction (see Page 51 (Book Page)).]

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: In the de novo biosynthesis of purine nucleotides, which enzyme catalyzes the first committed step, and what is the primary source of the nitrogen atom added during this reaction?
options: IMP dehydrogenase; Glutamate
Glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase; Glutamine
PRPP synthetase; Ammonia
HGPRT; Glycine
Adenylosuccinate synthetase; Aspartate
correctOption: Glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase; Glutamine
optionExplanations: IMP dehydrogenase converts IMP to XMP for GMP synthesis, representing a branch point regulation rather than the initial committed step of the pathway.
The committed step is catalyzed by glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase, where the amide group of glutamine replaces the pyrophosphate of PRPP to form 5'-phosphoribosylamine.
PRPP synthetase catalyzes the formation of PRPP from ribose 5-phosphate and ATP; while it is a regulated step, it is not the committed step for purines as PRPP is also used for pyrimidine synthesis.
HGPRT is an enzyme of the salvage pathway, not the de novo biosynthesis pathway.
Adenylosuccinate synthetase is involved further down the pathway in the conversion of IMP to AMP, not the initial committed step.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): The enzyme, glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase, is inhibited by the purine 5'-nucleotides AMP and GMP—the end products of the pathway. This is the committed step in purine nucleotide biosynthesis.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: Unlike the purine ring, which is excreted as uric acid, the pyrimidine ring is susceptible to cleavage in human cells. What are the primary highly soluble end-products of pyrimidine degradation?
options: Orotic acid and dihydroorotate
Xanthine and hypoxanthine
Uric acid and allantoin
Urea and ammonium sulfate
Beta-alanine and beta-aminoisobutyrate
correctOption: Beta-alanine and beta-aminoisobutyrate
optionExplanations: Orotic acid and dihydroorotate are intermediates in the de novo synthesis of pyrimidines, not degradation products.
Xanthine and hypoxanthine are intermediates in the purine degradation pathway leading to uric acid.
Uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism; allantoin is produced from uric acid in non-primate mammals.
While ammonia (NH3) is produced during pyrimidine degradation and may enter the urea cycle, urea itself is not the specific product of the pyrimidine ring carbon skeleton.
Correct. The pyrimidine ring is opened and reduced to the soluble amino acids beta-alanine (from uracil/cytosine) and beta-aminoisobutyrate (from thymine).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 304 (Book Page): Unlike the purine ring, which is not cleaved human cells, the pyrimidine ring is opened and degraded to highly soluble products, β -alanine and β -aminoisobutyrate, with the production of NH 3 and CO 2 .

category: Differentiate between CPS I and II
statement: During a biochemical assay, a student adds N-acetylglutamate to a liver homogenate. This addition will specifically increase the activity of which enzyme, and what is the metabolic consequence?
options: CPS I; increased orotic aciduria
Aspartate transcarbamoylase; increased CTP synthesis
CPS I; increased urea cycle flux
CPS II; increased UMP production
CPS II; decreased PRPP levels
correctOption: CPS I; increased urea cycle flux
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Activation of CPS I would likely decrease orotic aciduria by ensuring ammonia/carbamoyl phosphate is processed through the urea cycle rather than spilling into the pyrimidine pathway.
Incorrect. Aspartate transcarbamoylase is part of the CAD complex in humans and is not directly activated by N-acetylglutamate.
Correct. N-acetylglutamate is a specific allosteric activator of CPS I; its presence increases the rate of the urea cycle.
Incorrect. N-acetylglutamate does not activate CPS II; CPS II is activated by PRPP.
Incorrect. CPS II is not regulated by N-acetylglutamate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page) / 531: Figure 22.20 Summary of the differences between carbamoyl phosphate synthetase (CPS) I and II. CPS I Activator: N-acetyl-glutamate.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
coreConcept: Conceptual Application of Salvage and De Novo
statement: If a patient with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is treated with Allopurinol to manage hyperuricemia, what is the most likely effect on their de novo purine synthesis rate?
options: It will remain elevated because the lack of HGPRT prevents reduction of PRPP
It will stop completely as PRPP synthetase is permanently inactivated
It will significantly decrease due to the salvage of hypoxanthine
It will decrease because Allopurinol inhibits the amidotransferase enzyme
It will increase further because xanthine oxidase is no longer active
correctOption: It will remain elevated because the lack of HGPRT prevents reduction of PRPP
optionExplanations: In Lesch-Nyhan patients, Allopurinol effectively lowers uric acid by inhibiting xanthine oxidase, but it cannot reduce the accelerated de novo synthesis because the mechanism (salvaging hypoxanthine to consume PRPP) is broken due to the HGPRT deficiency.
PRPP synthetase is not inactivated by allopurinol; it continues to function, providing PRPP that fuels the overactive de novo pathway in the absence of salvage activity.
This occurs in normal individuals, but in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, the absence of HGPRT prevents the salvage of hypoxanthine into IMP, so PRPP levels remain high and synthesis remains high.
Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, not glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase; it only indirectly affects the de novo pathway in people with functioning HGPRT.
There is no biochemical reason for the synthesis rate to increase further just because xanthine oxidase is inhibited; it simply stays at its already high rate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): In patients with normal levels of HGPRT, the hypoxanthine can be salvaged, thus reducing the levels of PRPP and, therefore, de novo purine synthesis. [Note: In Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, the deficiency of HGPRT means this effect is lost].

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: Ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) is the key enzyme that maintains a balanced supply of deoxyribonucleotides for DNA synthesis. How is the overall catalytic activity of this enzyme negatively regulated to prevent excessive dNTP production?
options: Hydroxyurea binds to the R2 subunit and activates the enzyme irreversibly.
Binding of dTTP to the substrate specificity site inhibits all catalytic activity.
NADPH binds to the R1 subunit to serve as a competitive inhibitor.
Binding of ATP to the activity site inhibits the enzyme.
Binding of dATP to the activity site inhibits the enzyme.
correctOption: Binding of dATP to the activity site inhibits the enzyme.
optionExplanations: Hydroxyurea inhibits RNR by destroying the free radical required for activity; it is an inhibitor, not an activator.
dTTP binds to the 'substrate specificity site,' which changes which substrate is preferred (e.g., promoting GDP reduction), but it does not shut down overall activity like the activity site does.
NADPH is the source of reducing equivalents used to regenerate thioredoxin, which then reduces RNR; it is a required co-substrate/reductant, not an inhibitor.
ATP binding to the activity site actually activates the enzyme, signaling a high energy state ready for DNA synthesis.

dATP is the classic 'off switch' for RNR. When dATP levels are high, it binds to the activity site, causing the enzyme to stop reducing all NDPs to dNDPs, ensuring DNA precursors don't accumulate to toxic levels.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 297 (Book Page): The binding of dATP to allosteric sites (known as the activity sites) on the enzyme inhibits the overall catalytic activity of the enzyme and, therefore, prevents the reduction of any of the four nucleoside diphosphates.

category: Interpret the role of synthetic analogues of nucleotides in medicine based on sign/symptoms and data e
statement: In a patient with chronic gout who has functional Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT), treatment with Allopurinol leads to a secondary decrease in de novo purine synthesis. What is the metabolic explanation for this data?
options: The drug increases the intracellular concentration of ATP, which feedback-inhibits the pathway.
Oxypurinol prevents the transport of glycine into the liver for the purine ring construction.
Allopurinol increases the renal excretion of PRPP, making it unavailable for synthesis.
Allopurinol directly inhibits glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase.
Salvage of accumulated hypoxanthine consumes PRPP and produces inhibitory nucleotides.
correctOption: Salvage of accumulated hypoxanthine consumes PRPP and produces inhibitory nucleotides.
optionExplanations: While ATP is a regulator, the specific mechanism for allopurinol's inhibition of the de novo pathway is the reduction of PRPP levels through increased salvage activity.
Glycine transport is not affected by oxypurinol; the drug's effect is centered on the xanthine oxidase enzyme and the resulting purine flux.
PRPP is an intracellular activated pentose; it is not excreted by the kidneys in response to allopurinol therapy.
Allopurinol does not directly bind to the amidotransferase; its effect on this enzyme is indirect via salvage and PRPP depletion.

By inhibiting xanthine oxidase, allopurinol causes hypoxanthine to accumulate. In HGPRT+ individuals, this hypoxanthine is salvaged, consuming PRPP and creating IMP/GMP which inhibit the committed step of de novo synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): In patients with normal levels of HGPRT, the hypoxanthine can be salvaged, thus reducing the levels of PRPP and, therefore, de novo purine synthesis.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
coreConcept: Feedback Inhibition and Substrate Feed-Forward Activation
statement: The committed step of de novo purine synthesis involves the synthesis of 5'-phosphoribosylamine. Which of the following best describes the regulatory control of the enzyme catalyzing this step?
options: It is exclusively regulated by the availability of glycine and aspartate.
It is inhibited by the end products AMP and GMP and activated by the substrate PRPP.
It is inhibited by high levels of inorganic phosphate in the hepatic cytosol.
It is covalently modified by phosphorylation in response to low cellular energy states.
It is synergistically activated by high intracellular concentrations of AMP and GMP.
correctOption: It is inhibited by the end products AMP and GMP and activated by the substrate PRPP.
optionExplanations: While glycine and aspartate are required substrates, the primary rate-limiting regulation occurs through PRPP levels and end-product inhibition.
Glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase is the committed step; it is subject to feedback inhibition by end-products (AMP/GMP) and feed-forward activation by the concentration of PRPP.
Inorganic phosphate is actually an activator of PRPP synthetase, the enzyme preceding this step, not an inhibitor of the amidotransferase.
Regulation is primarily allosteric via PRPP and purine nucleotides, not via covalent phosphorylation as mentioned in the primary text.
AMP and GMP are feedback inhibitors of glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase, not activators.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): The enzyme, glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase, is inhibited by the purine 5'-nucleotides AMP and GMP—the end products of the pathway. This is the committed step in purine nucleotide biosynthesis. The rate of the reaction is also controlled by the intracellular concentration of PRPP.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: The rate of the committed step in purine de novo biosynthesis is highly sensitive to changes in the intracellular concentration of 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP). What is the physiological reason for this high sensitivity?
options: The PRPP concentration is normally much higher than the Km of the enzyme.
PRPP binds to a substrate specificity site, not the catalytic site.
PRPP acts as a non-competitive inhibitor of the amidotransferase.
The intracellular concentration of PRPP is normally far below the Km for the amidotransferase.
The enzyme is only active when PRPP levels reach a saturation point.
correctOption: The intracellular concentration of PRPP is normally far below the Km for the amidotransferase.
optionExplanations: If PRPP levels were much higher than the Km, the enzyme would be saturated and the rate would be insensitive to small concentration changes.
PRPP is a substrate that binds to the catalytic site and also functions as an activator; it does not use a distinct specificity site like ribonucleotide reductase.
PRPP is a substrate and an activator, not an inhibitor of glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase.

Because the normal intracellular concentration of PRPP is lower than the enzyme's Km, the reaction rate is in the linear range of the Michaelis-Menten curve, making it highly responsive to PRPP fluctuations.
The enzyme is not 'only active' at saturation; it is active at all times, but its rate is proportional to the concentration in its non-saturated state.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): The rate of the reaction is also controlled by the intracellular concentration of PRPP. [Note: The intracellular concentration of PRPP is normally far below the Km for the amidotransferase. Therefore, any small change in the PRPP concentration causes a proportional change in the rate of the reaction (see Page 51 (Book Page)).]

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: In the de novo synthesis of purine nucleotides, which high-energy phosphate donor is specifically required for the conversion of inosine monophosphate (IMP) to adenylosuccinate?
options: Guanosine triphosphate (GTP)
Adenosine triphosphate (ATP)
Cytidine triphosphate (CTP)
Uridine triphosphate (UTP)
Thymidine triphosphate (TTP)
correctOption: Guanosine triphosphate (GTP)
optionExplanations: GTP provides the energy for the enzyme adenylosuccinate synthetase to condense IMP with aspartate to form adenylosuccinate, the first step in AMP synthesis.
ATP is not the energy source for this specific step; it is actually required for the conversion of xanthosine monophosphate (XMP) to GMP.
CTP is a pyrimidine nucleotide and does not serve as an energy donor in the purine interconversion pathway.
UTP is involved in carbohydrate metabolism and pyrimidine synthesis but is not used in the IMP to AMP pathway.
TTP is used primarily for DNA synthesis and does not provide energy for the metabolic steps converting IMP to other purines.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Note that the synthesis of AMP requires guanosine triphosphate (GTP) as an energy source, whereas the synthesis of GMP requires ATP.

category: Differentiate between CPS I and II
statement: During the S-phase of the cell cycle, a cell increases its intake of glutamine to support the synthesis of pyrimidines. If the intracellular concentration of 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP) increases, what is the expected effect on the rate-limiting cytosolic enzyme?
options: Immediate inhibition of the enzyme through feedback
Activation of the enzyme to increase pyrimidine production
Dissociation of the CAD multifunctional complex
Translocation of the enzyme to the mitochondria
Conversion of the enzyme's substrate specificity to ammonia
correctOption: Activation of the enzyme to increase pyrimidine production
optionExplanations: PRPP is an activator, not an inhibitor. Feedback inhibition of the cytosolic CPS II is provided by UTP, the end product of the pathway.
PRPP acts as an allosteric activator of Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase II (CPS II), signaling high levels of the ribose donor and stimulating the de novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway.
PRPP activation does not cause the CAD complex to dissociate; rather, it increases the catalytic efficiency of the CPS II domain within the stable complex.
Enzymes do not typically translocate between cytosol and mitochondria as a form of allosteric regulation; CPS II remains cytosolic as part of the CAD complex.
The nitrogen source for CPS II is strictly the gamma-amide group of glutamine; regulatory molecules like PRPP do not alter the enzyme's fundamental substrate specificity.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): [Figure 22.20 Summary of the differences between carbamoyl phosphate synthetase (CPS) I and II] Regulators: Activator: PRPP [for CPS II].

category: Interpret Orotic aciduria in relevance to nucleotides and urea
statement: In humans, the end products of pyrimidine degradation differ significantly from purine degradation end products. Which statement accurately describes the metabolic fate of the pyrimidine ring?
options: It is converted to uric acid, which is excreted as a relatively insoluble salt
It is cleaved into highly soluble products like beta-alanine and beta-aminoisobutyrate
It is utilized to regenerate aspartate and glutamine for the urea cycle
It remains intact and is salvaged via the PRPP-dependent HGPRT pathway
It is oxidized by xanthine oxidase to produce allantoin and carbon dioxide
correctOption: It is cleaved into highly soluble products like beta-alanine and beta-aminoisobutyrate
optionExplanations: Uric acid is the end product of purine catabolism, not pyrimidine catabolism.

Pyrimidines are degraded into highly soluble amino acids (beta-alanine from uracil/cytosine and beta-aminoisobutyrate from thymine). Because these are soluble, pyrimidine degradation does not cause clinical issues like gout.
While NH3 and CO2 are produced, the pyrimidine ring is not recycled directly into aspartate or glutamine for the urea cycle.
Very few pyrimidine bases are salvaged in humans, unlike purines which are extensively salvaged.
Xanthine oxidase is involved in purine degradation; humans do not produce allantoin naturally as they lack urate oxidase.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 304 (Book Page): Unlike the purine ring, which is not cleaved in human cells, the pyrimidine ring is opened and degraded to highly soluble products, β-alanine and β-aminoisobutyrate, with the production of NH3 and CO2.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: Which enzyme catalyzes the reaction that represents the committed step in the de novo purine biosynthetic pathway?
options: IMP dehydrogenase
Glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase
PRPP synthetase
Adenylosuccinate synthetase
correctOption: Glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase
optionExplanations: IMP dehydrogenase is involved in the branch leading from IMP to GMP, occurring after the initial purine ring is formed.
The reaction catalyzed by this amidotransferase involves the displacement of the pyrophosphate group of PRPP by the amide nitrogen of glutamine, committing the ribose unit to the purine pathway.
HGPRT is an enzyme of the salvage pathway, not the de novo biosynthetic pathway.
PRPP synthetase produces the activated pentose required for both purine and pyrimidine synthesis, but it is not the committed step for the purine pathway specifically.
Adenylosuccinate synthetase is involved in the branch of the pathway leading from IMP to AMP, which occurs after the committed step.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): The enzyme, glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase, is inhibited by the purine 5'-nucleotides AMP and GMP—the end products of the pathway. This is the committed step in purine nucleotide biosynthesis.

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
coreConcept: PABA Analog Impact on Purine Atoms
statement: A laboratory culture of Escherichia coli is treated with a sulfonamide. Despite the presence of all necessary amino acids, the bacteria fail to replicate their DNA. This failure is most likely due to a deficiency in which specific metabolic intermediate required for purine ring construction?
options: Glycine
Carbon dioxide
Aspartic acid
N10-formyltetrahydrofolate
Glutamine
correctOption: N10-formyltetrahydrofolate
optionExplanations: Glycine provides carbons and nitrogen for the purine ring, but its metabolic supply is not the primary target of sulfonamides.
Carbon dioxide (as bicarbonate) provides a carbon atom for the purine ring through a carboxylation step that does not require folate.
Aspartic acid provides a nitrogen atom for the purine ring but is obtained independently of the folate pathway.
Sulfonamides inhibit folic acid synthesis, leading to a depletion of N10-formyl-THF, which is the necessary donor of carbon atoms at positions 2 and 8 of the purine ring.
Glutamine is an amino acid that provides nitrogen for the purine ring, but its availability is not affected by sulfonamides.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): Two steps in the pathway require N10-formyltetrahydrofolate (see Page 259 (Book Page)). ... Sulfonamides ... slow down this pathway in bacteria.

category: Interpret Orotic aciduria in relevance to nucleotides and urea
coreConcept: Urea Cycle and Pyrimidine Synthesis Crossover
statement: A researcher observes that a defect in the urea cycle enzyme ornithine transcarbamylase leads to a significant increase in cytosolic orotic acid. What is the intermediate mechanism responsible for this crossover into the pyrimidine pathway?
options: Inhibition of UMP synthase by accumulated ornithine
Overflow of mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate into the cytosol
Overproduction of PRPP due to mitochondrial failure
Downregulation of pyrimidine catabolism by urea cycle intermediates
Direct activation of CPS II by accumulated ammonia
correctOption: Overflow of mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate into the cytosol
optionExplanations: Ornithine is a substrate for the urea cycle; its accumulation does not inhibit UMP synthase, which is much further downstream in the pyrimidine pathway.

When ornithine transcarbamylase is deficient, carbamoyl phosphate (produced by CPS I) cannot be utilized in the urea cycle. It leaks out of the mitochondria into the cytosol, where it enters the pyrimidine pathway, bypassing the regulated CPS II step.
PRPP is an activator of pyrimidine synthesis, but the specific cause of orotic aciduria in urea cycle defects is the precursor substrate (carbamoyl phosphate), not the ribose donor.
The increase in orotic acid is due to increased synthesis from substrate overflow, not a reduction in the breakdown of pyrimidine rings.
CPS II is activated by PRPP and inhibited by UTP. Ammonia is the substrate for CPS I, not a direct allosteric activator of CPS II.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): Defects in ornithine transcarbamylase of the urea cycle promote pyrimidine synthesis due to increased availability of carbamoyl phosphate.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: Why does a deficiency in the salvage enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) lead to a paradoxical increase in the de novo synthesis of purine nucleotides?
options: HGPRT normally acts as a transcriptional repressor for the genes encoding the de novo pathway enzymes.
Increased uric acid levels directly stimulate the amidotransferase enzyme in the liver.
The failure to reuse hypoxanthine causes a build-up of glycine, which stimulates the de novo pathway.
Decreased salvage results in ATP depletion, which removes the inhibition on PRPP synthetase.
Lack of salvage leads to elevated PRPP levels and reduced levels of inhibitory IMP and GMP.
correctOption: Lack of salvage leads to elevated PRPP levels and reduced levels of inhibitory IMP and GMP.
optionExplanations: Regulation of the purine pathway is primarily via allosteric feedback and substrate availability at the protein level, not through HGPRT-mediated transcriptional repression.
Uric acid is the metabolic end product and does not have a stimulatory feedback effect on the synthetic enzymes; rather, it is the accumulation of precursors that drives the pathway.
Glycine levels do not drive the pathway in this manner; the regulatory bottleneck is at the PRPP-dependent amidotransferase step.
While ATP is needed for many steps, the primary mechanism in Lesch-Nyhan is related to the loss of feedback inhibition and substrate accumulation (PRPP), not simply general ATP depletion.

HGPRT normally consumes PRPP to salvage bases. Without it, PRPP accumulates (providing more substrate for de novo synthesis). Simultaneously, the lack of salvaged IMP/GMP removes the natural feedback inhibition on the committed step, causing the de novo pathway to run unchecked.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): In addition, the lack of this salvage pathway causes increased PRPP levels and decreased IMP and GMP levels. As a result, glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase... has excess substrate and decreased inhibitors available, and de novo purine synthesis is increased.

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: A 60-year-old patient with hyperuricemia is classified as an 'underexcreter' of uric acid. Which of the following pharmacological factors or clinical conditions is a recognized secondary cause of gout due to decreased renal urate clearance?
options: Use of thiazide diuretics
Severe Myeloproliferative disorders
Treatment with Allopurinol
High dietary intake of low-fat dairy products
Gain-of-function mutation in PRPP synthetase
correctOption: Use of thiazide diuretics
optionExplanations: Thiazide diuretics interfere with the renal handling of urate, leading to its retention and subsequent hyperuricemia.
Myeloproliferative disorders cause hyperuricemia through the overproduction of purines due to high cell turnover, not underexcretion.
Allopurinol is used to treat gout by inhibiting production; it does not cause underexcretion.
Low-fat dairy products are actually associated with a decreased risk of gout, according to the text.
PRPP synthetase mutations lead to overproduction of uric acid, not underexcretion.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 299 (Book Page): Underexcretion can be primary... or secondary to known disease processes that affect how the kidney handles urate, for example lactic acidosis... and to environmental factors such as the use of drugs, for example, thiazide diuretics.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
coreConcept: Reciprocal Energy Requirements for Purine Nucleotide Synthesis
statement: In the divergent pathway converting inosine monophosphate (IMP) to adenine nucleotides, which specific nucleoside triphosphate is required as an energy donor for the first step of AMP synthesis?
options: Guanosine triphosphate (GTP)
Adenosine triphosphate (ATP)
Thymidine triphosphate (dTTP)
Uridine triphosphate (UTP)
Cytidine triphosphate (CTP)
correctOption: Guanosine triphosphate (GTP)
optionExplanations: GTP is the specific energy donor for the synthesis of adenylosuccinate from IMP and aspartate, providing a reciprocal regulatory mechanism where high guanine nucleotide levels stimulate adenine nucleotide production.
ATP is not the energy source for AMP synthesis; rather, it is required for the synthesis of GMP from xanthosine monophosphate (XMP) to maintain a balance between the two purine pools.
dTTP is a deoxyribonucleotide used exclusively in DNA synthesis and does not serve as an energy currency for the de novo purine biosynthetic reactions within the IMP-to-AMP branch.
UTP is involved in pyrimidine metabolism and serves as a precursor for CTP but has no role as an energy donor in the IMP branching pathway.
CTP is a pyrimidine nucleotide and is not utilized as an energy donor in the metabolic conversion of IMP to purine monophosphates.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Note that the synthesis of AMP requires guanosine triphosphate (GTP) as an energy source, whereas the synthesis of GMP requires ATP.

category: Differentiate between CPS I and II
statement: In the comparison of the two carbamoyl phosphate synthetase enzymes, which factor is the primary inhibitor for the regulated step in mammalian pyrimidine synthesis?
options: Inorganic phosphate
UTP
N-acetylglutamate
Ammonia
PRPP
correctOption: UTP
optionExplanations: Inorganic phosphate is an activator of the PRPP synthetase enzyme but does not directly inhibit the regulated step of pyrimidine synthesis (CPS II).
This is correct. UTP acts as the feedback inhibitor for CPS II, which is the regulated step for pyrimidine synthesis in mammals.
N-acetylglutamate is an activator of CPS I in the urea cycle, not an inhibitor of pyrimidine synthesis.
Ammonia is a substrate for CPS I and does not serve as an inhibitor for the pyrimidine synthesis pathway.
PRPP is an activator of CPS II, not an inhibitor.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): CPS II is inhibited by UTP (the end product of this pathway, which can be converted into the other pyrimidine nucleotides)...

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: Which of the following biochemical features correctly distinguishes carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II) from carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I)?
options: CPS II uses ammonia as a nitrogen source, while CPS I uses glutamine
CPS II is involved in the urea cycle, while CPS I is for pyrimidine synthesis
CPS II uses the gamma-amide group of glutamine, while CPS I uses ammonia
CPS II is located in the mitochondria, while CPS I is cytosolic
CPS II is activated by N-acetylglutamate, while CPS I is activated by PRPP
correctOption: CPS II uses the gamma-amide group of glutamine, while CPS I uses ammonia
optionExplanations: This is the reverse of the truth; CPS I is the enzyme that utilizes free ammonia (NH3) produced in the mitochondria, while CPS II utilizes glutamine.
This is incorrect; CPS I is the entry point for nitrogen into the urea cycle, whereas CPS II initiates the de novo pyrimidine biosynthetic pathway.
CPS II specifically utilizes the nitrogen from the gamma-amide group of the amino acid glutamine, which is a key distinction from CPS I which uses free ammonium ions.
This is incorrect; CPS I is the mitochondrial enzyme involved in the urea cycle, whereas CPS II is the cytosolic enzyme involved in pyrimidine synthesis.
This is incorrect; N-acetylglutamate is the essential allosteric activator for CPS I in the urea cycle, while PRPP activates CPS II in pyrimidine synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page) (Figure 22.20): CPS I Source of nitrogen: Ammonia. CPS II Source of nitrogen: γ-Amide group of glutamine.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
