statement: Which of the following classes of molecules serves as the direct substrate for the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase during the synthesis of DNA precursors?
options: Deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs)
Ribonucleoside monophosphates (NMPs)
Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs)
Ribonucleoside triphosphates (NTPs)
Ribonucleoside diphosphates (NDPs)
correctOption: Ribonucleoside diphosphates (NDPs)
optionExplanations: Deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs) are the products of the ribonucleotide reductase reaction, not the substrates.
Ribonucleoside monophosphates (NMPs) are the substrates for nucleoside monophosphate kinases, not ribonucleotide reductase, which requires a diphosphate form.
Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) are the final products used by DNA polymerase; they are formed by phosphorylating dNDPs, but they do not serve as substrates for RNR.
Ribonucleoside triphosphates (NTPs) are used in RNA synthesis or serve as allosteric regulators for ribonucleotide reductase, but they are not the substrates for the reduction reaction itself.
Ribonucleotide reductase specifically acts on ribonucleoside diphosphates (ADP, GDP, CDP, and UDP) to reduce them into their corresponding deoxy-forms (dADP, dGDP, dCDP, and dUDP).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 297 (Book Page): Ribonucleotide reductase (ribonucleoside diphosphate reductase) is composed of two nonidentical dimeric subunits, R1 and R2, and is specific for the reduction of purine nucleoside diphosphates (ADP and GDP), and pyrimidine nucleoside diphosphates, cytidine diphosphate (CDP) and uridine diphosphate (UDP) to their deoxy-forms.

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
coreConcept: Lymphocyte Dependence on De Novo Synthesis
statement: Why is the deprivation of nucleic acid components by mycophenolic acid particularly detrimental to T and B lymphocytes compared to other cell types?
options: Other cell types can convert AMP back into IMP to maintain GMP levels.
Lymphocytes rely more heavily on de novo purine synthesis for proliferation.
The drug is actively concentrated within the lymphatic system.
Lymphocytes lack the enzymes for the purine salvage pathway.
Mycophenolic acid binds specifically to the TCR and BCR receptors.
correctOption: Lymphocytes rely more heavily on de novo purine synthesis for proliferation.
optionExplanations: While some interconversion is possible, it is insufficient to overcome the block in the de novo pathway during the intense proliferation seen in immune responses.
Rapidly proliferating T and B cells are significantly more dependent on the de novo purine synthesis pathway for generating the nucleotides needed for DNA replication compared to most other tissues.
The selectivity is metabolic (enzymatic dependency), not based on the drug's anatomical distribution or concentration.
Lymphocytes do possess salvage enzymes, but their rapid proliferation requires a high volume of nucleotides that salvage alone cannot provide.
The drug targets an intracellular enzyme (IMP dehydrogenase), not surface receptors like TCR or BCR.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): The drug deprives rapidly proliferating T and B cells of key components of nucleic acids. The drug is an immunosuppressant used to prevent graft rejection.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: A patient undergoing aggressive chemotherapy with Methotrexate develops symptoms of both purine and pyrimidine deficiency. While Methotrexate directly targets dihydrofolate reductase, its effect on pyrimidine metabolism is localized to which specific conversion?
options: dUMP to dTMP
Orotic acid to OMP
UDP to dUDP
UTP to CTP
OMP to UMP
correctOption: dUMP to dTMP
optionExplanations: Thymidylate synthase requires N5,N10-methylene THF to convert dUMP to dTMP. Methotrexate depletes THF by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase, thus halting dTMP production.
The conversion of orotic acid to OMP requires PRPP and orotate phosphoribosyltransferase; it is not a folate-dependent reaction.
The conversion of UDP to dUDP is performed by ribonucleotide reductase, which uses thioredoxin as a cofactor rather than folate derivatives.
The conversion of UTP to CTP requires glutamine and ATP but does not require any tetrahydrofolate derivatives, so it is not directly affected by Methotrexate.
The decarboxylation of OMP to UMP is catalyzed by orotidylate decarboxylase, which is independent of folate coenzymes.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 304 (Book Page): [By decreasing the supply of THF, these folate analogs... by preventing methylation of dUMP to dTMP, they also lower the cellular concentration of this essential component of DNA.]

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: In a patient with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, why does the de novo purine synthesis pathway become hyperactive, despite the absence of the salvage enzyme HGPRT?
options: Decreased levels of IMP and GMP reduce feedback inhibition, while PRPP levels rise.
Decreased production of hypoxanthine and guanine leads to activator buildup.
Absence of HGPRT prevents the degradation of glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase.
High uric acid levels act as an allosteric activator of PRPP synthetase.
PRPP is diverted from pyrimidine synthesis to purine synthesis exclusively.
correctOption: Decreased levels of IMP and GMP reduce feedback inhibition, while PRPP levels rise.
optionExplanations: HGPRT normally consumes PRPP to salvage bases. Without HGPRT, PRPP (the activator/substrate of the committed step) accumulates. Simultaneously, the lack of salvaged IMP and GMP removes the natural 'brakes' (feedback inhibition) on the de novo pathway.
Hypoxanthine and guanine are not activators; their failure to be salvaged leads to their degradation into uric acid, but the regulatory change happens at the nucleotide level.
The regulation of the amidotransferase is based on allosteric inhibition and substrate availability (PRPP), not the proteolytic degradation of the enzyme itself.
Uric acid is the end product of degradation and is metabolic 'waste'; it does not activate PRPP synthetase. Purine nucleotides themselves inhibit the synthetase.
While PRPP is used in both, the increase in purine synthesis is due to lack of inhibition and increased substrate concentration within the purine pathway itself, not a 'diversion' from pyrimidines.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): The lack of this salvage pathway causes increased PRPP levels and decreased IMP and GMP levels. As a result, glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase... has excess substrate and decreased inhibitors available, and de novo purine synthesis is increased.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: Unlike the purine ring which remains intact in humans, the pyrimidine ring is cleaved and degraded into highly soluble metabolites. Which of the following is a primary end product of pyrimidine degradation?
options: Beta-aminoisobutyrate
Hypoxanthine
Uric acid
Xanthine
Allantoin
correctOption: Beta-aminoisobutyrate
optionExplanations: Pyrimidines (cytosine, uracil, and thymine) are degraded into the highly soluble amino acids beta-alanine and beta-aminoisobutyrate.
Hypoxanthine is a purine base that is either salvaged or oxidized to xanthine in the purine degradation pathway.
Uric acid is the final product of purine degradation in humans, resulting from the oxidation of xanthine and hypoxanthine.
Xanthine is an intermediate in the purine degradation pathway, which is eventually converted to uric acid by xanthine oxidase.
Allantoin is produced from uric acid in non-primate mammals that possess the enzyme urate oxidase, which humans lack.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 304 (Book Page): Unlike the purine ring, which is not cleaved human cells, the pyrimidine ring is opened and degraded to highly soluble products, β-alanine and β-aminoisobutyrate, with the production of NH3 and CO2.

category: Interpret Orotic aciduria in relevance to nucleotides and urea
statement: Which of the following molecules provides both a carbon and a nitrogen atom for the de novo construction of the pyrimidine ring before it is attached to the ribose 5-phosphate moiety?
options: Aspartic acid
N10-formyltetrahydrofolate
Glycine
Ammonia
Arginine
correctOption: Aspartic acid
optionExplanations: Aspartic acid provides multiple atoms to the pyrimidine ring (C4, C5, C6, and N1). It is an essential building block that reacts with carbamoyl phosphate.
N10-formyltetrahydrofolate is a one-carbon donor used exclusively in purine synthesis (for C2 and C8); pyrimidines do not use folate derivatives until the dUMP to dTMP conversion stage.
Glycine is a major precursor for the purine ring, providing carbons 4 and 5 and nitrogen 7, but it is not utilized in the synthesis of the pyrimidine ring.
Ammonia is the nitrogen source for carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) in the urea cycle, but pyrimidine synthesis via CPS II specifically uses the amide group of glutamine.

Arginine is an intermediate of the urea cycle and a product of the urea cycle in some tissues, but it is not a direct substrate for the de novo pyrimidine biosynthetic pathway enzymes like CAD or UMP synthase.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): [Note: Glutamine and aspartic acid are thus required for both purine and pyrimidine synthesis.] ... The sources of the atoms in the pyrimidine ring are glutamine, CO 2 , and aspartic acid (Figure 22.19).

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
coreConcept: Hydroxyurea Clinical Impact on DNA Substrates
statement: A 55-year-old male with chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is initiated on hydroxyurea therapy. After three weeks, his laboratory results show a significant decrease in his leukocyte count, but he also develops a macrocytic anemia and mild neutropenia. Which of the following biochemical changes in the patient's hematopoietic cells is the most direct cause of the therapeutic effect of this drug?
options: Inhibition of the methylation of deoxyuridine monophosphate
Covalent binding of the drug to thymidylate synthase
Depletion of the intracellular pools of deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates
Accumulation of ribonucleoside triphosphates in the cytosol
Increased production of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) in myeloid precursors
correctOption: Depletion of the intracellular pools of deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates
optionExplanations: Inhibition of dUMP methylation is the mechanism of methotrexate or 5-fluorouracil, not hydroxyurea.
Hydroxyurea is not a suicide inhibitor of thymidylate synthase; that description applies to 5-fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate (5-FdUMP).
By inhibiting ribonucleotide reductase, hydroxyurea prevents the conversion of NDPs to dNDPs, depleting the substrates required for DNA replication, which is the goal in treating CML.
Inhibiting RNR leads to a lack of deoxyribonucleotides, but it does not necessarily cause a significant or therapeutically relevant accumulation of ribonucleoside triphosphates.
While hydroxyurea increases HbF, this is its mechanism for treating sickle cell disease, not the primary mechanism for its anti-leukemic effect in CML.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 298 (Book Page): Hydroxyurea destroys the free radical required for enzymic activity of ribonucleotide reductase, and thus inhibits the generation of substrates for DNA synthesis.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: Which of the following describes a key enzymatic difference between base-specific nucleoside monophosphate kinases and nucleoside diphosphate kinase?
options: Diphosphate kinase is only found in the liver, while monophosphate kinases are ubiquitous.
Monophosphate kinases use GTP as the phosphate donor, while diphosphate kinase uses ATP.
Monophosphate kinases only act on deoxyribose sugars, while diphosphate kinase acts on ribose sugars.
Only monophosphate kinases are inhibited by mycophenolic acid.
Monophosphate kinases are specific for the nitrogenous base, while diphosphate kinase has broad specificity.
correctOption: Monophosphate kinases are specific for the nitrogenous base, while diphosphate kinase has broad specificity.
optionExplanations: Both enzymes are widely distributed in various tissues to ensure local availability of nucleotides for synthesis.
ATP is generally the source of the transferred phosphate for both types of kinases because it is present in higher concentrations than other triphosphates.
Neither kinase discriminates between ribose and deoxyribose in their substrates; both are active on both types of sugars.
Mycophenolic acid inhibits IMP dehydrogenase; it does not inhibit either the monophosphate or diphosphate kinases.

Nucleoside monophosphate kinases (like adenylate kinase or guanylate kinase) are specific to the base (A or G). In contrast, nucleoside diphosphate kinase can transfer phosphates between almost any NDP and NTP regardless of the base.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): Nucleoside diphosphates and triphosphates are interconverted by nucleoside diphosphate kinase—an enzyme that, unlike the monophosphate kinases, has broad specificity.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: Unlike the purine ring which is excreted as uric acid, the pyrimidine ring is uniquely degraded into which of the following pairs of highly soluble products?
options: Urea and Ammonia
Orotic acid and UMP
Allantoin and CO2
Xanthine and Hypoxanthine
Beta-alanine and Beta-aminoisobutyrate
correctOption: Beta-alanine and Beta-aminoisobutyrate
optionExplanations: While NH3 and CO2 are produced (which can form urea), the specific ring-cleavage carbon skeletons are beta-amino acids.
Orotic acid and UMP are intermediates in the synthesis (de novo pathway) of pyrimidines, not their final degradation products.
Allantoin is the degradation product of uric acid in non-primate mammals; it is not related to pyrimidine ring cleavage.
Xanthine and hypoxanthine are intermediates in purine degradation, not pyrimidine degradation.
The pyrimidine ring is fully opened. Uracil and cytosine yield beta-alanine, while thymine yields beta-aminoisobutyrate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 304 (Book Page): Unlike the purine ring, which is not cleaved in human cells, the pyrimidine ring is opened and degraded to highly soluble products, beta-alanine and beta-aminoisobutyrate, with the production of NH3 and CO2.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: How does the drug Allopurinol reduce the rate of de novo purine synthesis in patients with functional HGPRT?
options: By directly inhibiting the enzyme PRPP synthetase.
By increasing the renal excretion of PRPP, making it unavailable for the amidotransferase.
By acting as a structural analog of Glycine to competitively inhibit the third step of the pathway.
By causing the accumulation of hypoxanthine, which is salvaged to IMP, subsequently inhibiting the committed step.
By irreversibly binding to the ATP-binding site of glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase.
correctOption: By causing the accumulation of hypoxanthine, which is salvaged to IMP, subsequently inhibiting the committed step.
optionExplanations: Allopurinol does not directly inhibit PRPP synthetase; its primary target is xanthine oxidase.
PRPP is an intracellular intermediate and is not excreted by the kidneys; uricosuric agents like probenecid affect uric acid excretion, not PRPP.
Allopurinol is a structural analog of hypoxanthine, not glycine, and it does not interfere with glycine incorporation into the purine ring.

Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, leading to increased levels of hypoxanthine. Hypoxanthine is salvaged by HGPRT to IMP, which consumes PRPP and provides feedback inhibition to the amidotransferase, thus slowing the de novo pathway.
While the end products (IMP/AMP/GMP) inhibit the amidotransferase, allopurinol itself does not bind to this enzyme; the effect is mediated via the salvaged nucleotides.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): In patients with normal levels of HGPRT, the hypoxanthine can be salvaged, thus reducing the levels of PRPP and, therefore, de novo purine synthesis.

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
statement: A 40-year-old male who recently underwent a liver transplant is prescribed a medication that acts as a reversible, uncompetitive inhibitor of inosine monophosphate (IMP) dehydrogenase. Which of the following is the most likely clinical goal of this pharmacological intervention?
options: Selective inhibition of DNA synthesis in pathogenic bacteria.
Prevention of the immune system from attacking the transplanted organ.
Destruction of free radicals required for ribonucleotide reductase activity.
Treatment of megaloblastic anemia caused by UMP synthase deficiency.
Reduction of hyperuricemia and prevention of gouty arthritis.
correctOption: Prevention of the immune system from attacking the transplanted organ.
optionExplanations: Selective inhibition of bacterial synthesis is the role of sulfonamides or trimethoprim, whereas mycophenolic acid targets human enzymes.
Mycophenolic acid is an immunosuppressant that prevents graft rejection by inhibiting IMP dehydrogenase, selectively limiting the guanine nucleotide pool in T and B cells.
Hydroxyurea is the drug that destroys the free radical required for the enzymatic activity of ribonucleotide reductase, not mycophenolic acid.
Megaloblastic anemia in UMP synthase deficiency (orotic aciduria) is treated with uridine, which bypasses the metabolic block.
Reduction of hyperuricemia is achieved with xanthine oxidase inhibitors like allopurinol, not IMP dehydrogenase inhibitors.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): The drug [Mycophenolic acid] is an immunosuppressant used to prevent graft rejection.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
coreConcept: Mechanism of Sulfonamides in the context of folate/purine synthesis
statement: How do sulfonamides specifically interfere with the production of purines in bacteria without affecting human purine synthesis?
options: They inhibit the amination of UTP to CTP in bacterial cells only.
They inhibit the human enzyme dihydrofolate reductase.
They prevent the salvage of preformed dietary purine bases in the gut.
They act as irreversible suicide inhibitors of xanthine oxidase.
They are structural analogs of PABA that inhibit bacterial folic acid synthesis.
correctOption: They are structural analogs of PABA that inhibit bacterial folic acid synthesis.
optionExplanations: The conversion of UTP to CTP is a pyrimidine synthesis step (catalyzed by CTP synthetase) and is not the target of sulfonamides.
Dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by methotrexate, not sulfonamides. Methotrexate affects both human and bacterial cells (though humans are the primary target in cancer therapy).
Sulfonamides target de novo synthesis pathways via folate depletion, not the salvage of dietary bases in the intestinal mucosa.
Allopurinol is the inhibitor of xanthine oxidase. Sulfonamides do not target this enzyme of purine degradation.

Sulfonamides compete with PABA in the bacterial synthesis of folic acid. Since humans lack this pathway and ingest folate as a vitamin, their purine synthesis (which requires THF) remains unaffected by sulfa drugs.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page): [Sulfonamides are structural analogs of para-aminobenzoic acid that competitively inhibit bacterial synthesis of folic acid... Humans cannot synthesize folic acid, and must rely on external sources of this vitamin. Therefore, sulfa drugs do not interfere with human purine synthesis.]

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: In the regulation of deoxyribonucleotide synthesis, the drug hydroxyurea is used clinically to treat certain cancers and sickle cell disease. Which of the following describes its mechanism of action regarding nucleotide metabolism?
options: It prevents the reduction of thioredoxin by inhibiting thioredoxin reductase
It irreversibly binds to the catalytic site of thymidylate synthase as a suicide inhibitor
It competitively inhibits the binding of dATP to the activity site of ribonucleotide reductase
It destroys the free radical required for the enzymatic activity of ribonucleotide reductase
It acts as a structural analog of folic acid to inhibit dihydrofolate reductase
correctOption: It destroys the free radical required for the enzymatic activity of ribonucleotide reductase
optionExplanations: While thioredoxin is the electron donor for RNR, hydroxyurea does not target thioredoxin reductase; it targets RNR directly.
5-fluorouracil (converted to 5-FdUMP) is the suicide inhibitor of thymidylate synthase, not hydroxyurea.
dATP is a natural allosteric inhibitor that binds to the activity site. Hydroxyurea does not mimic this binding; it acts on the catalytic mechanism itself by targeting the required free radical.

Ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) requires a tyrosyl free radical (usually on the R2 subunit) for its mechanism of reducing ribonucleoside diphosphates. Hydroxyurea quenches this radical, effectively halting the production of deoxyribonucleotides (dADP, dGDP, dCDP, dUDP).
Methotrexate is the drug that acts as a structural analog of folic acid to inhibit dihydrofolate reductase.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 298 (Book Page): The drug hydroxyurea destroys the free radical required for enzymic activity of ribonucleotide reductase, and thus inhibits the generation of substrates for DNA synthesis.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
coreConcept: Feedback inhibition and substrate regulation of purine synthesis
statement: During the de novo synthesis of purine nucleotides, the reaction catalyzed by glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase serves as the committed step. How is this enzyme primarily regulated within the cellular environment?
options: Inhibited by both AMP and GMP and controlled by PRPP concentration
Activated by AMP and inhibited by high concentrations of PRPP
Inhibited by inorganic phosphate and activated by GMP
Stimulated by high levels of IMP and inhibited by glycine
Activated by ATP and inhibited by fumarate levels
correctOption: Inhibited by both AMP and GMP and controlled by PRPP concentration
optionExplanations: The enzyme is subject to feedback inhibition by its distal end-products (AMP and GMP) and its rate is sensitive to the availability of its substrate, PRPP, which is usually below the enzyme's Km.
The enzyme is inhibited by AMP, not activated, and it is activated by PRPP, not inhibited.
Inorganic phosphate is an activator of PRPP synthetase, not an inhibitor of the amidotransferase; GMP is a feedback inhibitor, not an activator.
IMP is the parent nucleotide produced later in the pathway; glycine is a substrate but not a primary regulatory inhibitor for this specific enzyme.
ATP is not the primary activator of this step; fumarate is a byproduct of later steps (adenylosuccinate lyase) and does not regulate this committed step.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): The enzyme, glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase, is inhibited by the purine 5'-nucleotides AMP and GMP—the end products of the pathway. This is the committed step in purine nucleotide biosynthesis. The rate of the reaction is also controlled by the intracellular concentration of PRPP.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
coreConcept: Enzymatic steps in AMP synthesis from IMP
statement: A researcher studying purine synthesis discovers a mutation in adenylosuccinate lyase. In a cell line carrying this mutation, which of the following metabolic outcomes is most likely during the attempt to synthesize AMP from the parent nucleotide IMP?
options: Inability to release fumarate and failure to form AMP
Accumulation of XMP and depletion of ATP
Rapid conversion of IMP to uric acid via xanthine oxidase
Activation of the amidotransferase step due to low IMP
Excessive production of glutamate from glutamine
correctOption: Inability to release fumarate and failure to form AMP
optionExplanations: Adenylosuccinate lyase (also called adenylosuccinase) is responsible for cleaving adenylosuccinate to produce AMP and fumarate. A mutation here prevents both the release of fumarate and the formation of AMP.
XMP is an intermediate in the GMP branch; a defect in the AMP branch (adenylosuccinate lyase) would not directly cause XMP accumulation.

While IMP might be degraded if it cannot be converted to AMP, the direct biochemical result of this specific enzyme failure is the accumulation of adenylosuccinate, not immediate uric acid production.
A block at adenylosuccinate lyase would likely cause an accumulation of IMP or its precursors, which would inhibit, rather than activate, the amidotransferase step via feedback.
Glutamate production is associated with the GMP branch (XMP to GMP), which uses glutamine. This is unaffected by adenylosuccinate lyase deficiency.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page) / 531: Figure 22.8 shows Adenylosuccinate is converted to AMP by Adenylosuccinase (Adenylosuccinate lyase), releasing Fumarate.

category: Interpret the Lesh-Nhyan syndrome
statement: Which enzyme deficiency is the underlying biochemical cause of the hyperuricemia and neurological symptoms in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?
options: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase
Xanthine oxidase
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase
Adenosine deaminase
correctOption: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase
optionExplanations: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT) is involved in salvaging adenine to AMP; its deficiency does not cause Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency causes a rare immunodeficiency affecting primarily T-cells, distinct from the Lesch-Nyhan phenotype.
Xanthine oxidase is the enzyme that *produces* uric acid; its inhibition (by allopurinol) is a treatment for gout, not a cause of Lesch-Nyhan.

Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) is the specific enzyme that, when deficient, leads to the accumulation of uric acid and the characteristic neurological symptoms of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.
Adenosine deaminase deficiency leads to Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID), not the hyperuricemia and self-mutilation of Lesch-Nyhan.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): This syndrome is a rare, X-linked, recessive disorder associated with a virtually complete deficiency of HGPRT.

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: A 54-year-old male presents with sudden, agonizing pain and swelling in his first metatarsophalangeal joint. Arthrocentesis is performed to confirm the suspected diagnosis. Which of the following findings in the synovial fluid would definitively establish a diagnosis of gout?
options: Elevated concentrations of hypoxanthine and xanthine
Positively birefringent rhomboid-shaped crystals
Negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals
Presence of allantoin crystals within neutrophils
High levels of uric acid without crystal visualization
correctOption: Negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals
optionExplanations: While hypoxanthine and xanthine are precursors, their elevation is seen in xanthine oxidase inhibition (e.g., allopurinol therapy) rather than as a diagnostic hallmark of acute gout.
Positively birefringent rhomboid crystals are characteristic of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout), not gout.
Gout is definitively diagnosed by identifying monosodium urate crystals, which appear needle-shaped and show negative birefringence under polarized light.
Humans do not produce allantoin as they lack urate oxidase; this is a characteristic of other mammals.
Hyperuricemia is often asymptomatic and does not confirm gout; the diagnosis requires the identification of crystals in synovial fluid.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 299 (Book Page): The definitive diagnosis of gout requires aspiration and examination of synovial fluid (Figure 22.17) from an affected joint (or material from a tophus) using polarized light microscopy to confirm the presence of needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals (Figure 22.18).

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: The substrate specificity of ribonucleotide reductase is complex. Binding of deoxythymidine triphosphate (dTTP) to the substrate specificity site results in which of the following enzymatic shifts?
options: Stimulation of the reduction of UDP to dUDP
Activation of the reduction of GDP to dGDP
Inhibition of the reduction of all purines and pyrimidines
Induction of the degradation of the R2 subunit dimer
Enhancement of the affinity for ribonucleoside triphosphates
correctOption: Activation of the reduction of GDP to dGDP
optionExplanations: The text explicitly links dTTP binding to GDP reduction, not UDP reduction, as part of the balanced synthesis model.

Correct. The binding of dTTP at the specificity site specifically promotes the reduction of GDP, ensuring that as thymidine levels rise, guanine deoxyribonucleotides are also produced to maintain balance.
dTTP binding to the specificity site does not shut down the enzyme; that is the role of dATP at the activity site.
dTTP is a regulatory ligand; it does not cause the structural degradation of the enzyme subunits.

Ribonucleotide reductase uses diphosphates (NDPs) at its catalytic site, not triphosphates; the specificity site binds triphosphates only for regulation, not for increasing substrate affinity for triphosphates.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 298 (Book Page): For example, deoxythymidine triphosphate (dTTP) binding at the specificity sites causes a conformational change that allows reduction of GDP to dGDP at the catalytic site.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: A 55-year-old patient with colorectal cancer is prescribed 5-fluorouracil. This drug is converted to 5-FdUMP, which acts as a 'suicide inhibitor' to block the synthesis of dTMP. Which enzyme is the direct target of 5-FdUMP?
options: Ribonucleotide reductase
Dihydrofolate reductase
UMP synthase
CTP synthetase
Thymidylate synthase
correctOption: Thymidylate synthase
optionExplanations: Ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited by hydroxyurea and dATP; it is not the target for 5-fluorouracil metabolites.
Dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by methotrexate, which starves the cell of THF, but it is not the direct target of 5-FdUMP.
UMP synthase is involved in de novo UMP production; it is upstream of the reaction targeted by 5-fluorouracil.
CTP synthetase converts UTP to CTP; it is not affected by 5-fluorouracil or its metabolites.
5-FdUMP binds covalently to thymidylate synthase and its cofactor, permanently inactivating the enzyme and preventing the methylation of dUMP to dTMP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): 5-Fluorouracil is metabolically converted to 5-FdUMP, which becomes permanently bound to the inactivated thymidylate synthase; for this reason, the drug is called a 'suicide' inhibitor.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for the conversion of Guanosine Monophosphate (GMP) to Guanosine Diphosphate (GDP)?
options: Xanthine oxidase
Nucleoside diphosphate kinase
Guanylate kinase
Adenylate kinase
AMP deaminase
correctOption: Guanylate kinase
optionExplanations: Xanthine oxidase is a degradative enzyme that converts hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid; it is not a kinase.
Nucleoside diphosphate kinase acts on diphosphates (like GDP) to form triphosphates (like GTP); it does not act on monophosphates.
Guanylate kinase is the base-specific monophosphate kinase that phosphorylates GMP to GDP using ATP as the phosphate donor.
Adenylate kinase is base-specific for adenine nucleotides (AMP); it does not act on GMP.
AMP deaminase converts AMP to IMP by removing an amino group; it is part of the purine degradation or cycle pathway, not a phosphorylation step.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): Nucleoside diphosphates are synthesized from the corresponding nucleoside monophosphates by base-specific nucleoside monophosphate kinases (Figure 22.9). [Figure 22.9 specifically shows: GMP + ATP --(Guanylate kinase)--> GDP + ADP].

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
coreConcept: Secondary Gout in von Gierke Disease
statement: A 45-year-old male with a history of Type I glycogen storage disease (von Gierke disease) presents with excruciating pain and swelling in the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Laboratory findings show lactic acidosis and hyperuricemia. What is the metabolic explanation for the hyperuricemia in this specific patient?
options: Lactic acid increases the solubility of monosodium urate, leading to faster crystal deposition.
Lactate and urate compete for the same renal secretory transporter, reducing uric acid excretion.
Lactate competitively inhibits the xanthine oxidase enzyme in the liver.
Glycogen accumulation in the kidney directly blocks the physical passage of uric acid through the ureters.
High lactate levels stimulate the salvage of guanine back into the de novo pathway.
correctOption: Lactate and urate compete for the same renal secretory transporter, reducing uric acid excretion.
optionExplanations: Lactic acid does not increase the solubility of urate; in fact, lower pH can decrease the solubility of uric acid, but the primary clinical mechanism here is renal handling.

In von Gierke disease, glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency leads to hypoglycemia and compensatory lactic acidosis. In the kidneys, lactate competes with uric acid for the same organic acid secretory transporters. This results in the underexcretion of uric acid, leading to hyperuricemia and secondary gout.
Lactate does not inhibit xanthine oxidase; xanthine oxidase inhibition would actually decrease uric acid production.
The mechanism is biochemical and transporter-based in the nephron, not a mechanical obstruction by glycogen in the ureters.
Lactate does not stimulate purine salvage; salvage is primarily regulated by the availability of PRPP and free bases.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 299 (Book Page): Underexcretion can be primary... or secondary to known disease processes that affect how the kidney handles urate, for example lactic acidosis (lactate and urate compete for the same renal transporter).

category: Interpret the role of synthetic analogues of nucleotides in medicine based on sign/symptoms and data e
statement: In patients with Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency, the accumulation of specific metabolites leads to severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). What is the intermediate mechanism that prevents lymphocyte proliferation in these individuals?
options: Elevated dATP levels allosterically inhibit ribonucleotide reductase, stalling DNA synthesis.
High levels of hypoxanthine lead to the competitive inhibition of thymidylate synthase.
ADA deficiency prevents the conversion of IMP to AMP, causing adenine starvation.
Accumulated uric acid crystals cause apoptosis of T-cell precursors in the bone marrow.
Excess adenosine directly inhibits the phosphorylation of PRPP.
correctOption: Elevated dATP levels allosterically inhibit ribonucleotide reductase, stalling DNA synthesis.
optionExplanations: ADA deficiency causes adenosine and deoxyadenosine to accumulate. Cellular kinases convert deoxyadenosine to dATP. High dATP binds to the 'activity site' of ribonucleotide reductase, inhibiting the production of all other dNTPs, which halts DNA replication.
Hypoxanthine is a normal intermediate and does not inhibit thymidylate synthase; 5-FU and methotrexate are the typical inhibitors discussed for that enzyme.
ADA is involved in the degradation of adenosine/AMP to inosine/IMP, not the reverse synthesis pathway.
While ADA deficiency affects purine degradation, the immunodeficiency is caused by dNTP depletion, not uric acid crystal inflammation (gout).
Adenosine does not directly inhibit PRPP synthetase; the toxicity is mediated through its deoxy-form, dATP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): As dATP levels rise, ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited, thus preventing the production of all deoxyribose-containing nucleotides (see Page 289 (Book Page)). ... Page 297 (Book Page): The binding of dATP to allosteric sites (known as the activity sites) on the enzyme inhibits the overall catalytic activity.

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: Ribonucleotide reductase demonstrates a broad substrate range, allowing it to process both purine and pyrimidine precursors. Which specific set of molecules serves as the direct substrates for this enzyme in humans?
options: Adenosine, Guanosine, Cytidine, and Uridine
ADP, GDP, CDP, and UDP
ATP, GTP, CTP, and UTP
AMP, GMP, CMP, and UMP
dAMP, dGMP, dCMP, and dTMP
correctOption: ADP, GDP, CDP, and UDP
optionExplanations: These are nucleosides (base + sugar), which lack the phosphate groups required for recognition and processing by ribonucleotide reductase.
The enzyme is formally known as ribonucleoside diphosphate reductase because it specifically reduces the 2'-OH of the diphosphate forms of A, G, C, and U.
Nucleoside triphosphates serve as allosteric regulators (binding to specificity or activity sites) but they are not the substrates that are reduced by the enzyme.
Nucleoside monophosphates must first be phosphorylated to diphosphates by kinases before they can be acted upon by ribonucleotide reductase.
These are the deoxyribonucleoside monophosphates, which are products/downstream metabolites, not the substrates of the reduction reaction.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 297 (Book Page): specific for the reduction of purine nucleoside diphosphates (ADP and GDP), and pyrimidine nucleoside diphosphates, cytidine diphosphate (CDP) and uridine diphosphate (UDP)

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: During the reduction of a ribonucleoside diphosphate, which specific chemical change occurs within the active site of the ribonucleotide reductase enzyme itself before it is regenerated?
options: A phosphate group is transferred from ATP to a serine residue on the R1 subunit.
The enzyme's two sulfhydryl groups are oxidized to form a disulfide bond.
The tyrosyl free radical is permanently consumed and must be replaced.
The enzyme's two sulfhydryl groups are reduced to form a disulfide bond.
A hydroxyl group is transferred from the substrate to an aspartate residue.
correctOption: The enzyme's two sulfhydryl groups are oxidized to form a disulfide bond.
optionExplanations: The reaction mechanism involves redox chemistry and free radicals, not phosphorylation of the enzyme structure.

The enzyme provides reducing equivalents from its own cysteine-derived sulfhydryl groups. In giving up these hydrogens to the ribose sugar, the sulfhydryls become oxidized and form a disulfide bridge.
The tyrosyl free radical is essential for the reaction but is not 'consumed' like a substrate; however, it can be destroyed by drugs like hydroxyurea.
The sulfhydryl groups start in the reduced state and donate hydrogens; they are not 'reduced' to form a bond; they are oxidized.
The hydroxyl group of the ribose is reduced to a hydrogen; it is not transferred as a whole group to the enzyme's amino acids.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 297 (Book Page): The immediate donors of the hydrogen atoms needed for the reduction of the 2'-hydroxyl group are two sulfhydryl groups on the enzyme itself, which, during the reaction, form a disulfide bond

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
coreConcept: Biochemical mechanism of Sulfonamides as PABA analogs
statement: A patient with a severe bacterial infection is treated with a combination of drugs that include sulfonamides. Which of the following best describes the specific biochemical step inhibited by these PABA analogs?
options: The competitive inhibition of bacterial dihydropteroate synthase to block folic acid assembly.
The uncompetitive inhibition of bacterial IMP dehydrogenase.
The methylation of dUMP to dTMP by thymidylate synthase.
The conversion of IMP to AMP via adenylosuccinate synthetase.
The reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate by dihydrofolate reductase.
correctOption: The competitive inhibition of bacterial dihydropteroate synthase to block folic acid assembly.
optionExplanations: Sulfonamides competitively inhibit the enzyme that incorporates PABA into the folic acid molecule (dihydropteroate synthase), thereby halting the synthesis of the folate precursor needed for purine production.
Mycophenolic acid, not sulfonamides, is the drug that inhibits IMP dehydrogenase (and it is uncompetitive).
This describes the mechanism of 5-Fluorouracil, which is an antitumor drug, not an antimicrobial PABA analog.
The conversion of IMP to AMP requires aspartate and GTP; it is not the target of sulfonamides.
This describes the mechanism of methotrexate (in humans) and trimethoprim (in bacteria), not sulfonamides.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page): Sulfonamides are structural analogs of para-aminobenzoic acid that competitively inhibit bacterial synthesis of folic acid.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: Which enzyme in the purine metabolic pathway is considered the primary 'committed step' and is subject to potent feedback inhibition by AMP and GMP?
options: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase
Xanthine oxidase
Glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase
PRPP synthetase
Adenylosuccinate lyase
correctOption: Glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase
optionExplanations: HGPRT is part of the salvage pathway, which allows the reuse of bases, rather than the de novo synthesis pathway starting from ribose 5-phosphate.
Xanthine oxidase is a degradative enzyme involved in the breakdown of purines to uric acid, not in their synthesis.
The transfer of an amide group from glutamine to PRPP to form phosphoribosylamine is the first step unique to the purine de novo pathway, making it the committed step.
PRPP synthetase provides the substrate for many pathways (purines, pyrimidines, salvage), so it is a regulated step but not the 'committed' step specific to purine de novo synthesis.
Adenylosuccinate lyase occurs much later in the pathway and is not the primary regulatory committed step.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): The enzyme, glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase, is inhibited by the purine 5'-nucleotides AMP and GMP—the end products of the pathway. This is the committed step in purine nucleotide biosynthesis.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: A researcher is studying the cross-regulation of deoxyribonucleotide synthesis. She observes that when deoxythymidine triphosphate (dTTP) levels rise, the reduction of guanosine diphosphate (GDP) to dGDP is enhanced. At which specific site on ribonucleotide reductase is this regulation occurring?
options: Substrate specificity site
Activity site
Disulfide-reduction site
Thioredoxin binding site
Primary catalytic site
correctOption: Substrate specificity site
optionExplanations: Substrate specificity sites are distinct allosteric sites that bind various nucleoside triphosphates to ensure a balanced production of the four different deoxyribonucleotides.
The activity site (where ATP or dATP binds) regulates the overall 'on/off' status of the enzyme, not the specific selection of GDP over other substrates.
The disulfide-reduction involves the cysteine residues on the enzyme but does not regulate substrate choice.
Thioredoxin is a coenzyme donor of hydrogen atoms; its binding does not determine which ribonucleoside diphosphate is reduced.
The catalytic site is where the actual reduction occurs, but the selection of which substrate is reduced is determined at a separate regulatory site.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 298 (Book Page): For example, deoxythymidine triphosphate (dTTP) binding at the specificity sites causes a conformational change that allows reduction of GDP to dGDP at the catalytic site.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: Ribonucleotide reductase is regulated not only by overall activity but also by substrate specificity to ensure a balanced pool of deoxyribonucleotides. The binding of which molecule to the substrate specificity site is required to specifically stimulate the reduction of GDP to dGDP?
options: ATP
dGTP
dATP
dTTP
dCTP
correctOption: dTTP
optionExplanations: ATP binding to the activity site activates the enzyme overall.
dGTP binding to the specificity site typically regulates the reduction of other nucleotides (like ADP to dADP).
dATP binding to the activity site inhibits the overall enzyme activity, regardless of substrate.
Correct. The substrate specificity sites use የተለያዩ nucleoside triphosphates to signal the need for other nucleotides. dTTP specifically induces the enzyme to reduce GDP into dGDP.
dCTP is not the primary regulator mentioned for stimulating GDP reduction in the provided text.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 298 (Book Page): For example, deoxythymidine triphosphate (dTTP) binding at the specificity sites causes a conformational change that allows reduction of GDP to dGDP at the catalytic site.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: The synthesis of carbamoyl phosphate by Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase II (CPS II) is the primary regulated step of pyrimidine biosynthesis. Which of the following best describes its regulatory profile?
options: Activated by N-acetylglutamate and inhibited by CTP
Inhibited by UTP and activated by PRPP
Inhibited by malonate and activated by aspartate
Activated by UTP and inhibited by ATP
Inhibited by inorganic phosphate and activated by AMP
correctOption: Inhibited by UTP and activated by PRPP
optionExplanations: Incorrect. N-acetylglutamate is the essential activator for CPS I (the mitochondrial urea cycle enzyme), while CTP inhibition of aspartate transcarbamoylase is the regulatory step primarily in prokaryotes, not humans.

Correct. CPS II is the cytosolic enzyme for pyrimidine synthesis; it is inhibited by UTP (feedback inhibition) and activated by PRPP (feed-forward activation), ensuring the pathway responds to substrate availability and product levels.
Incorrect. Neither malonate (a TCA cycle inhibitor) nor aspartate (a substrate) serve as the primary allosteric regulators for the CPS II-mediated step.
Incorrect. UTP serves as an end-product inhibitor of the pathway, not an activator, while ATP typically serves as a general energy indicator rather than the specific allosteric regulator for CPS II.
Incorrect. Inorganic phosphate and AMP are more closely associated with the regulation of PRPP synthetase in the purine pathway, not CPS II.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page): [CPS II is inhibited by UTP (the end product of this pathway, which can be converted into the other pyrimidine nucleotides), and is activated by PRPP.]

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: Which of the following classes of compounds serves as the direct substrate for the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase in the synthesis of deoxyribonucleotides?
options: Deoxyribonucleoside monophosphates (dNMPs)
Ribonucleoside triphosphates (NTPs)
Ribonucleoside monophosphates (NMPs)
Ribonucleoside diphosphates (NDPs)
Free purine and pyrimidine bases
correctOption: Ribonucleoside diphosphates (NDPs)
optionExplanations: Deoxyribonucleoside monophosphates are products further down the line (after dephosphorylation) and are not the substrates of the ribonucleotide reductase reaction itself.

Ribonucleoside triphosphates are not the substrates for the reduction reaction; they primarily serve as allosteric regulators (like ATP or dTTP) at the activity or substrate specificity sites of the enzyme.
Ribonucleoside monophosphates are not the substrates for ribonucleotide reductase; they must first be phosphorylated to diphosphates by base-specific kinases before reduction can occur.
Ribonucleotide reductase specifically acts on ribonucleoside diphosphates (ADP, GDP, CDP, and UDP) to reduce the 2'-hydroxyl group, converting them into dADP, dGDP, dCDP, and dUDP respectively.

Free bases are used in salvage pathways (via HGPRT or APRT) but are not directly reduced to deoxy-forms by ribonucleotide reductase, which requires the pentose sugar to be already attached as a diphosphate nucleotide.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 297 (Book Page): Ribonucleotide reductase (ribonucleoside diphosphate reductase) is composed of two nonidentical dimeric subunits, R1 and R2, and is specific for the reduction of purine nucleoside diphosphates (ADP and GDP), and pyrimidine nucleoside diphosphates, cytidine diphosphate (CDP) and uridine diphosphate (UDP) to their deoxy-forms.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: The conversion of Nucleoside Diphosphates (NDPs) to Nucleoside Triphosphates (NTPs), such as GDP to GTP, is catalyzed by which enzyme, characterized by its broad substrate specificity?
options: PRPP synthetase
Ribonucleotide reductase
5'-Nucleotidase
Nucleoside diphosphate kinase
Base-specific monophosphate kinase
correctOption: Nucleoside diphosphate kinase
optionExplanations: PRPP synthetase produces 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate from ATP and ribose 5-phosphate; it is an early step in de novo synthesis, not a terminal phosphorylation step.
Ribonucleotide reductase converts ribonucleoside diphosphates (NDPs) to deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs); it does not add phosphate groups.
5'-Nucleotidase is a degradative enzyme that removes the phosphate group from nucleotides to form nucleosides; it is the reverse of a kinase.

Nucleoside diphosphate kinase is the enzyme responsible for the final phosphorylation step to create triphosphates. Unlike monophosphate kinases, it can use any NDP (ribo or deoxyribo) and any NTP (usually ATP) as substrates.
Monophosphate kinases (like adenylate or guanylate kinase) are base-specific and only convert monophosphates to diphosphates.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): Nucleoside diphosphates and triphosphates are interconverted by nucleoside diphosphate kinase—an enzyme that, unlike the monophosphate kinases, has broad specificity.

category: Interpret Orotic aciduria in relevance to nucleotides and urea
coreConcept: Diagnostic Contrast: Urea Cycle vs. Pyrimidine Synthesis
statement: Which biochemical laboratory finding is most critical for distinguishing orotic aciduria caused by a urea cycle defect from that caused by UMP synthase deficiency?
options: Serum Vitamin B12 levels
Urinary β-alanine levels
Blood ammonia levels
Urinary orotic acid levels
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)
correctOption: Blood ammonia levels
optionExplanations: Vitamin B12 levels are usually normal in both conditions, as the megaloblastic anemia in UMP synthase deficiency is specifically due to a pyrimidine shortage, not a B12 or folate deficiency.
β-alanine is a degradation product of pyrimidines; its levels might be altered but do not serve as a primary diagnostic discriminator between the two genetic defects.

Hyperammonemia is a hallmark of urea cycle defects like OTC deficiency because ammonia cannot be processed into urea; UMP synthase deficiency affects only the pyrimidine pathway and presents with normal ammonia.
Urinary orotic acid is elevated in both ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency (urea cycle) and UMP synthase deficiency (pyrimidine pathway), so it cannot distinguish them.
An increased MCV (macrocytosis) is typical of the megaloblastic anemia seen in UMP synthase deficiency, but it does not rule out other causes of orotic aciduria or anemia.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 306 (Book Page) / 531: Blood ammonia level would expected to be elevated in ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency but not in UMP synthase deficiency.

category: Interpret the Lesh-Nhyan syndrome
statement: An elite researcher is studying the metabolic profile of a patient with an X-linked deficiency of HGPRT. The researcher notes that while salvage of certain purines is completely halted, the salvage of adenine remains entirely normal. This observation correctly excludes a deficiency in which of the following enzymes, and why?
options: Xanthine oxidase; because it is responsible for degradation rather than salvage
Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase; because it is a separate enzyme that salvages adenine using PRPP
Nucleoside diphosphate kinase; because it is non-specific for the base type
Adenosine deaminase; because it only acts on nucleosides, not free bases
PRPP synthetase; because its absence would prevent the synthesis of any purines at all
correctOption: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase; because it is a separate enzyme that salvages adenine using PRPP
optionExplanations: Xanthine oxidase converts hypoxanthine to xanthine and then to uric acid; it is not a salvage enzyme and does not use PRPP to create nucleotides from bases.
Lesch-Nyhan is a deficiency of HGPRT only. Adenine is salvaged by APRT, a distinct enzyme. Normal adenine salvage confirms that APRT is functional, pinpointing HGPRT as the isolated defect.
Nucleoside diphosphate kinase interconverts diphosphates and triphosphates; it acts much later in the pathway and is not responsible for the initial salvage of free purine bases.
Adenosine deaminase (ADA) converts adenosine to inosine; while relevant to purine metabolism, it is not the enzyme that salvages the free base adenine.
PRPP synthetase produces the substrate for both enzymes; if it were deficient, both HGPRT and APRT salvage would be impaired due to lack of PRPP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): Two enzymes are involved: adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT) and hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). Both enzymes use PRPP as the source of the ribose 5-phosphate group.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: In the de novo synthesis of pyrimidines, most enzymes are located in the cytosol. However, one specific enzyme is localized to the inner mitochondrial membrane. Which enzyme is this?
options: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase
Orotidylate decarboxylase
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II
Aspartate transcarbamoylase
correctOption: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
optionExplanations: Correct. As stated in the text, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is the only enzyme of the pyrimidine de novo pathway that is not cytosolic, being located on the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase is a cytosolic domain of the bifunctional enzyme UMP synthase.
Orotidylate decarboxylase is also a cytosolic domain of the UMP synthase enzyme, responsible for converting OMP to UMP.
CPS II is located in the cytosol and is part of the multifunctional CAD protein in eukaryotes.
Aspartate transcarbamoylase is the second domain of the cytosolic CAD protein.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page): The enzyme that produces orotate, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, is associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane. All other enzymes in pyrimidine biosynthesis are cytosolic.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: A 14-month-old child presents with failure to thrive, severe lethargy, and a laboratory-confirmed megaloblastic anemia that is unresponsive to vitamin B12 and folate supplementation. Urinalysis reveals white crystalline precipitate. Which pharmacological intervention is most appropriate for this patient?
options: Allopurinol
5-Fluorouracil
Adenosine deaminase
Hypoxanthine
Uridine
correctOption: Uridine
optionExplanations: Allopurinol is an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase used to treat gout; it would not address the pyrimidine deficiency causing megaloblastic anemia in this child.
5-Fluorouracil is a chemotherapy agent that inhibits thymidylate synthase; it would exacerbate the patient's condition by further inhibiting DNA synthesis.
Adenosine deaminase is an enzyme of purine metabolism; its deficiency causes SCID, which presents differently (immunodeficiency) than the megaloblastic anemia seen here.
Hypoxanthine is a purine base used in the purine salvage pathway; it cannot be converted into pyrimidines and thus cannot alleviate symptoms of orotic aciduria.

Uridine is a pyrimidine nucleoside that can be salvaged into UMP. This bypasses the defective UMP synthase, provides the necessary pyrimidines for DNA/RNA synthesis, and reduces orotic acid production via feedback inhibition of CPS II.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Administration of uridine results in improvement of the anemia and decreased excretion of orotate.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: A biochemistry student is mapping the cellular locations of enzymes involved in nucleotide biosynthesis. She notes that while most enzymes of the pyrimidine pathway are cytosolic, one specific enzyme is uniquely associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane. Which enzyme is she identifying?
options: Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II
Thymidylate synthase
Aspartate transcarbamoylase
correctOption: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
optionExplanations: Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase is a domain of UMP synthase, which is located in the cytosol.
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, which oxidizes dihydroorotate to orotate, is the only pyrimidine synthesis enzyme located on the inner mitochondrial membrane.
CPS II is part of the CAD complex and is located in the cytosol.
Thymidylate synthase is a cytosolic enzyme responsible for the synthesis of dTMP.
Aspartate transcarbamoylase is part of the CAD complex and is located in the cytosol.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): The enzyme that produces orotate, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, is associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane. All other enzymes in pyrimidine biosynthesis are cytosolic.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: A 4-year-old boy presents with cognitive impairment, spasticity, and a history of repetitive lip-biting and finger-chewing. Laboratory analysis reveals significant hyperuricemia. Which mechanistic change in the purine pathway best explains the increased de novo synthesis observed in this patient?
options: Increased inhibition of glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase by GMP.
Defective conversion of IMP to AMP due to adenylosuccinate lyase deficiency.
Accumulation of PRPP due to failure of the salvage pathway enzymes.
Enhanced conversion of xanthine to uric acid by xanthine oxidase.
Decreased intracellular levels of phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP).
correctOption: Accumulation of PRPP due to failure of the salvage pathway enzymes.
optionExplanations: In Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, the failure to salvage bases results in decreased levels of GMP and IMP, meaning there is less (not more) feedback inhibition of the de novo pathway.
Adenylosuccinate lyase deficiency is a separate metabolic disorder and does not explain the characteristic self-mutilation and salvage failure of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.
HGPRT deficiency prevents the consumption of PRPP in salvage. Elevated PRPP then acts as a substrate-level activator for glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase, the committed step of de novo synthesis.
While uric acid is high, the 'increased de novo synthesis' is caused by upstream PRPP accumulation, not by the kinetics of xanthine oxidase.
PRPP levels actually increase because it is not being consumed by the HGPRT-mediated salvage pathway.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): This deficiency results in an inability to salvage hypoxanthine or guanine... In addition, the lack of this salvage pathway causes increased PRPP levels and decreased IMP and GMP levels. As a result, glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase... has excess substrate and decreased inhibitors available, and de novo purine synthesis is increased.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: Which amino acid provides carbons 4 and 5, as well as nitrogen 7, to the purine ring during the de novo biosynthetic pathway?
options: Glutamate
Leucine
Glutamine
Glycine
Aspartic acid
correctOption: Glycine
optionExplanations: Glutamate is a product of the amidotransferase reaction (when glutamine donates its nitrogen) but does not directly donate atoms to the purine ring structure.
Leucine is a ketogenic amino acid and does not participate in the synthesis of the purine ring atoms described in the metabolic pathway.
Glutamine contributes the nitrogen atoms at positions 3 and 9 of the purine ring, not the carbon skeleton.
Glycine is unique in the purine synthesis pathway as it is incorporated as a whole molecule, contributing carbons 4 and 5 and nitrogen 7.
Aspartic acid (aspartate) provides only the nitrogen at position 1 of the purine ring.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 292 (Book Page): The atoms of the purine ring are contributed by a number of compounds, including amino acids (aspartic acid, glycine, and glutamine), CO 2 , and N 10 –formyltetrahydrofolate (Figure 22.5).

category: Interpret the role of synthetic analogues of nucleotides in medicine based on sign/symptoms and data e
statement: Structural analogs of folic acid are commonly used in oncology to limit the spread of cancer. Which of the following drugs is a folate analog that interferes with nucleotide synthesis by inhibiting the reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate?
options: Hydroxyurea
Methotrexate
Allopurinol
Mycophenolic acid
Sulfonamide
correctOption: Methotrexate
optionExplanations: Hydroxyurea is an inhibitor of ribonucleotide reductase and is not structurally related to folic acid.

Methotrexate is the classic structural analog of folic acid. It competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, preventing the regeneration of THF, which is essential for both purine and dTMP synthesis.
Allopurinol is an analog of hypoxanthine used to treat gout by inhibiting xanthine oxidase.
Mycophenolic acid is an inhibitor of IMP dehydrogenase and does not function as a folate analog.
Sulfonamides are structural analogs of para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), not folic acid itself. They inhibit the synthesis of folate in bacteria.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): [Other purine synthesis inhibitors, such as structural analogs of folic acid (for example, methotrexate 2), are used pharmacologically to control the spread of cancer by interfering with the synthesis of nucleotides]

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: During the conversion of Inosine Monophosphate (IMP) to Adenosine Monophosphate (AMP), the intermediate compound Adenylosuccinate is cleaved. What is the second product of this reaction besides AMP?
options: Fumarate
Pyruvate
Malate
Alpha-ketoglutarate
Succinate
correctOption: Fumarate
optionExplanations: Adenylosuccinate lyase (also called adenylosuccinase) cleaves adenylosuccinate into AMP and fumarate. This fumarate can then enter the TCA cycle, linking nucleotide metabolism to central energy pathways.
Pyruvate is the end product of glycolysis and is not involved in the purine branching reactions.
Malate is formed from fumarate in the TCA cycle by fumarase, but it is not the immediate product of the adenylosuccinate lyase reaction.
Alpha-ketoglutarate is produced by the deamination or transamination of glutamate; it is not produced during the cleavage of adenylosuccinate.
Succinate is a TCA cycle intermediate, but it is not the product released by adenylosuccinate lyase; the carbon skeleton of aspartate is released as the unsaturated dicarboxylic acid, fumarate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): [Figure 22.8 shows] Adenylosuccinate [catalyzed by] Adenylosuccinase [to produce] AMP + Fumarate.

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: In the physiological loop that maintains deoxyribonucleotide production, what is the correct flow of electrons starting from the primary donor to the final production of the deoxyribose moiety?
options: NADPH -> Ribonucleotide Reductase -> Thioredoxin -> DNA
FADH2 -> Thioredoxin Reductase -> Ribonucleotide Reductase -> Thioredoxin
NADH -> Thioredoxin -> Thioredoxin Reductase -> Ribonucleotide Reductase
NADPH -> Thioredoxin Reductase -> Thioredoxin -> Ribonucleotide Reductase
ATP -> Thioredoxin Reductase -> Thioredoxin -> Ribonucleotide Reductase
correctOption: NADPH -> Thioredoxin Reductase -> Thioredoxin -> Ribonucleotide Reductase
optionExplanations: The electrons flow through thioredoxin before reaching ribonucleotide reductase, and the final destination is the sugar moiety of the nucleotide, not the DNA polymer directly.
FADH2 is not the primary donor for this loop; the source of reducing equivalents is NADPH.
NADH is not the electron donor for this specific biosynthetic reduction; NADPH is used.

The pathway begins with NADPH donating electrons to thioredoxin reductase. These electrons are passed to thioredoxin (reducing its disulfide bond to sulfhydryl groups), which then reduces the disulfide bond in ribonucleotide reductase, allowing it to reduce a ribonucleotide.
ATP provides energy via phosphate transfer or acts as an allosteric activator, but it does not serve as a source of reducing equivalents (electrons).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 297 (Book Page): The necessary reducing equivalents are provided by NADPH + H+, and the reaction is catalyzed by thioredoxin reductase (see Figure 22.12).

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: A patient receiving chemotherapy for a solid tumor is prescribed 5-fluorouracil. Which specific metabolic step is inhibited by the active metabolite of this drug?
options: The reduction of ribonucleoside diphosphates to deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates
The conversion of UTP to CTP using glutamine
The conversion of orotate to OMP via PRPP addition
The reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate
The methylation of dUMP to dTMP
correctOption: The methylation of dUMP to dTMP
optionExplanations: Ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) catalyzes this reduction. RNR is inhibited by drugs like hydroxyurea or high levels of dATP, not 5-fluorouracil.
The conversion of UTP to CTP is catalyzed by CTP synthetase and is not the target of 5-fluorouracil.
Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase catalyzes the formation of OMP. This is part of the UMP synthase complex and is deficient in orotic aciduria, but not targeted by 5-FU.
This step is inhibited by methotrexate, which targets dihydrofolate reductase, leading to a deficiency of tetrahydrofolate (the carbon carrier).

5-fluorouracil is a 'suicide inhibitor.' It is converted to 5-FdUMP, which covalently binds to thymidylate synthase, preventing the methylation of dUMP into dTMP, thus depleting the cell of thymidine for DNA synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 303 (Book Page): dUMP is converted to dTMP by thymidylate synthase... Inhibitors of thymidylate synthase include thymine analogs such as 5-fluorouracil... Page 304 (Book Page): 5-Fluorouracil is metabolically converted to 5-FdUMP, which becomes permanently bound to the inactivated thymidylate synthase.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: In the treatment of certain cancers, 5-fluorouracil is administered to inhibit cellular proliferation. After metabolic conversion, this drug acts as a 'suicide' inhibitor. Which specific enzyme-substrate interaction is permanently disrupted by this pharmacological agent?
options: Thymidylate synthase with dUMP
Ribonucleotide reductase with UDP
Dihydrofolate reductase with dihydrofolate
Orotidylate decarboxylase with OMP
CPS II with glutamine and CO2
correctOption: Thymidylate synthase with dUMP
optionExplanations: 5-fluorouracil is converted to 5-FdUMP, which acts as a structural analog of dUMP. It binds covalently and irreversibly to thymidylate synthase, preventing the methylation of dUMP to dTMP.
Ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited by hydroxyurea (which destroys the free radical) or dATP (allosteric inhibition), but not by 5-fluorouracil.
Dihydrofolate reductase is inhibited by methotrexate, not 5-fluorouracil. Methotrexate acts as a competitive inhibitor of THF regeneration.
Orotidylate decarboxylase is part of the UMP synthase complex; its deficiency causes orotic aciduria, but it is not the primary target of 5-fluorouracil suicide inhibition.
CPS II is the regulated step inhibited by UTP. 5-fluorouracil focuses on the later steps of dTMP synthesis essential for DNA replication rather than early ring synthesis steps.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): 5-Fluorouracil is metabolically converted to 5-FdUMP, which becomes permanently bound to the inactivated thymidylate synthase; for this reason, the drug is called a “suicide” inhibitor.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: The synthesis of Guanosine Monophosphate (GMP) from Inosine Monophosphate (IMP) requires an oxidized intermediate and a specific nitrogen donor. Which combination of molecules represents the intermediate and the donor required for the final step catalyzed by GMP synthetase?
options: Intermediate: Hypoxanthine; Donor: Glutamate
Intermediate: Xanthosine monophosphate (XMP); Donor: Aspartate
Intermediate: Xanthosine monophosphate (XMP); Donor: Ammonia
Intermediate: Adenylosuccinate; Donor: Glutamine
Intermediate: Xanthosine monophosphate (XMP); Donor: Glutamine
correctOption: Intermediate: Xanthosine monophosphate (XMP); Donor: Glutamine
optionExplanations: Hypoxanthine is the base of IMP, not a separate intermediate in the conversion to GMP; the pathway remains at the nucleotide level.
Aspartate is the nitrogen donor for the AMP branch, not the GMP branch.
While ammonia is the source of nitrogen in some prokaryotic pathways or the urea cycle (CPS I), human GMP synthetase specifically utilizes the amide nitrogen of glutamine.
Adenylosuccinate is the intermediate in the AMP branch, and that branch uses aspartate, not glutamine.
IMP is first oxidized to XMP by IMP dehydrogenase (using NAD+). XMP then receives an amide group from glutamine to become GMP, a reaction that also requires ATP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): [Figure 22.8 shows IMP being converted to Xanthosine monophosphate... and XMP being converted to GMP using ATP and Glutamine.]

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
coreConcept: Reciprocal cross-regulation of purine nucleotide synthesis
statement: A balanced intracellular concentration of Adenosine Monophosphate (AMP) and Guanosine Monophosphate (GMP) is maintained through a cross-regulatory mechanism. Which of the following correctly describes this intermediate regulation during the conversion of Inosine Monophosphate (IMP)?
options: The conversion of IMP to adenylosuccinate requires ATP as an energy source.
The synthesis of xanthosine monophosphate (XMP) is driven by GTP-dependent phosphorylation.
AMP synthesis is inhibited by high concentrations of xanthine oxidase.
GMP inhibits the conversion of IMP to adenylosuccinate through competitive inhibition.
Synthesis of AMP from IMP requires GTP, while synthesis of GMP from IMP requires ATP.
correctOption: Synthesis of AMP from IMP requires GTP, while synthesis of GMP from IMP requires ATP.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The conversion of IMP to adenylosuccinate (the precursor to AMP) requires GTP, not ATP, to provide the energy for the reaction.
Incorrect. XMP is produced by IMP dehydrogenase using NAD+; it is the subsequent conversion of XMP to GMP that requires ATP as energy.
Incorrect. Xanthine oxidase is involved in the degradation of purines to uric acid, not the biosynthetic pathway from IMP to AMP.

Incorrect. GMP inhibits the first step of its own branch (IMP dehydrogenase), while AMP inhibits its own branch (adenylosuccinate synthetase). They do not typically cross-inhibit the opposing branch's first enzyme in this manner according to the text.
Correct. This reciprocal requirement ensures that if one purine (e.g., GTP) is abundant, it drives the synthesis of the other (e.g., AMP), maintaining a balanced ratio for nucleic acid synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Note that the synthesis of AMP requires guanosine triphosphate (GTP) as an energy source, whereas the synthesis of GMP requires ATP. Also, the first reaction in each pathway is inhibited by the end product of that pathway.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: A 3-year-old child presents with recurrent infections and significant neurodevelopmental delay. Laboratory testing shows a decrease in T-cell count, but B-cell and natural killer (NK) cell functions are relatively preserved. This clinical picture is most consistent with a deficiency in which of the following enzymes?
options: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP)
Adenylate kinase
AMP deaminase
Adenosine deaminase (ADA)
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase
correctOption: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP)
optionExplanations: PNP deficiency is rarer and specifically characterized by a T-cell immunodeficiency and neurodevelopmental delay, leaving B-cells less affected than in ADA deficiency.
Adenylate kinase is involved in interconverting AMP, ADP, and ATP in high-energy tissues; its deficiency does not cause this specific immunodeficiency pattern.
AMP deaminase is involved in the conversion of AMP to IMP in the purine degradation pathway; its deficiency is usually associated with muscle issues, not SCID-like symptoms.
ADA deficiency causes Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID), which affects T, B, and NK cells, unlike the T-cell specific pattern seen here.
HGPRT deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, which features hyperuricemia and self-mutilation, not a selective T-cell immunodeficiency.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): [[Note: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase ( PNP) deficiency results in a less severe immunodeficiency involving T-cells primarily.]]

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: In the de novo synthesis of pyrimidines, most enzymes are cytosolic. However, one specific enzyme is localized to the inner mitochondrial membrane. Which enzyme is this?
options: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
Aspartate transcarbamoylase
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II
Dihydroorotase
Orotidylate decarboxylase
correctOption: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
optionExplanations: Correct. Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is unique among pyrimidine biosynthetic enzymes because it is located on the inner mitochondrial membrane and utilizes FAD/quinone as electron acceptors.
Aspartate transcarbamoylase is the second domain of the cytosolic CAD multifunctional protein.
CPS II is part of the CAD cytosolic complex, distinct from the mitochondrial CPS I used in the urea cycle.
Dihydroorotase is the third domain of the cytosolic CAD multifunctional protein.
Orotidylate decarboxylase is a domain of the cytosolic UMP synthase complex.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): The enzyme that produces orotate, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, is associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane. All other enzymes in pyrimidine biosynthesis are cytosolic.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed step in the de novo purine nucleotide biosynthetic pathway and is subject to feedback inhibition by AMP and GMP?
options: Glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase
Orotidylate decarboxylase
Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase
PRPP synthetase
Adenylosuccinate synthetase
correctOption: Glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase
optionExplanations: Glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase is the committed step in purine biosynthesis. It replaces the pyrophosphate of PRPP with an amide group from glutamine. It is highly regulated by its products (AMP, GMP) and its substrate (PRPP).
Orotidylate decarboxylase is an enzyme involved in the de novo synthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides, converting OMP to UMP. It has no role in the purine biosynthetic pathway.
