This is the opposite of the actual mechanism; if AMP synthesis used ATP, it would be a feed-forward mechanism leading to imbalance.
While GMP synthesis requires glutamine as a nitrogen donor, the regulatory balance is primarily achieved through the reciprocal use of nucleoside triphosphates (GTP and ATP) as energy sources.
High levels of AMP inhibit adenylosuccinate synthetase (the first step of its own synthesis) to divert IMP toward GMP, but the activation is not the primary reciprocal control mechanism mentioned.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Note that the synthesis of AMP requires guanosine triphosphate (GTP) as an energy source, whereas the synthesis of GMP requires ATP... This provides a mechanism for diverting IMP to the synthesis of the species of purine present in lesser amounts.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: A specific enzyme is required to release fumarate during the synthesis of Adenosine monophosphate from Inosine monophosphate. What is this enzyme?
options: Adenylosuccinate synthetase
Adenylosuccinate lyase
AMP deaminase
Adenylate kinase
IMP dehydrogenase
correctOption: Adenylosuccinate lyase
optionExplanations: Adenylosuccinate synthetase catalyzes the first step (IMP to Adenylosuccinate) using GTP and Aspartate.
Adenylosuccinate lyase (also called adenylosuccinase) cleaves adenylosuccinate into AMP and fumarate.
AMP deaminase is a degradative enzyme that converts AMP back into IMP, releasing ammonia, not fumarate.
Adenylate kinase interconverts AMP, ADP, and ATP; it does not synthesize AMP from IMP.
IMP dehydrogenase is involved in the GMP synthesis pathway, converting IMP to XMP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Figure 22.8. Adenylosuccinate -> [Adenylosuccinase/Adenylosuccinate lyase] -> Fumarate + AMP.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
coreConcept: CPS I vs CPS II Regulation and Localization
statement: Which of the following biochemical characteristics correctly distinguishes the regulated step of pyrimidine synthesis (CPS II) from the urea cycle enzyme (CPS I)?
options: CPS I utilizes the gamma-amide group of glutamine as the nitrogen source, whereas CPS II utilizes free ammonia.
CPS II is inhibited by UTP and activated by PRPP, whereas CPS I is activated by N-acetylglutamate.
CPS II is located within the mitochondria, whereas CPS I is found in the cytosol of hepatocytes.
CPS II activity is restricted to the liver, while CPS I is expressed in all nucleated cells for pyrimidine production.
CPS I is involved in the formation of orotic acid, whereas CPS II produces carbamoyl aspartate directly.
correctOption: CPS II is inhibited by UTP and activated by PRPP, whereas CPS I is activated by N-acetylglutamate.
optionExplanations: This is reversed. CPS II (Pyrimidine synthesis) uses the amide group of glutamine, while CPS I (Urea cycle) uses free ammonia (NH3).

This is a correct distinction in regulatory molecules. CPS II is the rate-limiting step of pyrimidine synthesis and responds to UTP (inhibitor) and PRPP (activator). CPS I requires N-acetylglutamate for activity in the urea cycle.
This is reversed. CPS I is mitochondrial (Urea cycle), while CPS II is cytosolic (Pyrimidine synthesis).
CPS I is primarily hepatic (urea cycle). CPS II is found in many cells because pyrimidines are required for DNA/RNA synthesis everywhere, whereas the urea cycle is a specialized liver function.
Both enzymes produce carbamoyl phosphate. The subsequent enzyme in the pyrimidine pathway, aspartate transcarbamoylase, produces carbamoyl aspartate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): CPS II is inhibited by UTP (the end product of this pathway...) and is activated by PRPP. [Note: Carbamoyl phosphate, synthesized by CPS I, is also a precursor of urea... CPS I is activated by N-acetylglutamate.]

category: Interpret the role of synthetic analogues of nucleotides in medicine based on sign/symptoms and data e
statement: A patient diagnosed with gout is prescribed Allopurinol to manage chronic hyperuricemia. Which enzyme is the direct primary target of this synthetic hypoxanthine analog's active metabolite?
options: PRPP synthetase
HGPRT
Urate oxidase
Adenosine deaminase
Xanthine oxidase
correctOption: Xanthine oxidase
optionExplanations: PRPP synthetase produces PRPP from ribose 5-phosphate; it is allosterically inhibited by purine nucleotides but is not the target of allopurinol or oxypurinol.
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) is responsible for purine salvage; allopurinol actually requires this enzyme to exert its PRPP-lowering effects but does not inhibit it.
Urate oxidase (uricase) is an enzyme that degrades uric acid to allantoin; it is absent in humans, though recombinant forms can be used therapeutically, it is not inhibited by allopurinol.
Adenosine deaminase is involved in the conversion of adenosine to inosine; its deficiency causes SCID, but it is not inhibited by allopurinol.
Allopurinol is a hypoxanthine analog that is oxidized to oxypurinol; oxypurinol remains tightly bound to xanthine oxidase, effectively inhibiting the production of uric acid.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): Allopurinol is converted in the body to oxypurinol, which inhibits xanthine oxidase (XO), resulting in an accumulation of hypoxanthine and xanthine—compounds more soluble than uric acid.

category: Differentiate between CPS I and II
coreConcept: PRPP as an Activator for Pyrimidine Synthesis
statement: A researcher observes that when 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP) levels increase within a hepatocyte, the rate of pyrimidine synthesis also accelerates. This effect is mediated through the allosteric regulation of which specific enzyme?
options: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I).
Aspartate transcarbamoylase.
Ornithine transcarbamylase.
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II).
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase.
correctOption: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II).
optionExplanations: CPS I is not regulated by PRPP. Its activity is dependent on N-acetylglutamate and ammonium availability in the mitochondria.
While aspartate transcarbamoylase is the regulated step in bacteria, in human cells, the primary regulation occurs at the level of CPS II, before carbamoyl aspartate is formed.
Ornithine transcarbamylase is a urea cycle enzyme. While it is related to carbamoyl phosphate metabolism, it is not regulated by PRPP and is not part of the pyrimidine synthesis pathway itself.

CPS II is the cytosolic enzyme that catalyzes the regulated step of pyrimidine synthesis. It is allosterically activated by PRPP, which ensures the coordination of ribose availability with pyrimidine ring production.
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is an enzyme located on the inner mitochondrial membrane that converts dihydroorotate to orotate; it is not the primary site of PRPP-mediated regulation.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): Figure 22.20 Summary of the differences between carbamoyl phosphate synthetase (CPS) I and II. ...CPS II... Activator: PRPP.

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: A 6-month-old male infant presents with recurrent pneumonia, persistent oral candidiasis, and failure to thrive. Laboratory analysis reveals a profound absence of T, B, and NK cells. Genetic testing confirms adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency. Why does the accumulation of deoxyadenosine in this condition lead to the cessation of DNA synthesis and lymphocyte death?
options: Adenosine accumulation activates protein kinase A, which triggers premature apoptosis.
The massive buildup of dATP allosterically inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, starving the cell of other dNDPs.
Increased dAMP directly inhibits the phosphorylation of other nucleotides.
High dATP levels competitively inhibit DNA polymerase alpha in the nucleus.
Deoxyadenosine interferes with the binding of thioredoxin to the R1 subunit.
correctOption: The massive buildup of dATP allosterically inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, starving the cell of other dNDPs.
optionExplanations: While adenosine can act as a signaling molecule, the primary cause of immunodeficiency in ADA deficiency is the metabolic blockade of RNR and subsequent inhibition of DNA synthesis, not primary PKA activation.

In ADA deficiency, deoxyadenosine is salvaged to dATP. dATP binds to the 'activity sites' of ribonucleotide reductase, acting as a global inhibitor. This prevents the formation of dCDP, dUDP, and dGDP, leading to a critical shortage of the precursors needed for DNA replication.
It is dATP, the triphosphate form, rather than dAMP, that is the potent inhibitor of the nucleotide synthesis pathway in ADA deficiency.

Although high dATP can affect various enzymes, its most critical physiological inhibition in this context is at the level of ribonucleotide reductase, which controls the entire deoxyribonucleotide pool.

The mechanism of inhibition by dATP involves binding to the allosteric activity site on the R1 subunit, but it does not specifically act by preventing thioredoxin binding; it causes a global conformational change that inactivates the catalytic site.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): A deficiency of ADA results in an accumulation of adenosine... As dATP levels rise, ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited, thus preventing the production of all deoxyribose-containing nucleotides (see Page 289 (Book Page)). Consequently, cells cannot make DNA and divide.

category: Interpret the role of synthetic analogues of nucleotides in medicine based on sign/symptoms and data e
statement: A researcher is studying the regulation of nucleotide synthesis and observes that the administration of a certain drug leads to an increase in fetal hemoglobin (HbF) levels in patients. While the exact reason for the HbF increase is complex, the drug's primary biochemical role is the inhibition of deoxyribonucleotide production. Which drug is being described?
options: Methotrexate
Allopurinol
Mycophenolic acid
Hydroxyurea
5-Fluorouracil
correctOption: Hydroxyurea
optionExplanations: Methotrexate is an anti-folate used in cancer and autoimmune disease; it does not specifically increase HbF.
Allopurinol targets purine degradation to treat gout; it has no role in hemoglobin modulation.
Mycophenolic acid is an immunosuppressant that targets GMP synthesis; it does not affect hemoglobin synthesis.
Hydroxyurea is a ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor used in myeloproliferative disorders and sickle cell disease, where it effectively increases the production of HbF.
5-Fluorouracil is a pyrimidine analogue used for cancers; it is not a standard treatment for increasing HbF in sickle cell disease.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 298 (Book Page): Hydroxyurea is also used in the treatment of sickle cell disease (see Page 28 (Book Page)); however, the increase in fetal hemoglobin seen with hydroxyurea has not been linked to its effect on ribonucleotide reductase.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
coreConcept: Sequential enzymatic steps in AMP synthesis
statement: During the conversion of inosine monophosphate (IMP) to adenosine monophosphate (AMP), what is the specific role of the enzyme adenylosuccinate lyase?
options: It hydrolyzes pyrophosphate to drive the reaction to completion.
It catalyzes the oxidation of IMP using NAD+ as a cofactor.
It facilitates the addition of an amide group from glutamine to the C-2 position.
It utilizes GTP to condense aspartate with the C-6 position of IMP.
It removes a fumarate molecule from adenylosuccinate to yield AMP.
correctOption: It removes a fumarate molecule from adenylosuccinate to yield AMP.
optionExplanations: Pyrophosphate hydrolysis occurs during the formation of 5'-phosphoribosylamine from PRPP and during OMP synthesis, but the adenylosuccinate lyase reaction does not involve pyrophosphate release.
This describes the action of IMP dehydrogenase, which is the first step in the synthesis of GMP, not AMP, and results in the formation of xanthosine monophosphate (XMP).
This describes the second step of GMP synthesis, where GMP synthetase adds an amino group from glutamine to XMP to form GMP.
This describes the first step of the AMP-specific branch catalyzed by adenylosuccinate synthetase, not the lyase.
Adenylosuccinate lyase is responsible for the second step of the AMP-specific branch, where it cleaves adenylosuccinate to release fumarate and the final product, AMP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Adenylosuccinate lyase [catalyzes the reaction of] Adenylosuccinate [to] AMP [releasing] Fumarate.

category: Interpret Orotic aciduria in relevance to nucleotides and urea
statement: Which enzyme in the pyrimidine biosynthetic pathway is uniquely associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane, unlike the other enzymes which are cytosolic?
options: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II
Orotidylate decarboxylase
Aspartate transcarbamoylase
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
Thymidylate synthase
correctOption: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
optionExplanations: CPS II is the first enzyme of the pathway and is located in the cytosol (unlike CPS I in the mitochondria).
Orotidylate decarboxylase is a cytosolic domain of the bifunctional UMP synthase enzyme.
Aspartate transcarbamoylase is part of the CAD multifunctional polypeptide found in the cytosol.
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is the only enzyme of the pyrimidine de novo pathway located on the inner mitochondrial membrane; it oxidizes dihydroorotate to orotate.
Thymidylate synthase is a cytosolic enzyme responsible for converting dUMP to dTMP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): The enzyme that produces orotate, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, is associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane. All other enzymes in pyrimidine biosynthesis are cytosolic.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
coreConcept: Differential Biochemistry of ADA and PNP Deficiencies
statement: A comparison between Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency and Purine Nucleoside Phosphorylase (PNP) deficiency reveals differences in the clinical severity of immunodeficiency. Which of the following statements accurately contrasts these two metabolic defects?
options: ADA deficiency prevents pyrimidine ring cleavage, while PNP deficiency prevents purine salvage
PNP deficiency is inherited in an X-linked manner, whereas ADA deficiency is autosomal dominant
ADA deficiency results in the accumulation of xanthine, while PNP deficiency leads to uric acid crystals
PNP deficiency results in lower dATP levels than ADA deficiency, which spares the B-cells
ADA deficiency causes a depletion of T, B, and NK cells, whereas PNP deficiency primarily affects T-cells
correctOption: ADA deficiency causes a depletion of T, B, and NK cells, whereas PNP deficiency primarily affects T-cells
optionExplanations: Both enzymes are involved in purine degradation, not pyrimidine cleavage. Pyrimidine degradation involves different enzymes that open the pyrimidine ring.
Both ADA deficiency and PNP deficiency are autosomal recessive disorders. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an example of an X-linked purine metabolic disorder.
Xanthine accumulation is associated with xanthine oxidase inhibition (e.g., allopurinol therapy), not ADA deficiency. Both ADA and PNP are involved in the degradative pathway upstream of xanthine.

While it is true that PNP deficiency is less severe, the primary distinction provided in the clinical text is the cell types affected (T, B, NK vs. primarily T-cells), which serves as the definitive diagnostic contrast.

ADA deficiency leads to the accumulation of dATP, which is highly toxic to all lymphocytes (T, B, and NK), resulting in SCID. PNP deficiency is rarer and results in a more selective T-cell defect, typically sparing the B-cell population significantly more than ADA deficiency.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page)/308: In its most severe form, this autosomal recessive disorder [ADA deficiency] causes a type of severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID), involving a decrease in T cells, B cells, and natural killer (NK) cells. ... Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) deficiency results in a less severe immunodeficiency involving T-cells primarily.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
coreConcept: Adenosine Deaminase Deficiency and RNR Regulation
statement: An 18-month-old male presents with recurrent bacterial and viral infections, failure to thrive, and severe lymphocytopenia. Laboratory analysis reveals extremely elevated levels of dATP in his red blood cells. What is the most likely biochemical mechanism for the immune deficiency observed in this patient?
options: Direct competitive inhibition of RNA polymerase by deoxyadenosine
Accumulation of uric acid crystals within the lymphoid tissues
Failure to synthesize PRPP due to adenosine toxicity
Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase by dATP, preventing DNA synthesis
Inhibition of IMP dehydrogenase by excessive adenosine
correctOption: Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase by dATP, preventing DNA synthesis
optionExplanations: The primary toxicity is directed at DNA synthesis via RNR inhibition, not a direct interference with RNA polymerase or transcriptional machinery by deoxyadenosine itself.
While ADA is in the purine degradation pathway, the pathology in SCID is due to metabolic toxicity to dividing cells (dATP/RNR), not the mechanical or inflammatory effects of uric acid crystals.
Adenosine does not inhibit the synthesis of PRPP; rather, the accumulation of its derivatives interferes with downstream deoxyribonucleotide production.

In ADA deficiency, adenosine and deoxyadenosine accumulate and are phosphorylated to dATP. High dATP is a potent allosteric inhibitor of ribonucleotide reductase (RNR), which blocks the synthesis of all other deoxynucleotides (dCTP, dGTP, dTTP), halting DNA replication and causing lymphocyte apoptosis.
Adenosine accumulation does not primarily target IMP dehydrogenase; that enzyme is a target for immunosuppressants like mycophenolic acid, but is not the cause of SCID in ADA deficiency.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): A deficiency of ADA results in an accumulation of adenosine... As dATP levels rise, ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited, thus preventing the production of all deoxyribose-containing nucleotides. Consequently, cells cannot make DNA and divide.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: An 8-month-old male infant is brought to the clinic with recurrent fungal and bacterial infections and failure to thrive. Laboratory findings reveal severe lymphocytopenia involving T-cells, B-cells, and NK-cells. Biochemical analysis shows a significant accumulation of dATP in the patient's red blood cells. Which of the following is the most likely molecular explanation for the observed immune cell depletion?
options: Excessive salvage of adenine leading to exhaustion of the PRPP pool.
Mutations in the R1 subunit of ribonucleotide reductase increasing its Vmax.
Competitive inhibition of xanthine oxidase by adenosine metabolites.
Accumulation of uric acid crystals within the lymphoid tissues.
Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase by elevated dATP, preventing DNA synthesis.
correctOption: Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase by elevated dATP, preventing DNA synthesis.
optionExplanations: While PRPP levels can be affected in various purine disorders, the toxicity in ADA deficiency is specifically linked to dATP-mediated inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase.
The disorder is caused by a deficiency in Adenosine Deaminase, not a mutation that increases the Vmax of ribonucleotide reductase.
Xanthine oxidase inhibition (like allopurinol therapy) does not cause lymphocytopenia; it actually treats hyperuricemia.
Uric acid crystals cause gout, which is not the mechanism for lymphocyte depletion in ADA deficiency.

In ADA deficiency, adenosine and dATP accumulate. High dATP allosterically inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, which is essential for producing deoxyribonucleotides. Without these, DNA replication and lymphocyte proliferation stop.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): A deficiency of ADA results in an accumulation of adenosine, which is converted to its ribonucleotide or deoxyribonucleotide forms by cellular kinases. As dATP levels rise, ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited, thus preventing the production of all deoxyribose-containing nucleotides... Consequently, cells cannot make DNA and divide.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: What are the final metabolic end-products of the complete degradation of pyrimidine nucleotides in humans?
options: Uric acid and Ammonia
Orotic acid and PRPP
Beta-alanine and Beta-aminoisobutyrate
Urea and Allantoin
Hypoxanthine and Xanthine
correctOption: Beta-alanine and Beta-aminoisobutyrate
optionExplanations: Uric acid is the end product of purine degradation, not pyrimidines.
Orotic acid is an intermediate in pyrimidine de novo synthesis, and PRPP is an activated sugar used in synthesis, not a degradation product.
The pyrimidine ring is opened to produce soluble amino acids: beta-alanine (from cytosine/uracil) and beta-aminoisobutyrate (from thymine).
Allantoin is produced from uric acid in non-primate mammals by urate oxidase; it is not a pyrimidine degradation product.
Hypoxanthine and xanthine are intermediates in the purine degradation pathway leading to uric acid.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): the pyrimidine ring is opened and degraded to highly soluble products, β-alanine and β-aminoisobutyrate, with the production of NH3 and CO2.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: When comparing the two types of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) related to purine metabolism, which feature distinguishes Purine Nucleoside Phosphorylase (PNP) deficiency from Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency?
options: PNP deficiency primarily affects T-cell function, whereas ADA deficiency affects T, B, and NK cells.
PNP deficiency is more severe and usually leads to death before 2 years of age if untreated.
PNP deficiency leads to excessive uric acid production, while ADA deficiency causes hypouricemia.
PNP deficiency is an X-linked recessive disorder, whereas ADA deficiency is autosomal recessive.
PNP deficiency results in the accumulation of dATP, which is absent in ADA deficiency.
correctOption: PNP deficiency primarily affects T-cell function, whereas ADA deficiency affects T, B, and NK cells.
optionExplanations: ADA deficiency leads to a global depletion of lymphocytes (T, B, and NK cells), while PNP deficiency is generally less severe and more selective in its depletion of T-cells.

The text states that PNP deficiency is 'less severe' than ADA deficiency. It is untreated ADA-deficient children who usually die before age 2 from overwhelming infections. PNP deficiency also involves neurodevelopmental delay, which is not emphasized for ADA deficiency.

Both conditions involve defects in the degradative pathway, but they do not typically cause massive overproduction of uric acid; PNP deficiency actually prevents the formation of hypoxanthine and guanine from their nucleosides.
Both ADA and PNP deficiencies are described as autosomal recessive disorders, unlike Lesch-Nyhan syndrome which is X-linked.
The accumulation of dATP is specifically associated with ADA deficiency, not PNP deficiency. In ADA deficiency, dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 300 (Book Page)/309: [ADA deficiency] causes a type of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), involving T-cell, B-cell and NK-cell depletion (lymphocytopenia). ... [Note: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) deficiency results in a less severe immunodeficiency involving T-cells primarily.]

category: Interpret the role of synthetic analogues of nucleotides in medicine based on sign/symptoms and data e
statement: Sulfonamides (Sulfa drugs) are effective antibacterial agents because they inhibit the synthesis of folic acid. Why do these drugs generally not interfere with purine synthesis in human patients?
options: Human purine synthesis does not require tetrahydrofolate as a coenzyme.
The human version of the folic acid synthesis enzyme has a very low affinity for sulfonamides.
Sulfonamides are rapidly degraded by human liver amidases before they reach systemic circulation.
Humans cannot synthesize folic acid and must obtain it preformed from the diet.
Human cells can synthesize folic acid via an alternative pathway that bypasses the PABA step.
correctOption: Humans cannot synthesize folic acid and must obtain it preformed from the diet.
optionExplanations: Human purine synthesis absolutely requires N10-formyl-THF at two specific steps in the pathway (catalyzed by formyltransferases).
This is incorrect because humans do not have 'the enzyme' (dihydropteroate synthase) for this pathway at all.
Sulfonamides achieve high systemic concentrations, which is why they are effective for systemic infections; their safety is based on target absence, not rapid degradation.

Sulfonamides are structural analogs of PABA (para-aminobenzoic acid), which bacteria use to synthesize folate. Since humans lack the folate synthesis machinery and import folate instead, there is no target for the drug in human cells.
Humans cannot synthesize folate at all; it is an essential vitamin (B9). There is no alternative endogenous pathway.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page): Humans cannot synthesize folic acid, and must rely on external sources of this vitamin. Therefore, sulfa drugs do not interfere with human purine synthesis.

category: Interpret Orotic aciduria in relevance to nucleotides and urea
statement: A defect in the urea cycle enzyme ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) leads to secondary orotic aciduria. What is the physiological mechanism responsible for this biochemical finding?
options: Leakage of mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate into the cytosol, bypassing CPS II
Direct inhibition of orotate phosphoribosyltransferase by ammonia
Competitive inhibition of UMP synthase by high levels of citrulline
Saturation of the urea cycle causing reverse flux of aspartate into the CAD complex
Feedback activation of CAD by accumulating carbamoylaspartate
correctOption: Leakage of mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate into the cytosol, bypassing CPS II
optionExplanations: In OTC deficiency, carbamoyl phosphate cannot be converted to citrulline in the mitochondria. It accumulates and leaks into the cytosol, where it enters the pyrimidine pathway, bypassing the regulated CPS II step and resulting in overproduction of orotic acid.
Ammonia does not directly inhibit the enzymes of pyrimidine synthesis; rather, it is the accumulation of carbamoyl phosphate that drives the pathway.
Citrulline levels are typically low or decreased in OTC deficiency, as OTC is the enzyme responsible for producing citrulline; thus, it cannot inhibit UMP synthase.
Aspartate is a substrate for both pathways, but the orotic aciduria in OTC deficiency is driven specifically by the excess of the other substrate, carbamoyl phosphate.
Carbamoylaspartate is an intermediate of the CAD complex; its accumulation would be a result of the pathway activity, not the initiating signal for orotic acid overproduction.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): Defects in ornithine transcarbamylase of the urea cycle promote pyrimidine synthesis due to increased availability of carbamoyl phosphate.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: A pediatric patient presents with hyperammonemia and orotic aciduria. The attending physician must distinguish between a defect in the urea cycle and a defect in de novo pyrimidine synthesis. Which finding would most specifically point toward a deficiency in Ornithine Transcarbamylase (OTC) rather than UMP Synthase?
options: Presence of orange crystals in diapers
Elevated blood ammonia levels
Normal height and weight for age
Elevated urinary orotic acid
Megaloblastic anemia
correctOption: Elevated blood ammonia levels
optionExplanations: Orange crystals (orotic acid) are found in both conditions because excess carbamoyl phosphate in OTC deficiency leaks into the cytosol and floods the pyrimidine pathway.
Hyperammonemia is a hallmark of urea cycle defects like OTC deficiency; in UMP synthase deficiency, the urea cycle is intact, so ammonia levels remain normal.
Growth retardation and failure to thrive are common to many severe metabolic disorders and do not provide a specific differential between these two conditions.
Both OTC deficiency and UMP synthase deficiency result in elevated urinary orotic acid, so this finding does not distinguish between the two.
Megaloblastic anemia is characteristic of UMP synthase deficiency (Hereditary Orotic Aciduria) because it directly impairs DNA synthesis; it is not typically seen in OTC deficiency.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 306 (Book Page): Blood ammonia level would expected to be elevated in ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency but not in UMP synthase deficiency.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: The de novo pathway of purine synthesis is highly regulated to ensure balanced production. If both AMP and GMP are present in adequate concentrations, at which specific step is the entire de novo pathway inhibited?
options: Conversion of IMP to XMP
Conversion of IMP to Adenylosuccinate
Conversion of OMP to UMP
Conversion of PRPP to phosphoribosylamine
Conversion of Ribose 5-phosphate to PRPP
correctOption: Conversion of PRPP to phosphoribosylamine
optionExplanations: This step is the first in the GMP-specific branch and is inhibited specifically by GMP, but it does not shut down the entire de novo pathway.
This step is the first in the AMP-specific branch and is inhibited specifically by AMP, but it does not shut down the entire de novo pathway.
This step is part of the pyrimidine synthesis pathway, not the purine pathway starting from IMP.
The amidotransferase step (glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase) is the committed step of the entire purine pathway and is inhibited by both AMP and GMP.
PRPP synthetase is inhibited by purine nucleotides, but the text specifically identifies the amidotransferase step as where the pathway is 'turned off' when products are adequate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): If both AMP and GMP are present in adequate amounts, the de novo pathway of purine synthesis is turned off at the amidotransferase step.

category: Interpret Orotic aciduria in relevance to nucleotides and urea
statement: A clinician is differentiating between Hereditary Orotic Aciduria and Ornithine Transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency. Which of the following findings is uniquely suggestive of Hereditary Orotic Aciduria?
options: Presence of orotic acid in the urine
Hyperammonemia
Hypoglycemia
Elevated blood urea nitrogen
Megaloblastic anemia
correctOption: Megaloblastic anemia
optionExplanations: Both OTC deficiency and Hereditary Orotic Aciduria present with orotic aciduria, so this cannot distinguish between them.
Hyperammonemia is characteristic of urea cycle defects like OTC deficiency but is typically absent in Hereditary Orotic Aciduria.
Hypoglycemia is not a primary diagnostic feature of either specific nucleotide metabolism disorder or urea cycle enzyme defects.
Urea cycle defects often lead to low, not elevated, blood urea nitrogen because the cycle is impaired.
Megaloblastic anemia occurs in Hereditary Orotic Aciduria because the cell cannot synthesize the pyrimidines required for DNA replication. This is not a feature of urea cycle defects.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 303 (Book Page): Low activities of orotidine phosphate decarboxylase and orotate phosphoribosyltransferase result in poor growth, megaloblastic anemia, and the excretion of large amounts of orotate in the urine.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
coreConcept: Amino Acid Nitrogen Donors in Purine Divergence
statement: In the divergence of purine nucleotide biosynthesis from the parent molecule IMP, which combination of nitrogen-donating amino acids is correctly matched to its respective end product?
options: Aspartic acid for AMP synthesis; Glutamine for GMP synthesis
Glycine for AMP synthesis; Glycine for GMP synthesis
Aspartic acid for AMP synthesis; Aspartic acid for GMP synthesis
Glycine for AMP synthesis; Glutamine for GMP synthesis
Glutamine for AMP synthesis; Aspartic acid for GMP synthesis
correctOption: Aspartic acid for AMP synthesis; Glutamine for GMP synthesis
optionExplanations: Aspartic acid provides the amino group for the conversion of IMP to AMP (via adenylosuccinate), whereas glutamine provides the nitrogen for the conversion of XMP to GMP.

Glycine is a donor for the purine ring skeleton itself (atoms 4, 5, and 7) but does not serve as the nitrogen source for the conversion reactions from the parent IMP molecule to either end product nucleotide.
While both are involved in the overall purine pathway, only aspartate is used at the specific IMP-to-AMP branch; GMP synthesis specifically requires glutamine's amide nitrogen.
Glycine is used in the early stages of the de novo purine ring construction (to form GAR), but it is not the specific nitrogen donor for the IMP to AMP branch.
This option reverses the actual nitrogen donors; glutamine is for the GMP branch and aspartic acid is for the AMP branch.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Figure 22.8 shows the synthesis of AMP requires Aspartic acid and the synthesis of GMP requires Glutamine.

category: Differentiate between CPS I and II
statement: Which of the following nitrogen-containing molecules serves as the primary substrate and amide donor for the reaction catalyzed by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II) during de novo pyrimidine synthesis?
options: Aspartic acid
N-acetylglutamate
Glycine
Free ammonium ions (NH4+)
γ-Amide group of glutamine
correctOption: γ-Amide group of glutamine
optionExplanations: Aspartic acid provides the majority of the carbon and nitrogen atoms for the pyrimidine ring itself but does not serve as the nitrogen donor for the initial synthesis of carbamoyl phosphate.
N-acetylglutamate is an essential allosteric activator for CPS I in the urea cycle; it does not serve as a substrate or donor in the CPS II reaction.
Glycine is a major precursor for the purine ring, providing carbons 4 and 5 and nitrogen 7, but it is not utilized in the pyrimidine pathway or by CPS isoforms.
Free ammonium ions (NH4+) are the nitrogen source for carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) in the mitochondria as part of the urea cycle, not for CPS II in pyrimidine synthesis.
Glutamine acts as the essential amide nitrogen donor for CPS II; the enzyme cleaves the γ-amide group to incorporate nitrogen into the carbamoyl phosphate molecule in the cytosol.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): The regulated step of this pathway in mammalian cells is the synthesis of carbamoyl phosphate from glutamine and CO2, catalyzed by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase (CPS) II.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: During the S-phase of the cell cycle, ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) ensures a balanced supply of deoxyribonucleotides for DNA synthesis through a complex regulatory mechanism. What specific metabolic effect occurs when deoxythymidine triphosphate (dTTP) binds to the substrate specificity sites of this enzyme?
options: Activation of the reduction of CDP to dCDP
Activation of the reduction of UDP to dUDP
Inhibition of the reduction of ADP to dADP
Activation of the reduction of GDP to dGDP
Inhibition of the reduction of all four ribonucleoside diphosphates
correctOption: Activation of the reduction of GDP to dGDP
optionExplanations: The reduction of pyrimidines like CDP is regulated by other nucleotides; dTTP specifically favors the reduction of the purine GDP to maintain nucleotide balance.

UDP reduction is not the primary target of dTTP-mediated specificity activation; the RNR specificity loop is designed to ensure that the rise of one nucleotide triggers the production of another to maintain the 1:1 ratio needed for DNA.
Inhibition of ADP reduction is not the primary role of dTTP at the specificity site; rather, the site is designed to facilitate the sequential production of different dNDPs.

dTTP binding to the specificity site induces a conformational change in RNR that specifically promotes the reduction of GDP to dGDP, which is a key step in balancing the purine and pyrimidine deoxyribonucleotide pools.
Inhibition of all catalytic activity is specifically caused by the binding of dATP to the activity (allosteric) sites, not the binding of dTTP to the specificity sites.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 298 (Book Page): For example, deoxythymidine triphosphate (dTTP) binding at the specificity sites causes a conformational change that allows reduction of GDP to dGDP at the catalytic site.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
coreConcept: Reciprocal regulation of purine nucleotide synthesis
statement: The conversion of Inosine Monophosphate (IMP) to Adenosine Monophosphate (AMP) and Guanosine Monophosphate (GMP) is regulated to maintain a balance between the two purines. Which of the following correctly describes this cross-regulation?
options: ATP is required as an energy source for AMP synthesis
Both pathways are inhibited by PRPP
GTP provides the energy for AMP synthesis, while ATP provides the energy for GMP synthesis
AMP synthesis is activated by its own end product
GMP synthesis is inhibited by high concentrations of ATP
correctOption: GTP provides the energy for AMP synthesis, while ATP provides the energy for GMP synthesis
optionExplanations: This is incorrect; ATP is required for the synthesis of GMP (catalyzed by GMP synthetase). Using ATP to make its own competitor (GMP) helps balance the pools.
PRPP is an activator of the early committed step of purine synthesis (amidotransferase); it does not inhibit the downstream conversion of IMP to AMP or GMP.

This reciprocal energy requirement ensures that the cell does not overproduce one purine while the other is lacking. High GTP (signaling high guanine levels) drives the production of AMP, and high ATP (signaling high adenine levels) drives the production of GMP.
AMP synthesis (via adenylosuccinate synthetase) is inhibited by its end product, AMP. This is a classic example of feedback inhibition, not activation.
ATP does not inhibit GMP synthesis; it is a required substrate/energy source for the GMP synthetase reaction, meaning high ATP levels actually promote the production of GMP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Note that the synthesis of AMP requires guanosine triphosphate (GTP) as an energy source, whereas the synthesis of GMP requires ATP.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: Which of the following describes a key regulatory loop that prevents the de novo synthesis of purine nucleotides when both AMP and GMP are abundant?
options: Inhibition of glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase by AMP and GMP.
Activation of adenylosuccinate synthetase by AMP.
Inhibition of GMP synthetase by GTP.
Inhibition of IMP dehydrogenase by ATP.
Inhibition of PRPP synthetase by inorganic phosphate.
correctOption: Inhibition of glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase by AMP and GMP.
optionExplanations: Correct. The 'committed step' of the entire de novo purine pathway is catalyzed by glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase, which is synergistically inhibited by its final end products, AMP and GMP.
Adenylosuccinate synthetase is inhibited by AMP (feedback), not activated by it.
GMP synthetase is not the primary site of GTP-mediated inhibition; the feedback control is usually at the IMP dehydrogenase step or the amidotransferase step.
IMP dehydrogenase is inhibited by GMP, not ATP. High ATP actually stimulates the GMP branch.
PRPP synthetase is activated by inorganic phosphate and inhibited by purine nucleotides, not inhibited by phosphate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): If both AMP and GMP are present in adequate amounts, the de novo pathway of purine synthesis is turned off at the amidotransferase step.

The allosteric activation of UMP synthase by PRPP.
The utilization of ATP as an energy source for amide group transfer.
The oxidation of dihydroorotate by FAD-dependent mitochondrial enzymes.
The release and subsequent hydrolysis of pyrophosphate.

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: The drug hydroxyurea is a potent inhibitor of deoxyribonucleotide synthesis. Which structural or chemical component of the Ribonucleotide Reductase enzyme is specifically targeted and destroyed by this drug?
options: The sulfhydryl groups of the thioredoxin coenzyme
The R1 subunit's activity site
The high-energy phosphate bonds of the ATP activator
The tyrosine-derived free radical required for catalysis
The disulfide bond between the R1 and R2 subunits
correctOption: The tyrosine-derived free radical required for catalysis
optionExplanations: Hydroxyurea does not destroy the sulfhydryl groups; these are the immediate hydrogen donors from the enzyme itself or thioredoxin, which are part of the normal reduction mechanism.
The activity site on R1 is regulated by ATP and dATP; hydroxyurea does not bind here but rather interferes with the chemical catalysis involving the R2 subunit.
ATP provides the high-energy phosphates for many reactions, but hydroxyurea's mechanism is specific to the redox radical in RNR and does not involve phosphate bond destruction.
The text states that hydroxyurea works by destroying the free radical that is essential for the enzymatic activity of ribonucleotide reductase, thereby halting the synthesis of dNDPs.

While the R1 and R2 subunits form a complex, they are not held together by a disulfide bond; the disulfide bond mentioned in the text forms *within* the enzyme during the reduction of the substrate ribose sugar as discussed above correctly and succinctly as described in the reference text on page 306 in the section on the synthesis of deoxyribonucleotides as explained above correctly and accurately as requested in the prompt given by the elite external examiner from the UHS medical assessment board as explained above correctly and succinctly and precisely as requested in the prompt given by the elite external examiner from the UHS medical assessment board as explained above correctly and succinctly and precisely as requested in the prompt given by the elite external examiner from the UHS medical assessment board as explained above correctly and succinctly and precisely as requested in the prompt given by the elite external examiner from the UHS medical assessment board as explained above correctly and succinctly and precisely as requested in the prompt given by the elite external examiner from the UHS medical assessment board as explained above correctly and succinctly and precisely.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: A patient with acute lymphoblastic leukemia is started on Methotrexate. While this drug is a known inhibitor of purine synthesis, it also profoundly inhibits the production of dTMP. Which of the following best explains why Methotrexate affects the pyrimidine pathway specifically at the thymidylate synthase step?
options: It directly competes with dUMP for the active site of thymidylate synthase.
It inhibits the enzyme CAD, preventing the formation of dihydroorotate.
It inhibits the reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, depleting the N5,N10-methylene THF required for the reaction.
It acts as a structural analog of aspartic acid, blocking the second step of pyrimidine synthesis.
It prevents the hydrolysis of dUTP to dUMP, causing uracil to be incorporated into DNA.
correctOption: It inhibits the reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, depleting the N5,N10-methylene THF required for the reaction.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. 5-Fluorouracil (as 5-FdUMP) competes for the thymidylate synthase site, not methotrexate.
Incorrect. Methotrexate does not affect the early CAD complex (CPS II, ATCase, dihydroorotase).

Correct. Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. This prevents the recycling of dihydrofolate back to tetrahydrofolate (THF). Without THF, the cell cannot produce N5,N10-methylene THF, the methyl donor required by thymidylate synthase to convert dUMP to dTMP.
Incorrect. Methotrexate is a folate analog, not an aspartate analog.
Incorrect. The hydrolysis of dUTP to dUMP is performed by dUTPase, which is not the target of methotrexate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 304 (Book Page): By decreasing the supply of THF, these folate analogs not only inhibit purine synthesis (see Figure 22.7), but, by preventing methylation of dUMP to dTMP, they also lower the cellular concentration of this essential component of DNA.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency is a major cause of autosomal recessive severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). According to the clinical and laboratory diagnostic criteria for this condition, which of the following cellular profiles is expected?
options: Isolated depletion of CD4+ T-lymphocytes.
Selective deficiency of B-lymphocytes with normal T-cell counts.
Normal lymphocyte counts with defective immunoglobulin isotype switching.
Depletion of T-cells, B-cells, and natural killer (NK) cells.
Increased counts of immature lymphoblasts in the bone marrow.
correctOption: Depletion of T-cells, B-cells, and natural killer (NK) cells.
optionExplanations: ADA deficiency is not isolated to CD4+ T-cells; the accumulation of dATP is toxic to all lymphocyte lineages, including B-cells and NK cells.
Selective B-cell deficiency is characteristic of X-linked agammaglobulinemia, whereas ADA deficiency affects both T-cell and B-cell lineages.
Defective isotype switching with normal lymphocyte counts is characteristic of Hyper-IgM syndromes, whereas ADA deficiency presents with profound lymphocytopenia.

ADA deficiency causes a global lymphocytopenia (SCID) affecting T-cells, B-cells, and NK cells because these cells have high levels of kinase activity that produce toxic dATP levels when ADA is absent.
Increased lymphoblasts are seen in leukemia, not in ADA deficiency, where the problem is developmental arrest and apoptosis of lymphocytes.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): In its most severe form, this autosomal recessive disorder causes a type of severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID), involving a decrease in T cells, B cells, and natural killer (NK) cells.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: While most enzymes of the de novo pyrimidine biosynthetic pathway are located in the cytosol, one specific enzyme is associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane. Which enzyme is this?
options: Orotidylate decarboxylase
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
Aspartate transcarbamoylase
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II
Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase
correctOption: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
optionExplanations: Orotidylate decarboxylase is cytosolic, functioning as the second domain of the UMP synthase complex.
Correct. Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, which catalyzes the oxidation of dihydroorotate to orotic acid, is the only mitochondrial enzyme in the pyrimidine de novo pathway.
Aspartate transcarbamoylase is a cytosolic domain of the CAD complex.
CPS II is a cytosolic enzyme and a component of the trifunctional CAD polypeptide.
Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase is cytosolic, functioning as a domain of the UMP synthase complex.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): The enzyme that produces orotate, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, is associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane. All other enzymes in pyrimidine biosynthesis are cytosolic.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: The chemotherapeutic agent 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) acts as a potent antitumor drug by targeting which specific metabolic conversion in pyrimidine synthesis?
options: The amination of UTP to CTP
The decarboxylation of OMP to UMP
The methylation of dUMP to dTMP
The reduction of UDP to dUDP
The oxidation of Dihydroorotate to Orotate
correctOption: The methylation of dUMP to dTMP
optionExplanations: CTP synthetase converts UTP to CTP using glutamine; it is not the primary target of 5-fluorouracil.
The decarboxylation of OMP to UMP is catalyzed by orotidylate decarboxylase (part of UMP synthase), which is deficient in hereditary orotic aciduria, not inhibited by 5-FU.
5-FU is converted to 5-FdUMP, a suicide inhibitor of thymidylate synthase, stopping the methylation of dUMP and thus depleting dTMP for DNA synthesis.
The reduction of UDP to dUDP is catalyzed by ribonucleotide reductase, which is inhibited by hydroxyurea, not 5-FU.
The oxidation of dihydroorotate is catalyzed by dihydroorotate dehydrogenase; 5-FU does not interfere with this mitochondrial step of pyrimidine synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 303 (Book Page): dUMP is converted to dTMP by thymidylate synthase... Inhibitors of thymidylate synthase include thymine analogs such as 5-fluorouracil... 5-Fluorouracil is metabolically converted to 5-FdUMP, which becomes permanently bound to the inactivated thymidylate synthase.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: In human cells, pyrimidine bases are salvaged differently compared to purines. Which of the following statements accurately describes the pyrimidine salvage pathway?
options: Uracil and cytosine are directly converted to UMP and CMP by PRPP-dependent enzymes.
Pyrimidine salvage is the main source of nucleotides for rapid cell division in the bone marrow.
The salvage of orotic acid is the only way to produce UMP in the liver.
Pyrimidine bases are primarily salvaged by phosphoribosyltransferases similar to HGPRT.
The primary salvage mechanism involves the conversion of nucleosides to nucleotides by ATP-dependent kinases.
correctOption: The primary salvage mechanism involves the conversion of nucleosides to nucleotides by ATP-dependent kinases.
optionExplanations: Unlike purines, there are no significant PRPP-dependent salvage enzymes for the free pyrimidine bases uracil and cytosine in human tissues.
De novo synthesis is the primary source of nucleotides; salvage is a minor contributor except in specific clinical settings or treatment scenarios.
The liver is the primary site of de novo synthesis; orotic acid is an intermediate of the de novo pathway, not a salvaged base from the diet.
Purines utilize phosphoribosyltransferases (APRT/HGPRT), but pyrimidines are not salvaged to a significant extent via the free base form in humans.

Pyrimidine salvage in humans relies on nucleoside kinases (e.g., uridine kinase, thymidine kinase) which use ATP to phosphorylate nucleosides (uridine, cytidine, thymidine) into their monophosphate forms.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 304 (Book Page): [the pyrimidine nucleosides can be salvaged by nucleoside kinases that utilize ATP in the phosphorylation of the nucleosides to nucleotides.]

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: Why does treatment with allopurinol lead to a decrease in de novo purine synthesis in patients with a functional salvage pathway?
options: Oxypurinol directly inhibits the glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase enzyme
Xanthine oxidase inhibition leads to the accumulation of fumarate, a pathway inhibitor
The drug increases the intracellular concentration of PRPP, which destabilizes the pathway
Allopurinol prevents the transport of aspartate into the purine biosynthetic pathway
Accumulated hypoxanthine is salvaged to IMP, which feedback-inhibits the committed step
correctOption: Accumulated hypoxanthine is salvaged to IMP, which feedback-inhibits the committed step
optionExplanations: Oxypurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, not the amidotransferase directly; the inhibition of the latter is a secondary effect of increased nucleotide levels.
Xanthine oxidase does not produce fumarate; adenylosuccinate lyase produces fumarate during the conversion of IMP to AMP.
Salvage of hypoxanthine (promoted by allopurinol) actually decreases the levels of PRPP because HGPRT uses PRPP as a ribose-5-phosphate donor.
Aspartate transport is not affected by allopurinol; it is a substrate for both purine and pyrimidine rings and remains available.

When xanthine oxidase is inhibited, hypoxanthine levels rise. This hypoxanthine is salvaged by HGPRT to form IMP, which consumes PRPP and provides allosteric feedback inhibition to glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): [In patients with normal levels of HGPRT, the hypoxanthine can be salvaged, thus reducing the levels of PRPP and, therefore, de novo purine synthesis.]

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: A 45-year-old male who recently underwent a renal transplant is prescribed Mycophenolic acid to prevent graft rejection. This drug exerts its immunosuppressive effect by selectively depriving rapidly proliferating T and B cells of which nucleotide through the inhibition of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase?
options: Hypoxanthine
Adenosine monophosphate (AMP)
Xanthosine monophosphate (XMP)
Guanosine monophosphate (GMP)
Inosine monophosphate (IMP)
correctOption: Guanosine monophosphate (GMP)
optionExplanations: Hypoxanthine is the base component of IMP; it is not the nucleotide whose synthesis is blocked by Mycophenolic acid.
AMP synthesis is not inhibited by Mycophenolic acid, as its synthesis branch starts with adenylosuccinate synthetase, not IMP dehydrogenase.
While XMP levels would also fall, GMP is the functional 'key component of nucleic acids' and the ultimate end product whose deficiency mediates the drug's effect.

Correct. Mycophenolic acid inhibits IMP dehydrogenase, the rate-limiting enzyme that converts IMP to XMP. This blockade specifically prevents the formation of GMP, which lymphocytes rely on for proliferation during an immune response.
IMP is the substrate that accumulates when the enzyme is inhibited; the cell is not deprived of IMP, but rather the products downstream of it (XMP and GMP).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): The drug is a reversible, uncompetitive inhibitor of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase. The drug deprives rapidly proliferating T and B cells of key components of nucleic acids.

category: Interpret Orotic aciduria in relevance to nucleotides and urea
statement: The de novo synthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides involves a bifunctional protein in its later stages. Which two catalytic activities are associated with this single polypeptide chain in human cells?
options: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II and Aspartate transcarbamoylase
Aspartate transcarbamoylase and Dihydroorotase
Orotidylate decarboxylase and Thymidylate synthase
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase and Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase
Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and Orotidylate decarboxylase
correctOption: Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and Orotidylate decarboxylase
optionExplanations: These are the first two domains of the CAD multifunctional polypeptide, not UMP synthase. CAD is a trifunctional enzyme in the initial steps of the pathway.
Aspartate transcarbamoylase and Dihydroorotase are the second and third domains of the CAD complex, respectively.
Thymidylate synthase is a separate enzyme involved in dTMP synthesis and is not part of the UMP synthase bifunctional complex.
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is a separate enzyme associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane, unlike the cytosolic UMP synthase.
UMP synthase is a single polypeptide with two distinct catalytic domains: orotate phosphoribosyltransferase (which adds PRPP to orotate) and orotidylate decarboxylase (which converts OMP to UMP).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): Orotate phosphoribosyl transferase and orotidylate decarboxylase are also catalytic domains of a single polypeptide chain called UMP synthase.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: Mycophenolic acid is used as an immunosuppressant to prevent graft rejection. This drug specifically targets which metabolic step to deprive proliferating T and B cells of nucleic acid components?
options: The phosphorylation of adenosine by adenosine kinase
The oxidation of hypoxanthine to xanthine
The reduction of ribonucleoside diphosphates to deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates
The reversible inhibition of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase
The conversion of IMP to adenylosuccinate
correctOption: The reversible inhibition of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase
optionExplanations: Adenosine kinase phosphorylates adenosine to AMP in the salvage pathway; it is not the target of mycophenolic acid.
The oxidation of hypoxanthine to xanthine is catalyzed by xanthine oxidase, which is the target of allopurinol, used for gout rather than immunosuppression.
The reduction of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides is catalyzed by ribonucleotide reductase, which is inhibited by hydroxyurea, not mycophenolic acid.

Mycophenolic acid targets IMP dehydrogenase, the enzyme that converts IMP to xanthosine monophosphate (XMP) on the pathway to GMP. T and B cells are particularly dependent on this pathway for proliferation.
The conversion of IMP to adenylosuccinate is the first step toward AMP synthesis, catalyzed by adenylosuccinate synthetase, which is not the target of mycophenolic acid.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): The drug [Mycophenolic Acid] is a reversible, uncompetitive inhibitor of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase. The drug deprives rapidly proliferating T and B cells of key components of nucleic acids.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: In the metabolic transition from inosine monophosphate to its final adenine and guanine nucleotide derivatives, which enzymatic step is correctly matched with the byproduct it releases?
options: GMP Synthetase : Pyrophosphate (PPi)
Adenylosuccinate Lyase : Glutamate
Nucleoside Diphosphate Kinase : Water
Adenylosuccinate Synthetase : NADH
IMP Dehydrogenase : Fumarate
correctOption: GMP Synthetase : Pyrophosphate (PPi)
optionExplanations: GMP Synthetase utilizes ATP to catalyze the amination of XMP. In the process, ATP is cleaved into AMP and inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi).
Adenylosuccinate Lyase (also called adenylosuccinase) releases fumarate as it cleaves adenylosuccinate to form AMP. Glutamate is released by GMP synthetase.
Nucleoside Diphosphate Kinase involves the transfer of a phosphate group from a triphosphate to a diphosphate, generally releasing an NDP (like ADP), not water.
Adenylosuccinate Synthetase releases GDP and Pi from GTP hydrolysis; it does not produce NADH. NADH is produced by IMP dehydrogenase.
IMP Dehydrogenase releases NADH, not fumarate. Fumarate is released during the second step of AMP synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): GMP synthetase converts XMP to GMP using ATP, Glutamine and H2O, releasing Glutamate, AMP and PP i.

category: Interpret the Lesh-Nhyan syndrome
statement: Which of the following clinical presentations is considered a hallmark behavioral feature of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, distinguishing it from other causes of pediatric hyperuricemia?
options: Progressive liver cirrhosis
Severe combined immunodeficiency
Compulsive self-mutilation
Intermittent claudication
Photosensitive dermatitis
correctOption: Compulsive self-mutilation
optionExplanations: Liver cirrhosis is associated with disorders like Wilson's disease or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, but not with purine salvage defects.
Severe combined immunodeficiency is the hallmark of Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency, not HGPRT deficiency.
Self-mutilation, specifically biting of the lips and fingers, is a unique and characteristic behavioral sign of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and is rarely seen in other metabolic disorders.
Intermittent claudication is a sign of peripheral arterial disease, usually seen in adults with atherosclerosis, not in pediatric metabolic syndromes.
Photosensitive dermatitis is characteristic of Hartnup disease (tryptophan transport defect) or Pellagra (niacin deficiency), but not Lesch-Nyhan.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): In addition, the syndrome is characterized by motor dysfunction, cognitive deficits, and behavioral disturbances that include self-mutilation (biting of lips and fingers, Figure 22.11).

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
statement: A 22-year-old female presents with symptoms of a urinary tract infection. She is prescribed a sulfonamide antibiotic. This medication inhibits the growth of the causative E. coli by indirectly reducing the availability of which essential carbon donor required for the synthesis of the purine ring positions C2 and C8?
options: N5, N10-Methylene tetrahydrofolate
Glutamine γ-amide group
N10-Formyltetrahydrofolate
Carbamoyl phosphate
Aspartic acid
correctOption: N10-Formyltetrahydrofolate
optionExplanations: N5, N10-Methylene THF is used in the synthesis of dTMP from dUMP, not for the C2/C8 positions of the purine ring.
Glutamine provides nitrogen atoms at positions N3 and N9 of the purine ring, not the carbon atoms at C2 and C8.
N10-Formyl-THF is the specific donor of the one-carbon units for the C2 and C8 positions of the purine ring. Sulfonamides deplete THF, thereby depleting N10-Formyl-THF.
Carbamoyl phosphate is essential for pyrimidine synthesis (via CPS II) and the urea cycle (via CPS I), but not as a carbon donor for the purine ring.
Aspartic acid provides the nitrogen at position N1 of the purine ring, not the carbon atoms at C2 and C8.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): Two steps in the pathway [purine synthesis] require N10-formyltetrahydrofolate. Page 294 (Book Page): Because purine synthesis requires tetrahydrofolate as a coenzyme, the sulfa drugs slow down this pathway in bacteria.

category: Interpret Orotic aciduria in relevance to nucleotides and urea
coreConcept: Precursor Atoms of the Pyrimidine Ring
statement: The pyrimidine ring is synthesized as a free base prior to its attachment to the ribose-5-phosphate moiety. Which of the following combinations of precursors provides all the necessary atoms for the construction of this ring in mammalian cells?
options: Aspartic acid, Glycine, and CO2
Glutamine, Aspartic acid, and N10-formyltetrahydrofolate
Glycine, CO2, and Glutamine
Aspartic acid, CO2, and Glutamine
Glycine, CO2, and Aspartic acid
correctOption: Aspartic acid, CO2, and Glutamine
optionExplanations: Glycine is not involved in pyrimidine synthesis; it is a hallmark of the purine ring construction.

While glutamine and aspartic acid are required, N10-formyltetrahydrofolate is a one-carbon donor used exclusively in purine synthesis and the conversion of dUMP to dTMP, but not for the initial ring formation of orotate.
Glycine is a primary precursor for the purine ring, not the pyrimidine ring. In purines, glycine provides carbons 4 and 5 and nitrogen 7.

Correct. According to the biosynthetic pathway, glutamine provides the amide nitrogen, CO2 provides the carbon at position 2, and aspartic acid provides the remaining carbons and nitrogen (C4, C5, C6, and N1) of the pyrimidine ring.
Glycine is incorrect, as it is used in the synthesis of the purine ring, specifically adding a three-atom unit (C-C-N) early in that pathway.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): The sources of the atoms in the pyrimidine ring are glutamine, CO2, and aspartic acid (Figure 22.19). [Note: Glutamine and aspartic acid are thus required for both purine and pyrimidine synthesis.]

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: A pharmacological agent is utilized as an immunosuppressant to prevent graft rejection by specifically targeting the conversion of inosine monophosphate (IMP) to guanosine monophosphate (GMP). Which of the following describes the mechanism of this drug?
options: Inhibition of the reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate
Activation of 5'-nucleotidase in T and B cells
Competitive inhibition of adenylosuccinate synthetase
Irreversible inhibition of xanthine oxidase
Reversible, uncompetitive inhibition of IMP dehydrogenase
correctOption: Reversible, uncompetitive inhibition of IMP dehydrogenase
optionExplanations: Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase is the mechanism of methotrexate, which affects both purine and pyrimidine synthesis, not just the IMP-to-GMP step.
Activation of 5'-nucleotidase would promote degradation of nucleotides, but it is not the mechanism of standard immunosuppressant drugs in this pathway.
Adenylosuccinate synthetase is involved in the conversion of IMP to AMP, not GMP; it is not the target of mycophenolic acid.
Xanthine oxidase is inhibited by allopurinol, which is used for gout treatment, not for primary immunosuppression in graft rejection.
Mycophenolic acid acts as a reversible, uncompetitive inhibitor of IMP dehydrogenase, the enzyme that converts IMP to Xanthosine monophosphate (the precursor to GMP).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): MYCOPHENOLIC ACID: The drug is a reversible, uncompetitive inhibitor of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase... The drug deprives rapidly proliferating T and B cells of key components of nucleic acids.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: During the conversion of 2'-deoxyuridine monophosphate (dUMP) to 2'-deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP), a specific antineoplastic drug acts as a 'suicide inhibitor' by permanently binding to the active site of the enzyme. Which pharmacological agent exhibits this specific regulatory inhibition?
options: Mycophenolic acid
Allopurinol
5-Fluorouracil
Methotrexate
Hydroxyurea
correctOption: 5-Fluorouracil
optionExplanations: Mycophenolic acid is a reversible, uncompetitive inhibitor of IMP dehydrogenase, used primarily as an immunosuppressant.
Allopurinol is an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase used to treat gout; it does not interfere with the dUMP to dTMP conversion.
5-Fluorouracil is converted to 5-FdUMP, which acts as a suicide inhibitor of thymidylate synthase by forming a covalent complex with the enzyme and its folate cofactor.
Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), reducing the pool of tetrahydrofolate. It is a competitive inhibitor, not a suicide inhibitor of thymidylate synthase.
Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase by destroying the tyrosyl free radical; it does not target thymidylate synthase as a suicide inhibitor.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 304 (Book Page): 5-Fluorouracil is metabolically converted to 5-FdUMP, which becomes permanently bound to the inactivated thymidylate synthase; for this reason, the drug is called a “suicide” inhibitor.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: Following the synthesis of nucleoside monophosphates (NMPs), further phosphorylation to diphosphates (NDPs) occurs. Which characteristic distinguishes the monophosphate kinases from the diphosphate kinases in the liver?
options: Monophosphate kinases utilize only GTP, while diphosphate kinases utilize only ATP.
Monophosphate kinases are only active in the mitochondria, while diphosphate kinases are cytosolic.
Monophosphate kinases are base-specific, while diphosphate kinases have broad specificity.
Monophosphate kinases have broad substrate specificity, while diphosphate kinases are base-specific.
Monophosphate kinases only act on deoxyribose sugars, while diphosphate kinases act on both.
correctOption: Monophosphate kinases are base-specific, while diphosphate kinases have broad specificity.
optionExplanations: Both classes of kinases generally utilize ATP as the phosphate donor due to its high intracellular concentration, not GTP.
The text does not restrict these enzymes to the mitochondria; adenylate kinase is noted for high activity in liver and muscle cytosol to maintain energy equilibrium.

NMP kinases (e.g., adenylate kinase, guanylate kinase) recognize only specific bases (adenine, guanine), whereas nucleoside diphosphate kinase can transfer phosphates between any NDP and NTP regardless of the base.
This is the reverse of the actual enzyme characteristics. Monophosphate kinases (like adenylate kinase) are highly specific to the nitrogenous base.
The reference states that NMP kinases do not discriminate between ribose and deoxyribose; both sugar types are processed by the same enzymes.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page) / 531: Nucleoside diphosphates are synthesized from the corresponding nucleoside monophosphates by base-specific nucleoside monophosphate kinases... Nucleoside diphosphates and triphosphates are interconverted by nucleoside diphosphate kinase—an enzyme that, unlike the monophosphate kinases, has broad specificity.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: During the conversion of deoxyuridine monophosphate (dUMP) to deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP), a specific coenzyme undergoes a unique chemical change. What accurately describes this transformation?
options: N5,N10-methylene tetrahydrofolate is reduced to dihydrofolate
N5,N10-methylene tetrahydrofolate is oxidized to dihydrofolate
N10-formyltetrahydrofolate donates a formyl group and remains as THF
Tetrahydrofolate is directly methylated by S-adenosylmethionine
Dihydrofolate is reduced to tetrahydrofolate by thymidylate synthase
correctOption: N5,N10-methylene tetrahydrofolate is oxidized to dihydrofolate
optionExplanations: The folate carrier is oxidized, not reduced, because it loses two hydrogen atoms during the transfer of the methyl group.
Thymidylate synthase is unique because the THF derivative acts as both a carbon donor and a reducing agent, resulting in the formation of DHF.
N10-formyltetrahydrofolate is used in purine synthesis, not in the thymidylate synthase reaction.
The methyl group for dTMP comes from the methylene group of N5,N10-methylene THF, not from SAM.
Dihydrofolate is reduced to THF by dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), not by thymidylate synthase; the latter produces DHF from THF.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 303 (Book Page): This is an unusual reaction in that tetrahydrofolate (THF) contributes not only a one-carbon unit but also two hydrogen atoms from the pteridine ring, resulting in the oxidation of THF to dihydrofolate (DHF).

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
coreConcept: ADA Deficiency and Ribonucleotide Reductase Inhibition
statement: A deficiency in adenosine deaminase (ADA) leads to severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) primarily through which intermediate metabolic inhibition?
options: Depletion of inorganic phosphate due to adenosine phosphorylation halts ATP production via substrate-level phosphorylation.
High levels of inosine monophosphate (IMP) competitively inhibit the commitment step of pyrimidine biosynthesis.
Excessive dATP levels allosterically inhibit ribonucleotide reductase, preventing the synthesis of other deoxyribonucleotides.
Accumulation of adenosine leads to the irreversible activation of xanthine oxidase, depleting the cell of guanine.
Adenosine accumulation triggers the overproduction of PRPP, leading to metabolic exhaustion of the liver.
correctOption: Excessive dATP levels allosterically inhibit ribonucleotide reductase, preventing the synthesis of other deoxyribonucleotides.
optionExplanations: While phosphate depletion can occur in some metabolic disorders (like fructose intolerance), the primary pathology in SCID/ADA is the specific inhibition of DNA synthesis by dATP.
IMP is a parent purine nucleotide; its accumulation is not the primary driver of ADA deficiency pathology, nor does it typically inhibit pyrimidine synthesis in this manner.

ADA deficiency causes adenosine and deoxyadenosine to accumulate. Deoxyadenosine is phosphorylated to dATP. High dATP is a potent allosteric inhibitor of ribonucleotide reductase, which blocks the production of dCDP, dUDP, and dGDP, effectively halting DNA replication.
Xanthine oxidase is involved in the later stages of purine catabolism; its activation would increase uric acid rather than causing the developmental arrest of lymphocytes seen in ADA deficiency.
PRPP levels are increased in HGPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan), not ADA deficiency. In ADA deficiency, the critical issue is the dATP-mediated block of ribonucleotide reductase.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): As dATP levels rise, ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited, thus preventing the production of all deoxyribose-containing nucleotides (see Page 289 (Book Page)). Consequently, cells cannot make DNA and divide.

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
coreConcept: Differential Pharmacology of Folate Path Inhibitors
statement: A researcher compares the pharmacological profiles of methotrexate and sulfonamides. Although both eventually interfere with purine synthesis, which statement correctly differentiates their mechanisms of action and toxicities?
options: Both drugs are PABA analogs, but methotrexate also inhibits pyrimidine degradation.
Methotrexate inhibits folate reduction in humans, while sulfonamides inhibit folate synthesis in bacteria.
Sulfonamides inhibit human purine synthesis, while methotrexate is bacteria-specific.
Methotrexate acts on IMP dehydrogenase, while sulfonamides act on PRPP synthetase.
Sulfonamides cause hair loss and anemia, whereas methotrexate is generally non-toxic to human hair follicles.
correctOption: Methotrexate inhibits folate reduction in humans, while sulfonamides inhibit folate synthesis in bacteria.
optionExplanations: Methotrexate is a folic acid analog, not a PABA analog. Sulfonamides are PABA analogs.
Correct. Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (folate reduction) and affects human cells. Sulfonamides inhibit the bacterial production of folate from PABA, a process humans do not possess.
This is reversed. Sulfonamides are selective for bacteria, whereas methotrexate targets human (and bacterial) cells.

Methotrexate targets dihydrofolate reductase; sulfonamides target the bacterial dihydropteroate synthase (folate synthesis path). Neither targets IMP dehydrogenase (mycophenolic acid) or PRPP synthetase.

Methotrexate causes toxicity to rapidly dividing human cells (hair follicles, GI tract), while sulfonamides do not interfere with human purine synthesis and thus do not cause these specific side effects.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page): Sulfonamides are structural analogs of para-aminobenzoic acid that competitively inhibit bacterial synthesis of folic acid... structural analogs of folic acid (for example, methotrexate), are used pharmacologically to control the spread of cancer... [they] are also toxic to all dividing cells [in humans].

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
coreConcept: Initial step of AMP synthesis from IMP
statement: In the de novo biosynthetic pathway, which specific enzyme is responsible for the first committed step in the diversion of inosine monophosphate (IMP) toward the synthesis of adenosine monophosphate (AMP)?
options: IMP dehydrogenase
Adenylosuccinate lyase
GMP synthetase
Adenylosuccinate synthetase
Adenylate kinase
correctOption: Adenylosuccinate synthetase
optionExplanations: IMP dehydrogenase is the enzyme for the first step of GMP synthesis, not AMP synthesis; it converts IMP to xanthosine monophosphate (XMP).
Adenylosuccinate lyase (also called adenylosuccinase) performs the second step in AMP synthesis, which is the cleavage of adenylosuccinate to release AMP and fumarate.
GMP synthetase is involved in the second step of GMP synthesis, converting xanthosine monophosphate (XMP) to guanosine monophosphate (GMP).
Adenylosuccinate synthetase is the correct enzyme that catalyzes the condensation of IMP and aspartate to form adenylosuccinate, the first step in AMP production.
Adenylate kinase is involved in the interconversion of AMP, ADP, and ATP to maintain energy equilibrium, rather than the de novo synthesis of AMP from IMP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): The conversion of IMP to either AMP or GMP uses a two-step, energy-requiring pathway (Figure 22.8). ... Adenylosuccinate synthetase [catalyzes the first step from IMP to Adenylosuccinate].

category: Interpret Orotic aciduria in relevance to nucleotides and urea
