citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): [Figure 22.20 and Section VI.A] Carbamoyl phosphate, synthesized by CPS I, is also a precursor of urea. ...Defects in ornithine transcarbamylase of the urea cycle promote pyrimidine synthesis due to increased availability of carbamoyl phosphate.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: In the de novo synthesis of purine nucleotides, the reaction converting 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP) to 5'-phosphoribosylamine serves as the committed step. Which mechanism best describes the regulation of this step by intracellular nucleotides?
options: Induction of the enzyme glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase by hypoxanthine
Activation by high levels of AMP and GMP via allosteric binding to the catalytic site
Feed-forward activation by UTP to maintain a balance with pyrimidines
Inhibition by AMP and GMP and activation by the substrate PRPP
Competitive inhibition by ATP for the glutamine binding site
correctOption: Inhibition by AMP and GMP and activation by the substrate PRPP
optionExplanations: Hypoxanthine is a purine base involved in the salvage pathway; it does not induce the de novo enzyme but rather leads to feedback inhibition if salvaged into IMP/GMP.
Purine nucleotides (AMP, GMP) are end-products of the pathway and act as inhibitors, not activators, to prevent the wasteful overproduction of nucleotides when levels are sufficient.
UTP is a pyrimidine nucleotide and regulates the pyrimidine synthesis pathway via carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II; it does not activate the purine committed step.

The enzyme glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase is subject to feedback inhibition by AMP and GMP (end-product inhibition). Conversely, since the intracellular concentration of PRPP is usually low, increases in its concentration act as a potent activator to drive the pathway forward.

ATP is actually required as an energy source in subsequent steps of the pathway and is an activator of PRPP synthetase (when compared to inhibition by purine nucleotides) and ribonucleotide reductase; it is not a competitive inhibitor at the glutamine site for this specific enzyme according to the mechanistic details of end-product control cited on page 301/303 for the amidotransferase step specifically being inhibited by the mono-phosphates AMP/GMP specifically as stated in Figure 22.7 and the text in Section III.B page 301/302/303 references provided for purine synthesis inhibition controls specifically on the amidotransferase enzyme which the text explicitly says is inhibited by AMP and GMP specifically as end products of that path (de novo) specifically for purines.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): The enzyme, glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase, is inhibited by the purine 5'-nucleotides AMP and GMP—the end products of the pathway. This is the committed step in purine nucleotide biosynthesis. The rate of the reaction is also controlled by the intracellular concentration of PRPP.

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: Colchicine is frequently used to manage acute attacks of gouty arthritis. What is its specific mechanism of action in this context?
options: Prevention of microtubule formation to inhibit neutrophil migration
Inhibition of xanthine oxidase to lower plasma urate
Competitive inhibition of PRPP amidotransferase
Increasing the renal clearance of uric acid by inhibiting URAT1
Chemical dissolution of existing monosodium urate tophi
correctOption: Prevention of microtubule formation to inhibit neutrophil migration
optionExplanations: Colchicine binds to tubulin and prevents its polymerization into microtubules. Since neutrophils rely on microtubules for chemotaxis and movement, this drug effectively stops them from migrating into the joint space to respond to urate crystals.
Xanthine oxidase inhibition is the mechanism of allopurinol and febuxostat, which are used for chronic management, not acute inflammation.
PRPP amidotransferase is a de novo synthesis enzyme; colchicine does not interfere with the biochemical pathways of purine synthesis.
Uricosuric agents like probenecid increase renal clearance, but colchicine has no effect on the systemic or local levels of uric acid.
Colchicine is an anti-inflammatory agent and does not possess the chemical properties required to dissolve solid urate crystals or tophi.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): Colchicine prevents formation of microtubules, thus decreasing the movement of neutrophils into the affected area. Like the other anti-inflammatory drugs, it has no effect on uric acid levels.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: In the de novo synthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides, which of the following molecules acts as the primary contributor of the nitrogen atom at position 1 and the carbon atoms at positions 4, 5, and 6 of the pyrimidine ring?
options: Aspartic acid
N10-Formyltetrahydrofolate
Glutamine
Carbon dioxide
Glycine
correctOption: Aspartic acid
optionExplanations: Aspartic acid is the source of the majority of the pyrimidine ring, specifically providing nitrogen at N1 and carbons at C4, C5, and C6 via the formation of carbamoyl aspartate.

N10-Formyltetrahydrofolate is a one-carbon donor essential for purine synthesis (C2 and C8) but is not involved in the formation of the initial pyrimidine ring (Orotate). Methylation of dUMP to dTMP requires N5,N10-methylene THF, not N10-formyl THF for the ring itself.
Glutamine provides the amide nitrogen (N3) of the pyrimidine ring but does not contribute to the carbon skeleton at positions 4, 5, or 6.
Carbon dioxide (as bicarbonate) contributes only the carbon atom at position 2 (C2) of the pyrimidine ring through the action of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II.
Glycine is a major precursor for the purine ring (contributing C4, C5, and N7), but it is not utilized in the synthesis of the pyrimidine ring.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page): The sources of the atoms in the pyrimidine ring are glutamine, CO2, and aspartic acid (Figure 22.19).

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: In the reduction of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides, which of the following molecules provides the ultimate source of reducing equivalents to return thioredoxin to its reduced state?
options: Ascorbate
Glutathione
NADPH
NADH
FADH2
correctOption: NADPH
optionExplanations: Ascorbate (Vitamin C) acts as a reducing agent in many biochemical pathways, such as collagen synthesis, but it does not play a role in the regeneration of thioredoxin for DNA precursor synthesis.
While glutathione is a major cellular antioxidant and can participate in some redox reactions, the specific coenzyme pathway for ribonucleotide reductase involves thioredoxin and NADPH.
NADPH provides the hydrogen atoms needed to reduce the disulfide bond in oxidized thioredoxin, a reaction catalyzed by thioredoxin reductase.
NADH is primarily used in catabolic reactions for ATP production in the mitochondria; NADPH is the preferred cofactor for reductive biosynthesis, including thioredoxin reduction.
FADH2 is involved in the electron transport chain and other metabolic reactions like those of dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, but it is not the reducing agent for thioredoxin.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 289 (Book Page): The necessary reducing equivalents are provided by NADPH + H+, and the reaction is catalyzed by thioredoxin reductase.

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: In which of the following human cell types is the cytoplasmic enzyme Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) expressed with the highest level of activity?
options: Enterocytes
Myocytes
Hepatocytes
Osteocytes
Lymphocytes
correctOption: Lymphocytes
optionExplanations: Intestinal mucosal cells (enterocytes) degrade dietary purines to uric acid, but their ADA activity is lower than that of the lymphocyte population.
Muscle cells (myocytes) have high adenylate kinase activity for energy turnover, but they are not the primary site of high ADA expression.
While the liver (hepatocytes) is a major site of purine metabolism, it does not possess the highest levels of ADA activity compared to immune cells.
Osteocytes (bone cells) do not have a prominent role in the systemic purine degradation pathway or high levels of ADA expression.
The text explicitly states that although ADA is found in many tissues, it is most active in lymphocytes, which explains why they are most affected by its deficiency.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): ADA is expressed in a variety of tissues, but, in humans, lymphocytes have the highest activity of this cytoplasmic enzyme.

category: Interpret Orotic aciduria in relevance to nucleotides and urea
coreConcept: Secondary Orotic Aciduria in OTC Deficiency
statement: A 4-day-old male neonate is hospitalized for lethargy and poor feeding. Lab tests show a plasma ammonia of 450 µmol/L and significant orotic aciduria. There is no megaloblastic anemia. The high levels of orotic acid in this specific context are most likely the result of which physiological mechanism?
options: A deficiency in dihydroorotate dehydrogenase leading to precursor accumulation.
Inhibition of UMP synthase by high levels of ammonium ions.
Excess mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate entering the cytosol to saturate CPS II inhibitors.
Increased de novo synthesis of PRPP due to hyperammonemia.
Spillover of mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate into the cytosol, bypassing the CPS II regulated step.
correctOption: Spillover of mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate into the cytosol, bypassing the CPS II regulated step.
optionExplanations: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase deficiency is not associated with hyperammonemia. The clinical picture of high ammonia and orotic aciduria is classic for OTC deficiency.
High ammonia does not inhibit UMP synthase; it primarily affects neuronal function and the urea cycle.
The mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate does not 'saturate inhibitors'; it acts as a substrate that enters the pyrimidine pathway downstream of the CPS II regulated step.
Hyperammonemia does not directly increase PRPP synthesis; the elevation in orotic acid is substrate-driven by carbamoyl phosphate.

In OTC deficiency, carbamoyl phosphate cannot be converted to citrulline. It accumulates in the mitochondria and leaks into the cytosol, where it provides a massive amount of substrate for the pyrimidine pathway, bypassing the normal regulatory control of CPS II.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): [Note: Carbamoyl phosphate, synthesized by CPS I, is also a precursor of urea (see Page 245 (Book Page)). Defects in ornithine transcarbamylase of the urea cycle promote pyrimidine synthesis due to increased availability of carbamoyl phosphate.]

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: The purine ring is a complex bicyclic structure whose atoms are derived from multiple metabolic precursors. Which specific amino acid provides the atoms located at positions C4, C5, and N7 of the completed ring?
options: Aspartate
Serine
Glycine
Alanine
Glutamine
correctOption: Glycine
optionExplanations: Aspartate provides the nitrogen atom at position N1 of the purine ring.
Serine is not a direct donor of atoms to the purine ring, although its derivatives may contribute to the folate pool.
Glycine provides the entirety of the C4, C5, and N7 atoms, which are added in the early stages of the de novo pathway.
Alanine does not contribute any atoms to the synthesis of the purine ring.
Glutamine provides nitrogen atoms at positions N3 and N9 of the purine ring.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): The atoms of the purine ring are contributed by a number of compounds, including amino acids (aspartic acid, glycine, and glutamine), CO2, and N10–formyltetrahydrofolate (Figure 22.5). [Figure 22.5 shows Glycine contributing 4, 5, 7].

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: A 5-year-old male with a history of recurrent pulmonary infections and delayed neurodevelopment is found to have significantly low T-cell counts, while B-cell counts and immunoglobulin levels are within normal limits. Based on the selective depletion of T-cells, a deficiency in which purine degradation enzyme is most likely?
options: Adenosine deaminase (ADA)
5'-nucleotidase
Guanase
AMP deaminase
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP)
correctOption: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP)
optionExplanations: ADA deficiency is more severe, leading to SCID with depletion of T, B, and NK cells, not just T-cells.
5'-nucleotidase converts mononucleotides to nucleosides; its deficiency is not a recognized cause of T-cell specific immunodeficiency.
Guanase is involved in converting guanine to xanthine; its deficiency is not associated with this specific T-cell immunodeficiency pattern.
AMP deaminase deficiency primarily affects skeletal muscle (causing exercise-induced myalgia), not the immune system.
PNP deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder that selectively affects T-cell immunity, sparing B-cells, and is often accompanied by neurodevelopmental issues.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) deficiency results in a less severe immunodeficiency involving T-cells primarily.

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: Which molecule is correctly identified as the 'parent' purine nucleotide that serves as the immediate precursor for the branched synthesis of both AMP and GMP?
options: PRPP
Hypoxanthine
Adenosine monophosphate (AMP)
Inosine monophosphate (IMP)
5'-phosphoribosylamine
correctOption: Inosine monophosphate (IMP)
optionExplanations: PRPP is an activated pentose sugar used as a substrate at the beginning of the pathway, but it is not a purine nucleotide itself.
Hypoxanthine is the nitrogenous base found in IMP, but the term 'parent purine nucleotide' refers to the whole nucleotide structure (base + sugar + phosphate), which is IMP.
AMP is an end-product of one of the branches, not the parent precursor for both.

Inosine monophosphate (IMP) is known as the 'parent' purine nucleotide because it is the first complete purine nucleotide formed, and it serves as the common starting point for the two branches leading to AMP and GMP.
5'-phosphoribosylamine is the first intermediate formed in the committed step of the de novo pathway, but it does not have the purine ring structure yet.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): Synthesis of inosine monophosphate, the 'parent' purine nucleotide... [and Page 295 (Book Page)] E. Conversion of IMP to AMP and GMP.

category: Differentiate between CPS I and II
coreConcept: Subcellular Compartmentalization of CPS I and II
statement: Which of the following describes the correct cellular location for Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase I (CPS I) and Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase II (CPS II) in human hepatocytes?
options: CPS I: Mitochondria; CPS II: Cytosol
CPS I: Endoplasmic Reticulum; CPS II: Nucleus
CPS I: Cytosol; CPS II: Mitochondria
CPS I: Mitochondria; CPS II: Mitochondria
CPS I: Cytosol; CPS II: Cytosol
correctOption: CPS I: Mitochondria; CPS II: Cytosol
optionExplanations: This is correct. CPS I is localized within the mitochondrial matrix to facilitate the urea cycle, whereas CPS II is found in the cytosol to initiate de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis.
Neither CPS I nor CPS II are primarily associated with the endoplasmic reticulum or the nucleus for their catalytic functions.

CPS I is not found in the cytosol; it is a mitochondrial enzyme necessary for the first step of the urea cycle where it fixes ammonia. CPS II is not mitochondrial; it is the cytosolic initiating enzyme for pyrimidine synthesis.
While CPS I is indeed mitochondrial, CPS II is a cytosolic enzyme. Both enzymes are not located in the mitochondria.
While CPS II is indeed cytosolic, CPS I is a mitochondrial enzyme. Both enzymes are not located in the cytosol.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): [Figure 22.20 Summary of the differences between carbamoyl phosphate synthetase (CPS) I and II] Cellular location: CPS I - Mitochondria; CPS II - Cytosol

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
statement: Which of the following describes the nature of the interaction between Mycophenolic acid and its target enzyme, Inosine Monophosphate Dehydrogenase?
options: Allosteric activation of a regulatory subunit
Reversible, uncompetitive inhibition
Competitive inhibition for the IMP binding site
Irreversible covalent modification
Non-reversible suicide inhibition
correctOption: Reversible, uncompetitive inhibition
optionExplanations: The drug acts as an inhibitor of the catalytic function, not as an allosteric activator.
According to the text, the drug acts in a reversible and uncompetitive manner against IMP dehydrogenase. This means it binds to the enzyme-substrate complex rather than the free enzyme.
Uncompetitive inhibition is distinct from competitive inhibition; in uncompetitive inhibition, the inhibitor does not compete for the active site of the free enzyme.
Mycophenolic acid is described as reversible, not an irreversible covalent inhibitor.
Suicide inhibitors are irreversible and covalent (e.g., 5-fluorouracil for thymidylate synthase). Mycophenolic acid is reversible.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): [Figure 22.8] The drug is a reversible, uncompetitive inhibitor of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: In the de novo synthesis of purine nucleotides, the conversion of the parent molecule inosine monophosphate (IMP) to AMP and GMP is tightly regulated to ensure balanced nucleotide pools. What is a key feature of this reciprocal regulation?
options: IMP is converted to XMP by the action of adenylosuccinate synthetase
Both AMP and GMP inhibit the enzyme carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II
AMP synthesis requires ATP as an energy source
AMP synthesis requires GTP, while GMP synthesis requires ATP
GMP synthesis requires GTP as an energy source
correctOption: AMP synthesis requires GTP, while GMP synthesis requires ATP
optionExplanations: IMP is converted to XMP by IMP dehydrogenase; adenylosuccinate synthetase is the enzyme that converts IMP to adenylosuccinate in the AMP branch.
CPS II is the regulated enzyme for pyrimidine synthesis and is inhibited by UTP, not by the purine nucleotides AMP or GMP.
AMP synthesis requires GTP, not ATP. Using GTP ensures that if guanine nucleotides are abundant, adenine nucleotide synthesis is promoted.

This is the core of reciprocal regulation in purine metabolism: the synthesis of each purine nucleotide requires the 'opposite' purine triphosphate as an energy source, ensuring that the cell does not overproduce one while lacking the other.
GMP synthesis requires ATP, not GTP. This ensures that if adenine nucleotides are abundant (high ATP), guanine nucleotide synthesis is promoted.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): Note that the synthesis of AMP requires guanosine triphosphate (GTP) as an energy source, whereas the synthesis of GMP requires ATP. Also, the first reaction in each pathway is inhibited by the end product of that pathway. This provides a mechanism for diverting IMP to the synthesis of the species of purine present in lesser amounts.

category: Interpret the Lesh-Nhyan syndrome
statement: In Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, the deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase leads to a massive up-regulation of the de novo purine synthesis pathway. What specific metabolic change contributes to this up-regulation by affecting the rate-limiting amidotransferase enzyme?
options: Accumulation of ATP as a required energy source
Increased degradation of dietary nucleic acids
Decreased intracellular levels of IMP and GMP
Increased conversion of xanthine to uric acid
Direct allosteric activation by hypoxanthine
correctOption: Decreased intracellular levels of IMP and GMP
optionExplanations: While ATP is required for de novo synthesis, its levels do not drive the up-regulation in Lesch-Nyhan as significantly as the loss of feedback inhibition and substrate excess.
Dietary nucleic acids are primarily degraded and not utilized for tissue synthesis; their degradation does not drive the hepatic de novo pathway.
IMP and GMP are the end-product inhibitors of the committed step (amidotransferase). Their decreased production due to failed salvage removes the 'brake' on de novo synthesis.
The conversion of xanthine to uric acid is a downstream catabolic event and does not regulate the early de novo synthetic steps.
Hypoxanthine is a substrate for the salvage pathway, not an allosteric activator of the de novo amidotransferase enzyme.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): In addition, the lack of this salvage pathway causes increased PRPP levels and decreased IMP and GMP levels. As a result, glutamine:phosphoribosylpyrophosphate amidotransferase (the committed step in purine synthesis) has excess substrate and decreased inhibitors available.

category: Interpret Orotic aciduria in relevance to nucleotides and urea
statement: An elite researcher is studying the regulation of pyrimidine biosynthesis in human lymphocytes. They observe that as the cellular concentration of UTP increases, the rate of orotic acid production decreases significantly. This regulatory mechanism is best described as:
options: Transcriptional repression of the UMP synthase gene.
Proteolytic degradation of the CAD multifunctional polypeptide.
Allosteric inhibition of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II.
Competitive inhibition of orotate phosphoribosyltransferase.
Feed-forward activation of dihydroorotase by pyrimidine nucleotides.
correctOption: Allosteric inhibition of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II.
optionExplanations: While gene expression can be regulated, the immediate decrease in metabolite production described is characteristic of allosteric enzyme inhibition, which is the mechanism for CPS II.
Regulation is achieved through allosteric modulation of enzyme activity (reversible), not the irreversible proteolytic degradation of the enzyme complex itself.

UTP acts as an allosteric inhibitor of CPS II, the rate-limiting enzyme. By slowing down the production of carbamoyl phosphate, the entire downstream production of intermediates like orotic acid is reduced.
UTP does not competitively inhibit UMP synthase (orotate phosphoribosyltransferase); its primary regulatory site is at the start of the pathway.
Pyrimidine nucleotides like UTP act as inhibitors (feedback), not feed-forward activators of the pathway enzymes.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): The regulated step of this pathway in mammalian cells is the synthesis of carbamoyl phosphate from glutamine and CO2, catalyzed by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase (CPS) II. CPS II is inhibited by UTP...

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: An 8-month-old male infant presents with failure to thrive and recurrent infections, including persistent oral candidiasis and a history of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. Laboratory evaluation reveals a profound reduction in T cells, B cells, and natural killer (NK) cells. A deficiency in which enzyme is most consistent with this 'Severe Combined Immunodeficiency' (SCID) presentation?
options: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP)
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT)
Adenosine deaminase (ADA)
AMP deaminase
Xanthine oxidase (XO)
correctOption: Adenosine deaminase (ADA)
optionExplanations: PNP deficiency causes a less severe immunodeficiency that primarily affects T cells, rather than the total depletion of T, B, and NK cells seen in ADA-SCID.
HGPRT deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, characterized by hyperuricemia and self-mutilation, but not the severe pan-lymphocyte depletion seen in SCID.
ADA deficiency is unique among purine enzyme defects because it affects T, B, and NK cells, fitting the clinical description of SCID with multiple opportunistic infections.
AMP deaminase deficiency is typically associated with exercise-induced muscle myopathy, not immunodeficiency.
Xanthine oxidase deficiency leads to xanthinuria and low uric acid levels, but does not impair the immune system.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): In its most severe form, this autosomal recessive disorder causes a type of severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID), involving a decrease in T cells, B cells, and natural killer (NK) cells. It is estimated that in the United States, ADA deficiency accounts for approximately 14% of all cases of SCID.

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: A patient with chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is prescribed hydroxyurea to reduce their rapidly expanding white blood cell count. Which of the following best describes the specific biochemical mechanism by which this drug exerts its antineoplastic effect?
options: It prevents the amination of UTP to CTP by inhibiting CTP synthetase.
It functions as a competitive inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase.
It inhibits the conversion of IMP to GMP by blocking IMP dehydrogenase.
It acts as a suicide inhibitor that permanently binds to thymidylate synthase.
It destroys the free radical required for the catalytic activity of ribonucleotide reductase.
correctOption: It destroys the free radical required for the catalytic activity of ribonucleotide reductase.
optionExplanations: CTP synthetase is responsible for converting UTP to CTP using glutamine; it is not the target of hydroxyurea.
Methotrexate, not hydroxyurea, is the classic competitive inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase, used to deplete tetrahydrofolate pools.
Mycophenolic acid is the reversible inhibitor of IMP dehydrogenase, primarily used as an immunosuppressant, not hydroxyurea.
5-Fluorouracil (specifically its metabolite 5-FdUMP) is the suicide inhibitor that targets thymidylate synthase.
Hydroxyurea specifically targets the R2 subunit of ribonucleotide reductase, quenching a tyrosyl free radical that is essential for the initiation of the reduction mechanism.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 298 (Book Page): The drug hydroxyurea destroys the free radical required for enzymic activity of ribonucleotide reductase, and thus inhibits the generation of substrates for DNA synthesis. Hydroxyurea has been used in the treatment of cancers such as chronic myelogenous leukemia.

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
statement: For which clinical purpose is mycophenolic acid primarily utilized in modern medicine?
options: Management of hyperuricemia in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome
Prevention of bacterial cell wall synthesis
Prevention of rejection in organ transplant recipients
Treatment of acute gouty arthritis
Treatment of megaloblastic anemia
correctOption: Prevention of rejection in organ transplant recipients
optionExplanations: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is managed by reducing uric acid (e.g., allopurinol); mycophenolic acid does not address the underlying HGPRT deficiency.
Bacterial cell wall synthesis is targeted by antibiotics like penicillins, not by purine synthesis inhibitors like mycophenolic acid.

Mycophenolic acid is a potent immunosuppressant. By inhibiting IMP dehydrogenase, it selectively prevents the proliferation of T and B lymphocytes, which is crucial for preventing the immune system from attacking a transplanted organ.
Acute gout is treated with anti-inflammatory agents like colchicine or NSAIDs, not mycophenolic acid.
Megaloblastic anemia is often caused by folate or B12 deficiency; mycophenolic acid would likely worsen anemia rather than treat it by inhibiting nucleotide synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): The drug is an immunosuppressant used to prevent graft rejection.

category: Interpret the Lesh-Nhyan syndrome
coreConcept: Diagnostic Contrast: HGPRT vs PRPP Synthetase
statement: A clinician is differentiating between hyperuricemia caused by a PRPP synthetase mutation and that caused by Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Which mechanism is uniquely characteristic of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome rather than PRPP synthetase overactivity?
options: An increase in the Vmax for the synthesis of phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate.
Inability to utilize hypoxanthine or guanine for nucleotide production.
Insensitivity to the allosteric inhibition of purine nucleotides.
Presence of a decreased Km for ribose 5-phosphate.
Overproduction of uric acid leading to urolithiasis.
correctOption: Inability to utilize hypoxanthine or guanine for nucleotide production.
optionExplanations: Increased Vmax of PRPP synthetase is a feature of primary hyperuricemia due to enzyme mutation, not the salvage defect seen in Lesch-Nyhan.
Correct. Lesch-Nyhan is fundamentally a defect in the salvage pathway (HGPRT deficiency), whereas PRPP synthetase mutations involve the over-activation of the PRPP synthesis step itself.
Decreased sensitivity to allosteric inhibitors is a characteristic of mutated PRPP synthetase, whereas in Lesch-Nyhan, the inhibitors are simply not produced in sufficient quantities via salvage.
A decreased Km for ribose 5-phosphate is a specific feature of certain PRPP synthetase mutations, leading to increased PRPP production, not Lesch-Nyhan.
Both conditions result in hyperuricemia and can cause uric acid stones; this is not a distinguishing feature.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): This syndrome is a rare, X-linked, recessive disorder associated with a virtually complete deficiency of HGPRT. This deficiency results in an inability to salvage hypoxanthine or guanine.

category: Interpret the Lesh-Nhyan syndrome
statement: A 10-month-old male infant is brought to the pediatric clinic due to developmental delay and noticeable orange-colored crystals in his diapers. The mother reports that the child has recently started excessively biting his own lips and the tips of his fingers. Laboratory findings confirm hyperuricemia. Which physiological change most accurately describes the state of purine metabolism in this patient?
options: Decreased production of phosphoribosylamine.
Under-secretion of uric acid by the renal tubules.
Elevated salvage of adenine via adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT).
Accumulation of xanthine due to xanthine oxidase deficiency.
Increased degradation of purines resulting from overactive de novo synthesis.
correctOption: Increased degradation of purines resulting from overactive de novo synthesis.
optionExplanations: Phosphoribosylamine production is the committed step of de novo synthesis, which is significantly increased (not decreased) in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.
Lesch-Nyhan is a disorder of overproduction, though the kidney must handle the excess; the primary defect is not renal under-secretion (which is the more common cause of gout in adults).

While APRT is functional, the primary metabolic derangement is the loss of HGPRT and the secondary surge in de novo synthesis, not a compensatory 'elevation' of adenine salvage that would correct the syndrome.
The patient has hyperuricemia, which implies xanthine oxidase is functional. Xanthine oxidase deficiency would lead to hypouricemia.
Correct. The lack of salvage and the loss of feedback inhibition cause the de novo pathway to run unchecked, leading to massive purine production and subsequent degradation into uric acid.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): The combination of decreased purine reutilization and increased purine synthesis results in increased degradation of purines and the production of large amounts of uric acid, making Lesch-Nyhan a heritable cause of hyperuricemia.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: A 2-year-old child presents with failure to thrive and megaloblastic anemia that does not respond to vitamin B12 or folate supplementation. Urinalysis shows significant crystal-like sediment identified as orotic acid. Blood ammonia levels are within normal limits. A deficiency in which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: PRPP synthetase
Ornithine transcarbamylase
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
UMP synthase
correctOption: UMP synthase
optionExplanations: PRPP synthetase overactivity leads to gout/hyperuricemia, not orotic aciduria and megaloblastic anemia.
Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency also causes orotic aciduria (due to carbamoyl phosphate spillover), but it is critically associated with hyperammonemia, which this patient does not have.
CPS I deficiency causes hyperammonemia but results in decreased carbamoyl phosphate, which would decrease, not increase, orotic acid levels.
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase deficiency is not the standard cause of orotic aciduria; this enzyme precedes orotate formation. UMP synthase is the bifunctional enzyme downstream of orotate.

UMP synthase deficiency (hereditary orotic aciduria) prevents the conversion of orotic acid to UMP. This results in orotic aciduria and megaloblastic anemia (due to lack of pyrimidines for DNA) but has normal ammonia levels as the urea cycle is intact.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): Low activities of orotidine phosphate decarboxylase and orotate phosphoribosyltransferase [UMP synthase] result in poor growth, megaloblastic anemia, and the excretion of large amounts of orotate in the urine.

category: Differentiate between CPS I and II
coreConcept: Nitrogen Donor Specificity for CPS Isoforms
statement: A second-year medical student is studying the differences in substrate utilization between CPS I and CPS II. Which of the following compounds serves as the specific source of nitrogen for the reaction catalyzed by CPS II in pyrimidine synthesis?
options: N10-Formyltetrahydrofolate
Aspartic acid
Glycine
Free ammonium ions (NH4+)
Amide group of glutamine
correctOption: Amide group of glutamine
optionExplanations: N10-Formyltetrahydrofolate provides carbon atoms in purine synthesis; pyrimidine synthesis does not require folate derivatives at the CPS II step.
Aspartic acid provides several atoms to the pyrimidine ring later in the pathway via aspartate transcarbamoylase, but it is not the nitrogen donor for the CPS II step.
Glycine is a precursor for purine synthesis, contributing several atoms to the purine ring, but it is not involved in the CPS II reaction.
Free ammonia is the nitrogen source for CPS I in the mitochondria, which is used for the urea cycle, not pyrimidine synthesis.
CPS II specifically utilizes the gamma-amide group of glutamine as its nitrogen source to produce carbamoyl phosphate in the cytosol.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): CPS II | Source of nitrogen | γ-Amide group of glutamine

category: g Methotrexate, 5 Flurouracil and Allupurinol
statement: The synthesis of dTMP from dUMP is a critical step in providing precursors for DNA replication. Which enzyme in this cycle is responsible for restoring the coenzyme pool by reducing dihydrofolate, and is the target of methotrexate?
options: UMP synthase
Dihydrofolate reductase
Xanthine oxidase
Thymidylate synthase
Ribonucleotide reductase
correctOption: Dihydrofolate reductase
optionExplanations: UMP synthase is a bifunctional enzyme in the de novo pyrimidine pathway; its deficiency causes orotic aciduria.
Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) reduces DHF (produced by the thymidylate synthase reaction) back to THF, which is essential for continued dTMP and purine synthesis. It is inhibited by methotrexate.
Xanthine oxidase is involved in purine degradation and is the target of allopurinol.
Thymidylate synthase catalyzes the conversion of dUMP to dTMP and oxidizes THF to DHF; it is the target of 5-FU, not methotrexate.
Ribonucleotide reductase reduces ribonucleoside diphosphates to deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates; it is inhibited by hydroxyurea or dATP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 304 (Book Page): [DHF can be reduced to THF by dihydrofolate reductase (see Figure 28.3, Page 366 (Book Page)), an enzyme that is inhibited by drugs such as methotrexate.]

category: Interpret the role of synthetic analogues of nucleotides in medicine based on sign/symptoms and data e
statement: In the management of chronic gout, allopurinol is used to lower serum uric acid. What is the metabolic fate of allopurinol that leads to the inhibition of its target enzyme?
options: It is deaminated to alloxanthine, which prevents the reabsorption of urate in the kidney
It is conjugated with glycine to form a more soluble excretory product
It is phosphorylated to allopurinol ribotide, which inhibits PRPP synthetase
It is converted to oxypurinol, which acts as an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase
It is oxidized to uric acid analogs that lack the ability to form crystals
correctOption: It is converted to oxypurinol, which acts as an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase
optionExplanations: Oxypurinol inhibits production, not renal reabsorption; drugs that affect renal handling are called uricosurics (e.g., probenecid).
Allopurinol is not primarily metabolized via glycine conjugation for its therapeutic effect.
While allopurinol can be converted to a ribotide, its primary therapeutic action is through oxypurinol inhibiting xanthine oxidase, not PRPP synthetase.
Allopurinol is a hypoxanthine analog; xanthine oxidase converts it to oxypurinol (alloxanthine), which then binds tightly to the enzyme, inhibiting the production of uric acid.
The goal is to stop the production of uric acid, not to produce a different 'analog' of uric acid for excretion via the same pathway of oxidation by XO and crystal formation elsewhere.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): Allopurinol is converted in the body to oxypurinol, which inhibits xanthine oxidase (XO), resulting in an accumulation of hypoxanthine and xanthine.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: A 3-year-old child presents with a history of recurrent fungal and viral infections and developmental delay. Immunological profiling reveals a significant depletion of T-cells, but B-cell and natural killer (NK) cell counts are within normal limits. Tests for Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) are normal. A deficiency in which of the following enzymes most likely explains this specific presentation?
options: Xanthine oxidase
Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT)
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP)
Adenylate kinase
AMP deaminase
correctOption: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP)
optionExplanations: Xanthine oxidase deficiency leads to xanthinuria (low uric acid, high xanthine/hypoxanthine) and possible stones, but it is not a cause of SCID or T-cell depletion.
HGPRT deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, characterized by hyperuricemia and self-mutilation, but not the specific T-cell immunodeficiency described.
PNP deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder that specifically leads to T-cell dysfunction, unlike ADA deficiency which affects T, B, and NK cells.
Adenylate kinase maintains the balance between AMP, ADP, and ATP in tissues like muscle; its deficiency does not cause this specific immunological phenotype.
AMP deaminase deficiency is typically associated with exercise-induced muscle myopathy and fatigue, not recurrent infections or T-cell depletion.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) deficiency results in a less severe immunodeficiency involving T-cells primarily.

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
coreConcept: Allopurinol and De Novo Pathway Regulation
statement: Allopurinol is a structural analog of hypoxanthine that effectively treats gout by inhibiting xanthine oxidase. A secondary benefit of allopurinol in patients with normal HGPRT levels is the reduction of de novo purine synthesis. What is the mechanism for this secondary effect?
options: Salvage of accumulated hypoxanthine, which consumes PRPP and produces inhibitory nucleotides
Allopurinol acts as a competitive activator of ribonucleotide reductase
Direct inhibition of CPS II by allopurinol
Degradation of PRPP by oxypurinol
Conversion of allopurinol to UMP, which inhibits OMP decarboxylase
correctOption: Salvage of accumulated hypoxanthine, which consumes PRPP and produces inhibitory nucleotides
optionExplanations: When xanthine oxidase is inhibited, hypoxanthine accumulates and is salvaged by HGPRT. This salvage process consumes PRPP (the activator of the de novo pathway) and produces IMP/GMP (the inhibitors of the de novo pathway), effectively shutting down new purine production.

Allopurinol (or its metabolites) does not activate ribonucleotide reductase; in fact, its metabolites like dATP (if ADA were deficient) would inhibit it, but that is not the mechanism for reducing purine synthesis in gout.
CPS II is the regulator for pyrimidines, not purines; allopurinol does not inhibit it.
Oxypurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase; it does not directly degrade PRPP.
Allopurinol is a purine analog, not a pyrimidine analog; it is not converted to UMP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): In patients with normal levels of HGPRT, the hypoxanthine can be salvaged, thus reducing the levels of PRPP and, therefore, de novo purine synthesis.

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
coreConcept: Cell Cycle Regulation of Nucleotide Metabolism
statement: During which phase of the eukaryotic cell cycle is the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase primarily active to provide the necessary substrates for DNA replication?
options: S-phase
M-phase
G1 phase
G2 phase
G0 phase
correctOption: S-phase
optionExplanations: The S-phase (Synthesis phase) is when the genome is replicated; ribonucleotide reductase activity is maximal during this time to provide dNTPs.
M-phase (Mitosis) involves the segregation of chromosomes rather than the synthesis of new DNA, so ribonucleotide reductase is not at peak activity.
G1 is the gap phase where cells grow and prepare for DNA synthesis, but the peak activity of ribonucleotide reductase occurs when synthesis actually begins.
G2 is the phase following DNA synthesis where the cell prepares for mitosis; the requirement for new deoxyribonucleotide production has typically passed.
G0 is a quiescent phase where cells are not preparing for division, and therefore, the demand for deoxyribonucleotides is minimal.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 289 (Book Page): The nucleotides required for DNA synthesis, however, are 2'-deoxyribonucleotides, which are produced from ribonucleoside diphosphates by the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase during the S-phase of the cell cycle.

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
coreConcept: Carbon Sources in the Purine Ring
statement: A patient with a bacterial infection is treated with a sulfonamide. Which of the following best describes the metabolic consequence within the bacterial cell regarding purine ring assembly?
options: Reduced ability to incorporate the one-carbon units required for the C2 and C8 positions.
Failure to donate amino groups from glutamine to the C3 and C9 positions.
Inability to incorporate CO2 at the C6 position of the purine ring.
Blockade of the aspartate addition to the C6-carbon of the purine ring.
Inhibition of the closure of the five-membered imidazole ring.
correctOption: Reduced ability to incorporate the one-carbon units required for the C2 and C8 positions.
optionExplanations: N10-formyltetrahydrofolate is the carrier of one-carbon units. In the de novo purine pathway, these formyl groups are essential for providing the carbon atoms at positions 2 and 8 of the purine ring. Sulfa drugs decrease the availability of this coenzyme.
Glutamine provides the nitrogens at N3 and N9 via amidotransferase reactions that are independent of folic acid.
CO2 is incorporated into the C6 position by a carboxylase enzyme that does not require folate.
Aspartate provides the N1 atom (and its carbon framework is released as fumarate); it does not provide the C6 carbon, and this reaction is folate-independent.
Imidazole ring closure is a multi-step process involving ATP but does not directly depend on folate for the closure mechanism itself, although the precursors for the closure require folate.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): Two steps in the pathway require N10-formyltetrahydrofolate (see Page 259 (Book Page)).... Page 294 (Book Page): Because purine synthesis requires tetrahydrofolate as a coenzyme, the sulfa drugs slow down this pathway in bacteria.

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: A researcher is studying the molecular basis of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) caused by Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency. Which metabolic disturbance directly accounts for the developmental arrest and apoptosis of lymphocytes in these patients?
options: Inhibition of xanthine oxidase leading to hypoxanthine toxicity
Accumulation of uric acid causing DNA damage
Overactivation of thymidylate synthase causing uracil depletion
Depletion of PRPP stores for de novo synthesis
Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase by elevated dATP
correctOption: Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase by elevated dATP
optionExplanations: Xanthine oxidase inhibition (e.g., by allopurinol) is used to treat gout and does not cause the lymphocytopenia seen in SCID.
Uric acid accumulation is associated with gout, not the lymphocytic depletion seen in ADA-deficient SCID.
Thymidylate synthase is involved in dTMP synthesis; its overactivation is not a feature of ADA deficiency metabolism and does not cause SCID symptoms.
PRPP is an activated pentose used in nucleotide synthesis, but its depletion is not the primary toxic mechanism in ADA deficiency.
In ADA deficiency, adenosine and deoxyadenosine accumulate. Deoxyadenosine is phosphorylated to dATP, which allosterically inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, preventing DNA synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page) / 531: As dATP levels rise, ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited, thus preventing the production of all deoxyribose-containing nucleotides... The dATP and adenosine that accumulate in ADA deficiency lead to developmental arrest and apoptosis of lymphocytes.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
coreConcept: Regulation of Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase II (CPS II)
statement: What molecule serves as the primary allosteric inhibitor for the regulated, rate-limiting step of de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis in mammalian cells?
options: 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP)
Uridine triphosphate (UTP)
Cytidine triphosphate (CTP)
Inosine monophosphate (IMP)
Adenosine triphosphate (ATP)
correctOption: Uridine triphosphate (UTP)
optionExplanations: 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate (PRPP) is actually an allosteric activator of CPS II, not an inhibitor, providing feed-forward stimulation for pyrimidine production.
In mammalian cells, the synthesis of carbamoyl phosphate by CPS II is the regulated step; UTP, the pathway's end product, provides feedback inhibition to maintain homeostatic control.
While CTP is a regulator in prokaryotic cells (inhibiting aspartate transcarbamoylase), in mammalian cells, UTP is the primary inhibitor of the regulated step (CPS II).
Inosine monophosphate (IMP) is the 'parent' purine nucleotide and is involved in the feedback regulation of the purine pathway, not the pyrimidine pathway.
ATP acts as an activator of the activity sites of ribonucleotide reductase, but it is not the primary feedback inhibitor for the rate-limiting step of pyrimidine synthesis (CPS II).
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): CPS II is inhibited by UTP (the end product of this pathway, which can be converted into the other pyrimidine nucleotides), and is activated by PRPP.

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
statement: Why are T and B lymphocytes more sensitive to mycophenolic acid than other cell types in the human body?
options: They lack the enzymes for de novo purine synthesis.
They cannot salvage adenine via APRT.
They are particularly dependent on the de novo pathway for guanine nucleotides.
They overexpress IMP dehydrogenase, causing rapid drug accumulation.
They lack mitochondria, which are required to metabolize the drug.
correctOption: They are particularly dependent on the de novo pathway for guanine nucleotides.
optionExplanations: Lymphocytes do possess the de novo pathway; their sensitivity arises from their heavy reliance on it during proliferation.
While lymphocytes use APRT for adenine salvage, mycophenolic acid targets the guanine (GMP) branch of the pathway, which is distinct from adenine (AMP) synthesis.

Rapidly proliferating T and B cells have a high demand for guanine nucleotides for DNA synthesis and are uniquely dependent on the de novo pathway (via IMP dehydrogenase) rather than salvage to meet this demand.
The drug inhibits the enzyme; it is not that overexpression causes sensitivity, but that the high metabolic requirement for the enzyme's product (GMP) makes the cells vulnerable.
The presence or absence of mitochondria does not determine the sensitivity to mycophenolic acid's inhibition of cytosolic purine synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): The drug [mycophenolic acid] deprives rapidly proliferating T and B cells of key components of nucleic acids.

category: Discuss the regulation of purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis and degradation
statement: PRPP synthetase is a critical enzyme that produces the activated pentose for nucleotide synthesis. Which of the following represents its physiological activator and inhibitor?
options: Activated by Inorganic phosphate; Inhibited by purine nucleotides.
Activated by Glutamine; Inhibited by AMP.
Activated by Ribose 5-phosphate; Inhibited by Inorganic phosphate.
Activated by ATP; Inhibited by dATP.
Activated by UTP; Inhibited by PRPP.
correctOption: Activated by Inorganic phosphate; Inhibited by purine nucleotides.
optionExplanations: PRPP synthetase is uniquely activated by inorganic phosphate and feedback-inhibited by the end-products of the pathway, the purine ribonucleotides.
Glutamine is a substrate for later steps in the pathway but does not activate PRPP synthetase.
Ribose 5-phosphate is a substrate for the enzyme, while inorganic phosphate is an activator, not an inhibitor.
This describes the regulation of the activity site of ribonucleotide reductase, not PRPP synthetase.
This is incorrect; UTP inhibits CPS II, and PRPP is the product of PRPP synthetase, not an inhibitor.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): [This X-linked enzyme is activated by inorganic phosphate and inhibited by purine nucleotides (end-product inhibition).]

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
coreConcept: Renal handling of urate in acidosis
statement: Secondary hyperuricemia can occur in patients with lactic acidosis. What is the physiological basis for the increased serum uric acid levels in these individuals?
options: Acidosis causes the chemical precipitation of urate in the blood
Lactate acts as an allosteric activator of PRPP synthetase
Lactate competes with urate for the same renal transport mechanism
Lactate is a direct precursor for the synthesis of the purine ring
Lactic acid increases the rate of cell turnover in the bone marrow
correctOption: Lactate competes with urate for the same renal transport mechanism
optionExplanations: Acidosis can decrease the solubility of uric acid in urine, potentially leading to stones, but the increase in *serum* levels is due to excretory competition.
Lactate does not activate PRPP synthetase; PRPP synthetase is regulated by inorganic phosphate and purine nucleotides.
Uric acid excretion occurs in the kidneys; in conditions with high lactic acid, lactate competes with uric acid for secretion into the renal tubules, leading to urate retention.
The precursors of the purine ring are glycine, glutamine, aspartate, CO2, and folate derivatives; lactate is not a structural contributor to the purine ring.
High cell turnover increases purine degradation, but this is associated with myeloproliferative disorders, not specifically lactic acidosis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 299 (Book Page): Underexcretion can be primary... or secondary to known disease processes that affect how the kidney handles urate, for example lactic acidosis (lactate and urate compete for the same renal transporter).

category: Interpret the role of synthetic analogues of nucleotides in medicine based on sign/symptoms and data e
statement: A 28-year-old female receiving high-dose methotrexate for osteosarcoma develops severe oral mucositis, a maculopapular rash, and a significant drop in her white blood cell count. These symptoms are primarily due to the drug's toxic effect on rapidly dividing cells. Which metabolic consequence of methotrexate therapy is responsible for this clinical presentation?
options: Accumulation of orotic acid in the intestinal mucosa
Direct covalent inhibition of thymidylate synthase
Selective depletion of guanosine monophosphate in T cells
Inhibition of the CPS II enzyme in the cytosol
Depletion of tetrahydrofolate levels required for nucleotide synthesis
correctOption: Depletion of tetrahydrofolate levels required for nucleotide synthesis
optionExplanations: Orotic acid accumulation is characteristic of UMP synthase deficiency (orotic aciduria), not methotrexate use.
5-fluorouracil, not methotrexate, is a direct covalent (suicide) inhibitor of thymidylate synthase.
Selective GMP depletion in lymphocytes is the mechanism of mycophenolic acid, not methotrexate.
CPS II is inhibited by UTP; methotrexate targets dihydrofolate reductase, not the pyrimidine committed step.

Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, preventing the regeneration of THF. This starves the cell of 1-carbon units needed for both purine synthesis and dTMP synthesis, halting DNA replication in dividing tissues like GI mucosa and skin.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page): These drugs limit the amount of tetrahydrofolate available for use in purine synthesis and, thus, slow down DNA replication in mammalian cells. These compounds are... toxic to all dividing cells... adverse effects, including anemia, scaly skin, GI tract disturbance.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: In the management of certain malignancies, 5-fluorouracil is utilized to arrest cell proliferation. What is the specific mechanism by which this drug inhibits the synthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides required for DNA replication?
options: Covalent binding to thymidylate synthase as a suicide inhibitor
Destruction of the free radical on ribonucleotide reductase
Inhibition of IMP dehydrogenase to deplete guanine supplies
Competitive inhibition of orotate phosphoribosyltransferase
Reversible inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase
correctOption: Covalent binding to thymidylate synthase as a suicide inhibitor
optionExplanations: Correct. 5-FU is converted to 5-FdUMP, which acts as a suicide inhibitor of thymidylate synthase, preventing the conversion of dUMP to dTMP and thus stalling DNA synthesis.
Incorrect. Hydroxyurea is the agent that destroys the free radical on the R2 subunit of ribonucleotide reductase.
Incorrect. IMP dehydrogenase is a purine synthesis enzyme and is the target of mycophenolic acid, not 5-fluorouracil.
Incorrect. While 5-FU is a pyrimidine analog, its primary therapeutic target is thymidylate synthase, not the early stage orotate phosphoribosyltransferase enzyme.
Incorrect. Methotrexate is the drug that inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. 5-FU targets the methylation step directly.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 296 (Book Page): 5-Fluorouracil is metabolically converted to 5-FdUMP, which becomes permanently bound to the inactivated thymidylate synthase; for this reason, the drug is called a “suicide” inhibitor.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of purines (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: In the degradation of purine nucleotides, which enzyme is responsible for the oxidation of both hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to the final excretory product, uric acid?
options: Guanase
Adenosine deaminase
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase
Xanthine oxidase
5'-Nucleotidases
correctOption: Xanthine oxidase
optionExplanations: Guanase is responsible for the deamination of guanine to form xanthine, providing a second entry point into the final stages of the degradation pathway.
Adenosine deaminase converts adenosine to inosine by removing an amino group, but it does not catalyze the final oxidative steps to uric acid.
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) cleaves the glycosidic bond of inosine and guanosine to release the free bases hypoxanthine and guanine.
Xanthine oxidase is the key oxidative enzyme that converts hypoxanthine to xanthine and then xanthine to uric acid; it is the pharmacological target for allopurinol.
5'-Nucleotidases are responsible for the hydrolysis of the phosphate group from nucleotides like IMP, AMP, and GMP to produce their respective nucleosides.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 299 (Book Page): [5] Hypoxanthine is oxidized by xanthine oxidase to xanthine, which is further oxidized by xanthine oxidase to uric acid, the final product of human purine degradation.

category: Interpret the role of synthetic analogues of nucleotides in medicine based on sign/symptoms and data e
statement: In the management of colorectal cancer, 5-fluorouracil is utilized. Which metabolic transformation is required for this drug to exert its 'suicide' inhibition on thymidylate synthase?
options: Reduction to 5-fluorodihydrofolate
Conversion to 5-fluorocytidine triphosphate (FCTP)
Conversion to 5-fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate (5-FdUMP)
Phosphorylation to 5-fluorouridine monophosphate (FUMP)
Oxidation to 5-fluorourate by xanthine oxidase
correctOption: Conversion to 5-fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate (5-FdUMP)
optionExplanations: 5-FU is a pyrimidine analog, not a folate analog, so it is not reduced to a dihydrofolate form.
5-FU targets DNA synthesis via dTMP inhibition; FCTP would involve RNA pathways and is not the primary 'suicide' mechanism for thymidylate synthase.
5-FU must be converted to the deoxyribonucleotide form (5-FdUMP) to mimic dUMP and permanently bind the active site of thymidylate synthase.
FUMP may be formed, but the specific suicide inhibitor for thymidylate synthase is the deoxy form, 5-FdUMP.
Xanthine oxidase handles purines; 5-FU is a pyrimidine and is not oxidized to 'fluorourate' as a primary mechanism.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 304 (Book Page): 5-Fluorouracil is metabolically converted to 5-FdUMP, which becomes permanently bound to the inactivated thymidylate synthase; for this reason, the drug is called a “suicide” inhibitor.

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
statement: A single polypeptide chain in mammalian cells, known as CAD, contains the catalytic domains for the first three enzymes of de novo pyrimidine synthesis. Which enzymic activity is included in this multifunctional protein?
options: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase
Thymidylate synthase
Orotidylate decarboxylase
Aspartate transcarbamoylase
correctOption: Aspartate transcarbamoylase
optionExplanations: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is the fourth enzyme in the pathway and is uniquely located in the inner mitochondrial membrane; it is not part of the cytosolic CAD complex.
Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase is a domain of the bifunctional enzyme UMP synthase, which catalyzes the conversion of orotate to OMP, later in the pathway.
Thymidylate synthase is a separate enzyme responsible for converting dUMP to dTMP using a folate-dependent mechanism; it is not part of any multifunctional complex in this pathway.
Orotidylate decarboxylase is the second domain of the UMP synthase complex; it converts OMP to UMP and is not part of the CAD complex.
CAD is a tri-functional protein in mammals that includes Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II, Aspartate transcarbamoylase, and Dihydroorotase domains.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page): [Note: The first three enzymic activities in this pathway (CPS II, aspartate transcarbamoylase, and dihydroorotase) are actually three different catalytic domains of a single polypeptide chain known as CAD...]

category: Discuss the synthesis and degradation of pyrimidine (De-Novo and salvage pathway)
coreConcept: Role of dUTPase in DNA Integrity
statement: Which enzyme plays a critical role in preventing the erroneous incorporation of uracil into DNA by maintaining low cellular levels of dUTP?
options: Orotidylate decarboxylase
UMP kinase
CTP synthetase
Ribonucleotide reductase
dUTPase
correctOption: dUTPase
optionExplanations: Orotidylate decarboxylase is involved in the de novo synthesis of UMP from OMP; it has no role in handling deoxy-triphosphates.
UMP kinase phosphorylates UMP to UDP but does not protect DNA from uracil incorporation.
CTP synthetase converts UTP to CTP using glutamine; it is involved in producing cytosine nucleotides for RNA synthesis.
Ribonucleotide reductase produces dUDP from UDP, but it is the subsequent action of dUTPase that prevents the dUTP produced from entering DNA.
dUTPase (UTP diphosphatase) hydrolyzes dUTP to dUMP. This serves two purposes: it provides the substrate for dTMP synthesis and keeps dUTP levels low so DNA polymerase does not use it.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 303 (Book Page): dUDP is phosphorylated to dUTP, which is rapidly hydrolyzed to dUMP by UTP diphosphatase (dUTPase). dUTPase, then, plays an important role in reducing availability of dUTP as a substrate for DNA synthesis, thus preventing erroneous incorporation of uracil into DNA.

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: An 8-month-old male infant presents with recurrent pneumonia, persistent oral thrush, and severe lymphopenia. Genetic testing confirms a deficiency in adenosine deaminase (ADA). In the context of nucleotide metabolism, which of the following best explains the failure of his lymphocytes to proliferate?
options: Increased IMP levels cause feedback inhibition of the R1 subunit.
Accumulated dATP allosterically inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, preventing DNA precursor synthesis.
Accumulated adenosine competitively inhibits the binding of ADP to the R2 subunit of RNR.
High levels of dATP destroy the free radical required for RNR activity.
A lack of ATP prevents the activation of the RNR specificity sites.
correctOption: Accumulated dATP allosterically inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, preventing DNA precursor synthesis.
optionExplanations: IMP is a purine monophosphate and does not directly regulate ribonucleotide reductase; RNR regulation is mediated by nucleoside triphosphates (ATP/dNTPs).

In ADA deficiency, dATP accumulates to toxic levels. dATP binds to the 'activity sites' of ribonucleotide reductase, essentially locking the enzyme in an inactive state and halting the production of all dNTPs needed for DNA replication.
Adenosine itself is not a competitive inhibitor for the RNR catalytic site; it must be converted to dATP to exert its regulatory effect on RNR.
Destroying the free radical is the mechanism of the drug hydroxyurea, not dATP. dATP inhibits RNR through allosteric conformational changes.
While ATP is an activator, ADA deficiency causes a pathologic excess of dATP (an inhibitor) which overrides normal ATP activation, leading to cellular toxicity.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): As dATP levels rise, ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited, thus preventing the production of all deoxyribose-containing nucleotides... Consequently, cells cannot make DNA and divide.

category: Interpret the role of PABA analogs and mycophenolic acid in purine biosynthesis
coreConcept: Lymphocyte Dependence on De Novo Synthesis
statement: In a patient receiving mycophenolic acid therapy, why is the effect on T and B cells more profound than on other cell types like hepatocytes?
options: Hepatocytes lack the enzyme IMP dehydrogenase.
The salvage pathway for guanine is absent in hepatocytes.
Mycophenolic acid is selectively transported only into lymphoid tissues.
Lymphocytes are uniquely dependent on de novo purine synthesis for proliferation.
Hepatocytes have a much higher concentration of PRPP to overcome inhibition.
correctOption: Lymphocytes are uniquely dependent on de novo purine synthesis for proliferation.
optionExplanations: Hepatocytes possess IMP dehydrogenase as they are the primary site of de novo purine synthesis.
Hepatocytes have robust salvage pathways; it is the lymphocyte's specific reliance on the de novo route during proliferation that creates this sensitivity.
Mycophenolic acid distributes systemically, but its metabolic impact is felt most where the targeted pathway is most critical.

While most cells can use both salvage and de novo pathways, T and B lymphocytes are particularly dependent on de novo synthesis for their expansion during an immune response, making them highly susceptible to IMP dehydrogenase inhibition.
While PRPP levels affect the rate of synthesis, they do not bypass the block at the IMP dehydrogenase step.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page): The drug deprives rapidly proliferating T and B cells of key components of nucleic acids. [Note: Lymphocytes rely on de novo synthesis].

category: Outline the sequence of reactions that converts IMP to AMP and GMP and to their corresponding triphosphates
statement: A comparison of the pathways branching from Inosine Monophosphate (IMP) reveals distinct intermediate molecules. Which intermediate is unique to the branch leading to Guanosine Monophosphate (GMP)?
options: 5-Phosphoribosylamine
Hypoxanthine
Xanthosine monophosphate (XMP)
Adenylosuccinate
Orotidine 5'-monophosphate
correctOption: Xanthosine monophosphate (XMP)
optionExplanations: 5-Phosphoribosylamine is the first intermediate of the de novo purine synthesis pathway, occurring long before the formation of IMP.
Hypoxanthine is the nitrogenous base of IMP itself; it is the starting point of these two branches, not a unique intermediate of one branch.
Xanthosine monophosphate (XMP) is formed from IMP by the enzyme IMP dehydrogenase; it is then aminated to form GMP.
Adenylosuccinate is the unique intermediate in the conversion of IMP to Adenosine Monophosphate (AMP), not GMP.
Orotidine 5'-monophosphate (OMP) is an intermediate in pyrimidine synthesis, not purine synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 295 (Book Page) / 531: [Figure 22.8 illustrates the intermediate conversion of IMP to Xanthosine monophosphate via IMP dehydrogenase.]

category: g Methotrexate, 5 Flurouracil and Allupurinol
statement: A gout patient with normal HGPRT activity is treated with allopurinol. Beyond inhibiting uric acid production, how does this therapy additionally reduce the rate of 'de novo' purine synthesis in this specific patient?
options: Increased hypoxanthine salvage consumes PRPP and produces IMP/GMP which inhibit the committed step.
Oxypurinol prevents the uptake of glutamine into the liver, starving the purine pathway.
Allopurinol directly inhibits the amidotransferase enzyme through allosteric binding.
The accumulation of xanthine causes a competitive inhibition of PRPP synthetase.
The drug increases the renal clearance of PRPP, making it unavailable for synthesis.
correctOption: Increased hypoxanthine salvage consumes PRPP and produces IMP/GMP which inhibit the committed step.
optionExplanations: By inhibiting xanthine oxidase, hypoxanthine levels rise. If HGPRT is active, this hypoxanthine is salvaged to IMP. This process consumes PRPP (the activator) and increases IMP/GMP (the inhibitors of the committed step).
Oxypurinol targets xanthine oxidase; it does not interfere with the transport or availability of glutamine.
Allopurinol does not directly bind to glutamine:PRPP amidotransferase; its effect on the de novo pathway is indirect through salvage products.
Xanthine accumulation does not inhibit PRPP synthetase; PRPP synthetase is inhibited by purine nucleotides (end-product inhibition).
PRPP is an intracellular 'activated pentose' and is not cleared by the kidneys in a manner that regulates nucleotide synthesis; its concentration is regulated by PRPP synthetase and consumption.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 301 (Book Page): In patients with normal levels of HGPRT, the hypoxanthine can be salvaged, thus reducing the levels of PRPP and, therefore, de novo purine synthesis.

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: Ribonucleotide reductase activity is highly regulated in coordination with the cell cycle. During which specific phase is this enzyme most active to ensure an adequate supply of deoxyribonucleotides?
options: M-phase
G0 phase
G1 phase
G2 phase
S-phase
correctOption: S-phase
optionExplanations: The M-phase involves mitosis and cytokinesis. DNA has already been replicated by this stage, so the biosynthetic role of ribonucleotide reductase is significantly reduced compared to the S-phase.
G0 is a quiescent phase where the cell is not preparing for division, and thus the demand for deoxyribonucleotides and the activity of ribonucleotide reductase are minimal.
During G1, the cell prepares for DNA synthesis, but the actual peak activity of ribonucleotide reductase occurs when DNA replication is actively taking place.
G2 follows the S-phase and involves preparation for mitosis; while some dNTPs may be needed for repair, the primary biosynthetic surge of RNR occurs in the S-phase.
Correct. The S-phase (synthesis phase) is when DNA replication occurs, necessitating a large and balanced pool of dNTPs provided by ribonucleotide reductase.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 297 (Book Page): The nucleotides required for DNA synthesis, however, are 2'-deoxyribonucleotides, which are produced from ribonucleoside diphosphates by the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase during the S-phase of the cell cycle.

category: Discuss the role of Ribonucleotide reductase in Nucleotide metabolism (hydroxyurea)
statement: Ribonucleotide reductase is characterized by its ability to act on several different substrates to maintain balanced dNTP pools. According to its enzymatic classification and biochemical role, which of the following molecules serves as a valid substrate for this enzyme?
options: dTMP
UMP
dADP
CDP
ATP
correctOption: CDP
optionExplanations: dTMP is a deoxyribonucleoside monophosphate and is a product of the thymidylate synthase reaction, not a substrate for RNR.
UMP is a ribonucleoside monophosphate; RNR specifically requires nucleoside diphosphates (NDPs).
dADP is a product of the enzyme (after ADP is reduced), not a substrate for the reduction of ribose to deoxyribose.
CDP is one of the four specific ribonucleoside diphosphate substrates (ADP, GDP, CDP, UDP) that RNR reduces to their corresponding deoxy forms.
ATP acts as an allosteric activator at the activity site of RNR, but the substrate for reduction is the diphosphate form, ADP.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 297 (Book Page): Ribonucleotide reductase (ribonucleoside diphosphate reductase)... is specific for the reduction of purine nucleoside diphosphates (ADP and GDP), and pyrimidine nucleoside diphosphates, cytidine diphosphate (CDP) and uridine diphosphate (UDP) to their deoxy-forms.

category: Interpret the role of synthetic analogues of nucleotides in medicine based on sign/symptoms and data e
statement: Which enzyme is the primary pharmacological target of the structural folic acid analog methotrexate?
options: Xanthine oxidase
Thymidylate synthase
IMP dehydrogenase
Ribonucleotide reductase
Dihydrofolate reductase
correctOption: Dihydrofolate reductase
optionExplanations: Xanthine oxidase is the target of allopurinol and febuxostat, used in the treatment of gout to reduce uric acid production.
Thymidylate synthase is the target of 5-fluorouracil (via 5-FdUMP), which acts as a suicide inhibitor to block dTMP production.
IMP dehydrogenase is inhibited by mycophenolic acid, an immunosuppressant used to prevent graft rejection by depriving T and B cells of nucleotides.
Ribonucleotide reductase is the target of hydroxyurea, not methotrexate; it is responsible for converting ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides.
Methotrexate is a structural analog of folic acid that competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, thereby preventing the regeneration of tetrahydrofolate needed for purine and dTMP synthesis.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 294 (Book Page): Methotrexate and related compounds inhibit the reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, catalyzed by dihydrofolate reductase (see Page 366 (Book Page)).

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: A 10-month-old infant is diagnosed with an autosomal recessive form of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) due to adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency. Which metabolic alteration is directly responsible for the developmental arrest and apoptosis of lymphocytes in this patient?
options: Competitive inhibition of thymidylate synthase by adenosine
Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase by elevated dATP levels
Accumulation of xanthine and hypoxanthine in the mitochondrial matrix
Depletion of PRPP stores due to overactive purine salvage
Hyperuricemia resulting in intracellular monosodium urate crystallization
correctOption: Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase by elevated dATP levels
optionExplanations: Thymidylate synthase is inhibited by 5-fluorouracil; adenosine does not compete for its active site in the context of ADA deficiency.

In ADA deficiency, adenosine/deoxyadenosine accumulate and are phosphorylated to dATP. High dATP allosterically inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, preventing the synthesis of other dNDPs required for DNA replication.
Xanthine and hypoxanthine are soluble intermediates that accumulate in xanthine oxidase deficiency, not the primary toxic agents in SCID.
PRPP levels are actually low in conditions like Lesch-Nyhan syndrome salvage failure, but ADA deficiency is characterized by dATP-mediated inhibition of de novo pathways.
While ADA is in the purine pathway, the primary lymphoid toxicity is not due to uric acid crystals but due to nucleotide imbalance.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 293 (Book Page): As dATP levels rise, ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited, thus preventing the production of all deoxyribose-containing nucleotides (see Page 289 (Book Page)). Consequently, cells cannot make DNA and divide.

category: Interpret Orotic aciduria in relevance to nucleotides and urea
coreConcept: Differential Diagnosis of Orotic Aciduria with Hyperammonemia
statement: A neonate presents with irritability, vomiting, and stupor. Laboratory findings show extremely high blood ammonia levels and a marked increase in urinary orotic acid. The plasma citrulline level is notably low. These findings most strongly suggest a deficiency in which enzyme?
options: UMP synthase
PRPP synthetase
Argininosuccinate synthetase
Ornithine transcarbamylase
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
correctOption: Ornithine transcarbamylase
optionExplanations: UMP synthase deficiency (Hereditary Orotic Aciduria) presents with orotic aciduria but normal ammonia levels.
PRPP synthetase overactivity can lead to gout (hyperuricemia) but does not cause hyperammonemia or primary orotic aciduria.
Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency causes hyperammonemia and high citrulline, not the specific low-citrulline/high-orotate profile of OTC deficiency.
OTC deficiency leads to hyperammonemia and high orotic acid because the accumulated carbamoyl phosphate enters the pyrimidine pathway. Low citrulline confirms a block before its synthesis.
CPS I deficiency would cause hyperammonemia, but orotic acid levels would be low because carbamoyl phosphate cannot be produced.
citation: In book "Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry", Page 302 (Book Page): Defects in ornithine transcarbamylase of the urea cycle promote pyrimidine synthesis due to increased availability of carbamoyl phosphate.

category: Gout, SCID/ADA on basis of sign symptoms and data
statement: A 2-year-old boy presents with cognitive deficits, spasticity, and a history of orange-colored 'sand' in his diapers. Physical examination reveals several areas of tissue loss on his lower lip and fingertips where he has been compulsively biting himself. Which biochemical finding is expected in this patient?
options: Decreased levels of phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP)
Increased levels of adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT)
Elevated uric acid due to decreased hypoxanthine salvage
Megaloblastic anemia responsive to uridine administration
Accumulation of xanthine due to xanthine oxidase deficiency
correctOption: Elevated uric acid due to decreased hypoxanthine salvage
optionExplanations: PRPP levels are actually increased in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome because it is not being consumed by the HGPRT salvage reaction.
APRT handles adenine salvage; Lesch-Nyhan specifically involves HGPRT, which handles hypoxanthine and guanine.
